# crates/mcp/, engine/src/mcp/, app-server mcp_server, tui mcp: 11 verified defects from R22 (baseline bc58781ba)

## How to read this document (terms used below)

- **R<number>** — review unit, one area of the codebase; this document is about R22.
- **L<number>** — one of twelve review lenses (themes) applied to every unit; the table below names each lens.
- **P0 / P1 / P2** — priority rank: P0 highest, P2 lowest. It orders the work, not the severity of a finding.
- **Stage D** — the verification step: every cited line was opened at the baseline, the reachability was traced, and severity was re-scored. **Stage E** — the drafting step that produced this report.
- **Baseline `bc58781ba`** — the exact commit every quote refers to; re-check before acting if `main` has moved.
- **Confirmed** — a verifier opened the cited line, traced a reachable path and kept the finding; rejected and uncertain findings are not here.
- **Public** — this issue contains only findings cleared for a public report; security-class findings are handled through a separate private channel.
- **needs-test** — the written proof is static; a focused test named in the finding would settle the remaining question. No test was run in this audit.
- **Cell** — one audit cell: a review unit crossed with one lens; finding IDs keep the cell number, so a gap in numbering means a candidate was rejected, marked duplicate or routed to the private index.
- **NOT READ** — a scope marker in a cell: that region was not opened, so no claim is made about it.
- **not-applicable / sampled-rescan-passed** — negative-check outcomes: the lens did not apply to that cell, or a sampled rescan found no new signal.
- **Refs #N / UPSTREAM REFS** — existing tracked issues related to the theme or to the exact code site; they are cross-links, never a claim to close or fix those issues. A 500-issue open/closed sweep found no exact duplicate of these findings at the same file and line.
- **CALL PATH, TRIGGER, MECHANISM, IMPACT, EVIDENCE, FIX, REGRESSION CHECK** — copied verbatim from the verified finding file. CALL PATH = how a user reaches the code; TRIGGER = the condition that fires it; MECHANISM = what the code actually does; IMPACT = what the user sees; EVIDENCE = the supporting lines; FIX = recommended change; REGRESSION CHECK = the test that should be added.

Unit R22 (P2 — highest priority is P0, then P1, then P2), MCP restored by the owner; all twelve themes applied. Confirmed unique findings: **11** — **11 public** in this draft and **0** withheld as private-advisory or held. Finding IDs keep their original cell numbers; a gap means the candidate was rejected, marked duplicate or routed to the private index.

No finding in this unit is withheld as a private security advisory or held item.


## Coverage

- Unit R22 at baseline `bc58781ba`. The full analysis, verbatim quotes and verification notes are in the following comments.
- 11 confirmed public findings. No test, build or product run happened in this audit.

## Findings (condensed)

The verbatim quote, full mechanism, evidence, verifier note and regression check for each finding are in the following comment(s).

### R22-L3-01 — sanitize name empty accepted as runtime server name

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/engine/src/tools/runtime_mcp.rs:318`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** A model or user calls start_mcp_server with a valid server command/URL and a name whose characters are all non-ASCII-alphanumeric and not '-' (for example name="_", name="...", or a fully non-Latin name such as "服务"); sanitize_name maps every character to '-' and trim_matches('-') yields the empty string. The same result is reachable with no custom name when the inferred name is empty (e.g.

**Mechanism:** `server_name` is built at runtime_mcp.rs:318-321 as `custom_name.map(sanitize_name).unwrap_or(parsed.name).replace('_', "-")`. `sanitize_name` (188-199) keeps only `is_ascii_alphanumeric()` or '-', maps everything else to '-', then `trim_matches('-')`, so an all-non-ASCII-alphanumeric input returns "" — the existing test `sanitize_name_empty_input` (796-797) asserts this is possible.

**Impact:** A connected MCP server and its tools are registered under an empty-name key. The user-facing `/mcp` name parser rejects empty/whitespace names (crates/tui/src/commands/groups/utility/mcp.rs:148-152, `parse_name`), and `mcp_name_is_command_safe("")` is false (mcp.rs:7561-7566), so the operator cannot revoke, disable, or reference the server by name through the normal command surface.

**Fix:** After computing `server_name` at runtime_mcp.rs:318-321, reject an empty result before calling `pool.add_runtime_server_config`, e.g. `anyhow::ensure!(!server_name.is_empty(), "MCP server name must contain at least one ASCII alphanumeric or '-' character")` surfaced as `ToolError::invalid_input`; alternatively make `add_dynamic_server_config` (mcp.rs:7281) validate the name with `mcp_name_is_command_safe` so every dynamic-registration caller is covered.

### R22-L4-01 — swallow source error empty default

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/engine/src/mcp/external_import.rs:124-127`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** `~/.claude.json`, `.mcp.json`, or a marketplace path exists and is passed to discovery, but the file is malformed JSON / oversized / unreadable, or one entry is unsupported. `checked_source` returns `Err(...)` or `(candidates, problems)`; both the error and the content-free problem list are dropped before the caller sees anything.

**Mechanism:** `checked_source` (lines 137-153) is deliberately fallible: it returns `anyhow::Result<(Vec<ImportCandidate>, Vec<String>)>` and documents that a file-level failure is an `Err` while per-entry validation problems are reported in a second, content-free list so one bad entry cannot hide valid siblings. `discover_from_json_file` throws both away — `.map(|(candidates, _)| candidates)` drops the problem list and `.unwrap_or_default()` converts the `Err` into an empty vector.

**Impact:** A user asking to import MCP servers from Claude Code / a project `.mcp.json` / a marketplace sees an empty (or partial) candidate list with no indication that a source failed. Because the return type is `Vec<ImportCandidate>` and no `tracing` call exists anywhere in this file, the failure leaves no durable trace; support cannot distinguish "no servers to import" from "the source file was malformed".

**Fix:** Change `discover_from_json_file` to return `(Vec<ImportCandidate>, Vec<String>)` (or a small result struct) and have `discover_external_sources` aggregate and surface the per-source problems through its caller, preserving the content-free strings already produced by `checked_source`. Minimum acceptable fix: log before defaulting — `tracing::warn!(target: "mcp", source = %path.display(), error = %err, "skipping MCP import source");` — and never log raw file contents (the omission convention at lines 153/258).

### R22-L4-02 — discard reader error without log

Severity: major · Location: ``crates/engine/src/extension_host/mcp.rs:454`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** The launched MCP server writes a non-JSON line to stdout, a line exceeding `MAX_MCP_RESPONSE_BYTES`, or an invalid JSON-RPC frame; or the frame consumer is dropped. Any of these makes the `run` future return `Err(anyhow::Error)`, which is silently discarded at line 454.

**Mechanism:** The spawned stdout-reader task accumulates parse/read/dispatch failures into an explicit `Result<(), anyhow::Error>` (line 452). At line 454 the task binds that result to `_`, so the `anyhow::Error` — including the "MCP frame consumer closed" cause built at line 449, the invalid-frame cause from `observe` (line 131-134) and the capped-read cause from line 437 — is dropped without a `tracing` call, without being stored on the `Session`, and without being sent to any channel.

**Impact:** A server that emits one malformed or oversized stdout line loses its whole connection with no diagnostic anywhere in the log or tool result. The model/user sees an MCP server's tools disappear and cannot tell whether the server crashed, produced bad output, or hit the read cap.

**Fix:** Replace `let _ = run.await;` with explicit handling, e.g. `if let Err(err) = run.await { tracing::error!(target: "mcp", server = %reading.name, error = %err, "MCP stdio reader stopped"); }` (and, if the session type permits, store the cause so the tool result can surface it).

### R22-L8-01 — unknown lifecycle status passes as active

Severity: major · Location: ``crates/engine/src/tools/mcp_registry.rs:423`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** the upstream MCP Registry returns a lifecycle status value that is not exactly the lowercase string "deleted" or "deprecated" — e.g. a case variant ("DELETED"), a typo ("deleted "), a future enum member ("quarantined", "banned"), or any malformed value — for a server that should be retired.

**Mechanism:** The upstream `status` is documented in this file as a required enum `active | deprecated | deleted` (mcp_registry.rs:77-82), but it is deserialized as a free-form `Option<String>` — the typed enum is dropped into prose. The retirement gate is an exact-string denylist of only two values: `Some("deleted") | Some("deprecated")`.

**Impact:** A server the registry marked for removal — the comment at mcp_registry.rs:59-61 notes `deleted` entries include moderation takedowns for spam/malware/illegal content — stays in the local index and is offered to the model as a recommended connector whenever its status value differs from the two hard-coded spellings. `registry_start_tool` then launches its cached `run_command` (npx/uvx, arbitrary package spec) in the user's environment.

**Fix:** Deserialize `status` into a real enum (`active | deprecated | deleted`, with `#[serde(other)]` for unknown values) and fail closed: retain only confirmed `active` (or the documented absent-extension case), and drop or quarantine `deprecated`, `deleted`, and every unrecognized value. Log a `tracing::warn!` with the raw status string, server name and source page whenever an unrecognized value is seen, and keep that status in the cache entry so it can be rechecked before launch.

### R22-L8-02 — corrupt cache silently reported as missing

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/engine/src/tools/mcp_registry.rs:393`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** ~/.codewhale/mcp-index.json exists but is truncated, unreadable, or no longer parses as McpRegistryIndex (e.g. interrupted atomic write, disk corruption, manual edit).

**Mechanism:** `read_cache` collapses two distinct failures — a filesystem read error and a JSON/schema parse error — into `None` with `.ok()?`, discarding the `std::io::Error` and `serde_json::Error` and emitting no log line. The only caller-visible outcome is `None`.

**Impact:** An operator debugging a broken Registry cache is told the file is absent rather than corrupt, and no structured trace (server, path, parse error) survives for post-hoc diagnosis — the exact "failure leaves no trace" defect this theme targets. Blast radius is limited to the Registry cache diagnostic path; recovery (running `registry_sync`) is still available because `None` selects a full resync, so no data is lost.

**Fix:** Change `read_cache` to return `Result<Option<McpRegistryIndex>, ToolError>` (or log before returning `None`): emit `tracing::warn!(target: "mcp", path = %path.display(), error = %err, "could not read/parse MCP Registry cache; treating as missing")` for both read and parse failures, and distinguish "absent" from "corrupt" in the `registry_start_tool` message.

### R22-L9-01 — unbounded pagination loop cursor full body read

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/engine/src/tools/mcp_registry.rs:723`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** The registry endpoint (or a MITM / misbehaving upstream) returns a `metadata.nextCursor` that never becomes null — e.g. the same cursor on every page — while each page still returns `servers` entries.

**Mechanism:** `cursor` is taken verbatim from the remote response's `metadata.nextCursor` (:749) and is the loop's only termination condition (:750-752). There is no page-count cap, no total-entry cap, no repetition/dedup check on `cursor`, and no length cap on the cursor string.

**Impact:** A buggy, compromised, or MITM'd registry causes the MCP registry-sync tool to hang and OOM the Codewhale process: every 500 ms another page of entries is appended to `all_entries`, never returning to the caller and never triggering the configured per-request timeout. This is the unbounded-fan-out / cap-after-full-read failure mode named by #6554/#6560.

**Fix:** Bound the pagination explicitly in `fetch_registry_entries`: add `const MAX_PAGES: usize = ...` and `const MAX_REGISTRY_ENTRIES: usize = ...` (or a total byte ceiling) and break with an error when either is exceeded; keep a `HashSet<String>` of cursors seen and refuse to follow a cursor that repeats or is not strictly advancing; cap `next_cursor.len()` (e.g. 4096) before putting it in the next URL.

### R22-L9-02 — cache full read before deserialize no byte cap

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/engine/src/tools/mcp_registry.rs:393`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** `~/.codewhale/mcp-index.json` is larger than intended — written oversized by a prior sync (see R22-L9-01's unbounded `all_entries`) or inflated by a local actor with write access to the home directory.

**Mechanism:** `read_cache` materializes the entire cache file into a `String` at :394 with no `metadata().len()` pre-check, no `File::take()`, and no byte ceiling, then deserializes the whole string into an `McpRegistryIndex` at :395. The byte cost is paid in full before any size or validity decision, and there is no cap at all on the read.

**Impact:** An oversized `mcp-index.json` makes the registry tool allocate and parse the entire file with no visible refusal. On a memory-constrained host this stalls or OOMs the process running the tool; the input is local and has a workaround (delete/regenerate the cache), so the blast radius is limited — minor rather than major.

**Fix:** Before reading, call `std::fs::metadata(path)` and return `None` when `len()` exceeds a fixed ceiling (e.g. the 1 MiB MCP config bound used elsewhere in this unit); otherwise read through `BufReader::take(ceiling + 1)` and treat a length above the ceiling as a cache miss rather than allocating the whole file.

### R22-L9-03 — server settings full config read no byte cap

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/app-server/src/mcp_server.rs:64`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** `~/.deepseek/mcp_server.toml` is oversized — supplied by the operator or by a process able to write to the user home directory.

**Mechanism:** `McpServerSettings::load()` reads the whole `mcp_server.toml` into `contents` at :67 with no `metadata().len()` pre-check and no `File::take()`/byte ceiling, then parses it at :69. The full allocation is paid before any size or validity decision, and no cap exists on the read.

**Impact:** An oversized config makes the `serve --mcp` startup allocate and parse the entire file with no visible refusal, potentially stalling or OOMing that process before the server is usable. Because the input is a local operator config with an obvious workaround and the server is a separately launched process, this is minor.

**Fix:** Before `read_to_string`, call `std::fs::metadata(&path)` and return a clear error when `len()` exceeds a fixed ceiling (e.g. the 1 MiB MCP config bound used in `crates/engine/src/mcp.rs`, `MAX_MCP_CONFIG_BYTES`); otherwise read through `BufReader::take(ceiling + 1)` and refuse when the content exceeds the ceiling.

### R22-L10-01 — swallow approval receipt write after config commit

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/engine/src/mcp/project_authority.rs:123`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** An approved project-scoped `.codewhale/mcp.json` is edited through mutate_config (path parent `.codewhale`, file `mcp.json`, workspace trusted, stored receipt == digest(original)); the follow-up receipt write fails (disk/permission error) or the process crashes between the config commit at mcp.rs:8731 and the receipt write at project_authority.rs:118.

**Mechanism:** mutate_config (crates/engine/src/mcp.rs:8681-8735) persists the edited config first with write_atomic at line 8731, then calls carry_approval_across_product_edit at line 8733; the helper's whole job is to move the stored approval receipt from digest(original) to digest(written) so the new config stays approved. The receipt write at project_authority.rs:118 can fail, but the result is reduced to `.is_err()` and a tracing::warn at lines 123-125 — the function returns `()`, and mutate_config returns Ok regardless.

**Impact:** After such a failure, the user's next session finds the project's mcp.json Unapproved, so its approved MCP servers are no longer loaded and the user must re-run `/mcp review` + `/mcp approve` — a real user scenario breaks with only a log warning and no durable trace in the operation receipt. The config change itself is durable and reported successful, so the failure is silent at the point of action and surfaces only on restart.

**Fix:** Make the carry part of the same durability contract as the config write: either (a) have carry_approval_across_product_edit return Result and propagate it from mutate_config so the caller sees "config saved but approval receipt could not be updated — re-approve required" (never plain Ok), or (b) write the receipt before/at the same commit point as the config (e.g. stage both and commit under one lock), so a crash cannot leave the new config without its matching approval digest.

### R22-L11-01 — sync read cache in async tool handler

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/engine/src/tools/mcp_registry.rs:393`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** invoke the registry_search or registry_sync tool, or trigger the background sync on first Registry-launched server use; the handler reads the whole ~/.codewhale/mcp-index.json and deserializes it synchronously on a Tokio worker.

**Mechanism:** `read_cache` at :393-395 performs a synchronous `std::fs::read_to_string` followed by a synchronous `serde_json::from_str`. It has three callers, all `async fn` running on the Tokio runtime: `load_registry_catalog` (:662, itself awaited from `McpSearchRegistry::execute` :944), `sync_once` (:828, launched by `spawn_background_sync` :702), and `McpSyncRegistry::execute` (:1018).

**Impact:** Each registry tool invocation (or background sync) blocks a Tokio worker for the full duration of the file read and JSON parse. On a large index or a slow/network home directory this stalls unrelated engine tasks sharing the runtime.

**Fix:** Route the read through the blocking pool at each async call site, e.g. `let existing = tokio::task::spawn_blocking({ let p = path.to_path_buf(); move || read_cache(&p) }).await.ok().flatten();`, or introduce an async `read_cache_async` that does the same.

### R22-L11-02 — sync dir scan in async setup view

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/tui/setup/tools_mcp.rs:643`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** open the Setup wizard (OpenSetupWizard / OpenSetupWizardAt) while the UI event loop is running; the view is built synchronously on the async UI thread and enumerates the tools/, skills/ and plugins/ directories and parses plugin frontmatter inline.

**Mechanism:** `count_dir_entries` (:643) and `count_skill_dirs` (:654) call `std::fs::read_dir` synchronously. `SetupToolsMcpFacts::from_app_config` (:124) invokes `tools_dir_inventory` (which at :509 also calls `codewhale_engine::tools::plugin::scan_plugin_dir`, itself a synchronous `std::fs::read_dir` plus per-file `read_script_metadata` at plugin.rs:519/544), `skills_inventory` (:453) and `plugins_inventory` (:525, scanning each plugin dir at :571-572).

**Impact:** Each setup-wizard open blocks a Tokio worker with repeated directory enumerations and file reads proportional to the number of installed tools, skills and plugins. On a populated home directory or a slow filesystem this stalls UI event ingestion and rendering for the duration of the scans.

**Fix:** Build `SetupToolsMcpFacts` off the UI thread: on OpenSetupWizard, move the `from_app_config` call into `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` (as OpenConstitutionManager does) and store the resulting facts on the view when the task completes; or precompute/cache the inventory at startup and have the view consume the cached snapshot. Do not enumerate directories inline in `new_for_app`.

Unit R21 (P2 — highest priority is P0, then P1, then P2), CI, release, install, packaging, workflows, extension manifests. Confirmed unique findings: **14** — **14 public** in this draft and **0** withheld as private-advisory or held. Finding IDs keep their original cell numbers; a gap means the candidate was rejected, marked duplicate or routed to the private index.

No finding in this unit is withheld as a private security advisory or held item.


## Coverage

- Unit R21 at baseline `bc58781ba`. The full analysis, verbatim quotes and verification notes are in the following comments.

## Findings (condensed)

The verbatim quote, full mechanism, evidence, verifier note and regression check for each finding are in the following comment(s).

### R21-L1-01 — stale deepseek name in feishu startup log

Severity: minor · Location: ``integrations/feishu-bridge/src/index.mjs:98`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** Starting the Feishu/Lark bridge (`node src/index.mjs`, or `codewhale-feishu-bridge.service`); the very first line the process emits is the stale banner.

**Mechanism:** The Feishu bridge startup banner was copied from a predecessor and the product-name token was never updated; three sibling bridges in the same unit print "Starting CodeWhale <platform> bridge". This is the L1 card's "copy-paste with one name unchanged" pattern: the mechanism that fails is the log statement reached on every normal start, not an error path.

**Impact:** An operator who starts the Feishu bridge and reads stdout or `journalctl -u codewhale-feishu-bridge` sees a different product name from the other three bridges and from the installed binary (`codewhale`). This is cosmetic: it causes diagnostic confusion and makes the bridge look unmaintained or forked, but no request, turn, credential or state is affected.

**Fix:** Change line 98 to `console.log("Starting CodeWhale Feishu bridge");` to match the sibling bridges. If the two user-facing strings are to be updated in the same change, replace "DeepSeek phone bridge commands:" -> "CodeWhale phone bridge commands:" at `lib.mjs:227` and "Anything else is sent as a DeepSeek prompt." -> "Anything else is sent as a CodeWhale prompt." at `lib.mjs:239`; leave the `DEEPSEEK_*` env-var aliases untouched.

### R21-L2-01 — approval cleanup ignores configured timeout

Severity: minor · Location: ``integrations/wecom-bridge/src/index.mjs:48`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** operator sets CODEWHALE_APPROVAL_TIMEOUT_MS above 300000 (e.g. 900000) and a human answers a pending natural-language approval 6-10 minutes after it was recorded.

**Mechanism:** The cleanup timer at line 48 evicts a pending approval after a hardcoded 300_000 ms, while the natural-language approval check at line 270 honours `config.approvalTimeoutMs`, which is populated from `CODEWHALE_APPROVAL_TIMEOUT_MS` at line 70 (default 300000). When an operator raises that variable above five minutes, the map entry is deleted at the fixed five-minute mark on the next 120_000 ms tick, so `pendingApprovals.has(chatId)` at line 268 is false and the human's affirmative answer cannot be matched to its approval; execution falls through to `runPrompt` at line 283 as an ordinary prompt.

**Impact:** A WeCom operator who follows the documented remedy for an expired approval — raise `CODEWHALE_APPROVAL_TIMEOUT_MS` — gets no extra time for natural-language approval: answers arriving between 5 minutes and the configured timeout are silently treated as fresh prompts instead of approvals. Button approvals and the runtime's own authority are unaffected, so the failure is a broken convenience path rather than an authz bypass.

**Fix:** At index.mjs:48 compare against the configured value, e.g. `if (now - approval.timestamp > config.approvalTimeoutMs) pendingApprovals.delete(chatId);`, and derive the 120_000 ms sweep interval from the same setting so the documented knob governs both the check and the eviction.

### R21-L3-01 — feishu max reply chars upper bound missing

Severity: minor · Location: ``integrations/feishu-bridge/src/lib.mjs:175`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** FEISHU_MAX_REPLY_CHARS set to a large MAX-boundary value (e.g. "1000000"); any agent reply whose length exceeds the Feishu per-message size limit

**Mechanism:** The validator applies only two bounds to FEISHU_MAX_REPLY_CHARS: finite and >= 100 (src/lib.mjs:175-177). There is no upper bound.

**Impact:** An operator who sets a large value to reduce message splitting gets a green validation report, but oversized sendText calls can be rejected by the Feishu message API, so long agent replies fail to deliver with no config error pointing at the cause. The sibling Telegram bridge guards both sides of the same setting (src/lib.mjs:497-500 rejects > 4096; src/index.mjs:82 clamps with Math.min(..., 4096)), which shows the missing upper bound is local to Feishu rather than an intentional omission.

**Fix:** In validateBridgeConfig, extend the check at src/lib.mjs:176 to also reject values above the documented Feishu per-message limit (e.g. `|| maxReplyChars > <limit>`), and clamp at the runtime read in src/index.mjs:61 with Math.min(Number(...), <limit>) to match the Telegram bridge.

### R21-L4-01 — swallow second stream send failure

Severity: major · Location: ``integrations/wecom-bridge/src/lib.mjs:132`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** WeCom `client.replyStream` rejects on the original stream id and again on the rotated id during the `turn.completed` event (e.g. stream expired twice, or a transient WeCom API outage).

**Mechanism:** `update()` is `async` but its second `send` failure is consumed by `catch (e) { console.error(...) }` and never rethrown, so the returned promise resolves successfully. `streamTurnEvents` awaits `streamer.update(responseText.trim() || fallback, true)` at index.mjs:464 and immediately executes `return true` at :465; `streamer.update()` also returns void, so there is no status the caller could inspect.

**Impact:** When both stream sends fail, the WeCom user never receives the final turn answer (or the failed/canceled status), yet `streamTurnEvents` reports success to its caller. No fallback `replyText` is attempted and no durable per-turn record of the failed delivery is written, so an operator seeing `return true` believes the turn was delivered.

**Fix:** After the second failure, rethrow the original error (`catch (e) { console.error(...); throw e; }`) so `await streamer.update(...)` rejects; then let `streamTurnEvents`'s existing `catch` at index.mjs:478 attempt a non-stream `replyText` fallback and record the delivery failure. Alternatively return a boolean from `update()` and make index.mjs:465/474 return `false` on failure.

### R21-L4-02 — discard error in spawn report

Severity: minor · Location: ``integrations/dingtalk-bridge/src/lib.mjs:156`` · Upstream refs: #6555 (CLOSED)

**Trigger:** Any rejection from a spawned `drain`/`runTurn`/`flush` operation (e.g. transport timeout, store write error, or a thrown programming error) reaches the `catch` at lib.mjs:156.

**Mechanism:** The `catch` callback takes no `error` parameter and calls `this.report` with a constant string, so the rejection's message, stack, errcode and the `key` identifying which operation (`inbox:`, `turn:`, `output:`) failed are all discarded. `report` is wired to `console.error(message)` at index.mjs:33, so the only durable trace is that one generic line.

**Impact:** An operator investigating a DingTalk bridge that stops answering turns sees only "DingTalk transport work retained for recovery" repeated, with no way to distinguish a network timeout from a durable-store write failure from a code defect. The root cause is unrecoverable from the log, lengthening diagnosis of a user-visible delivery stall.

**Fix:** Change to `.catch((error) => this.report(\`DingTalk ${key} transport work retained for recovery: ${error?.stack || error?.message || String(error)}\`))`, including the operation key and the original cause; optionally retain the error on the task record for the recovery path.

### R21-L6-01 — cursor persisted before output effect

Severity: major · Location: ``integrations/feishu-bridge/src/index.mjs:370`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** The bridge process exits, is redeployed, or the stream drops after an `item.delta` record is consumed at lines 369-370 but before the terminal `turn.completed` handler at lines 402-410 sends `responseText`. On reattach, `sinceSeq` is taken from `state.lastSeq` (line 332) or the engine's `detail.latest_seq` (line 268), both >= the already-consumed delta's seq, so that delta is never re-read and the in-memory `responseText` rebuilds empty.

**Mechanism:** The resume cursor is durably persisted on every record at line 370, before the record is filtered by turn (372) and before any effect is produced. Deltas are appended only to the local `responseText` variable (line 375, declared at line 350) and reach the user only in the terminal `sendText` at line 409.

**Impact:** A Feishu user whose bridge restarts mid-turn (deploy, crash, stream timeout) receives the final message as "Turn completed." with no assistant content, or misses an approval prompt. The failure is silent: the turn is reported as completed even though its output was never delivered.

**Fix:** Follow the weixin/telegram pattern: store `responseText` and any pending approval text in the chat record and persist them in the same `threadStore.patchChat` that advances `lastSeq`, or delay advancing `lastSeq` until the effect is durably committed and replay from the last uncommitted seq on restart. Route messages through a durable, idempotent outbox as weixin does at index.mjs:616-644.

### R21-L8-01 — group status captures only last gate

Severity: major · Location: ``.github/workflows/catalog-refresh.yml:88`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** any run where `seed render --check`, `seed age --max-days 30`, or `catalog_models_dev_test.py` fails but the final `web/scripts/check-facts.mjs` succeeds (the group's last command).

**Mechanism:** With `set +e`, all four checks run but the brace group's exit status is the status of its last command only (line 86, check-facts.mjs). `status=$?` at line 88 therefore records only whether that final check passed; a failure in any of the first three checks is discarded.

**Impact:** A scheduled catalog refresh whose seed is malformed, too old, or whose unit tests fail is still turned from draft to ready-to-merge and the generated PR claims every check passed. A maintainer merging that PR publishes faulty offline model-seed data to the public /models page under a green receipt, with no durable record in the PR that three of four gates failed.

**Fix:** Accumulate each check's status explicitly, e.g. `ok=true; for cmd in ...; do "$cmd" || ok=false; done` or add `|| status=1` to each of the four commands before line 88, so any single failure produces `ok=false` and keeps the PR in draft (`gh pr ready --undo`).

### R21-L8-02 — always gate ignores failed upstream job as no change

Severity: minor · Location: ``.github/workflows/web-maintainer.yml:274`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** the `lane` job (or `derived` job) fails after `plan` succeeded — e.g. a lane times out or its DeepSeek key step at line 137-139 fails — so no `change.patch` artifact is uploaded for that lane.

**Mechanism:** The `publish` job declares `needs: [plan, derived, lane]` but its `if` gate (line 274) checks only `needs.plan.result`; `derived.result` and `lane.result` are never tested. With `always()`, the job runs even when a lane failed.

**Impact:** Scheduled web-maintainer automation whose lane crashes or times out is reported as a clean "no change proposed" no-op in the job summary. A maintainer reading the summaries (not each matrix job) cannot tell that automation broke, so a broken lane can persist unnoticed; the receipt misrepresents a failure as an intentional no-op.

**Fix:** Make the publish gate distinguish skipped from failed dependencies, e.g. `if: needs.plan.result == 'success' && (needs.derived.result == 'success' || needs.derived.result == 'skipped') && (needs.lane.result == 'success' || needs.lane.result == 'skipped') && vars.WEB_MAINTAINER_ENABLED == 'true'`, and emit an explicit `::error::`/summary line when any dependency result is `failure`, instead of the generic "No lane proposed a change".

### R21-L9-01 — unbounded sse frame buffer

Severity: major · Location: ``extensions/vscode/src/sse.ts:26`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** Any SSE response whose bytes arrive without a "\n\n" or "\r\n\r\n" frame terminator. A single oversized event frame (for example a very large agent_message delta) or a malformed/hostile runtime stream keeps nextBoundary() at -1, so every 'data' chunk is concatenated into this.buffer with no ceiling.

**Mechanism:** push() appends each raw network chunk to a single string field with no byte or character limit. nextBoundary() only searches for "\n\n"/"\r\n\r\n"; if none is present the buffer is retained in full across pushes.

**Impact:** A runaway, buggy or hostile runtime SSE stream drives unbounded heap growth inside the VS Code extension host until the host stops responding or is killed by OOM. The user loses the extension session and any unsaved UI state; the same gap exists on every supported platform because the parser is pure TypeScript with no platform gate.

**Fix:** Add a MAX_SSE_BUFFER_BYTES limit (mirror bridge-core's 2 MiB) to SseParser. In push(), accumulate the byte length of chunk plus the retained buffer before appending; when it would exceed the cap, emit an onError/throw and drop or reset the buffer instead of growing it.

### R21-L9-02 — unbounded json response accumulation

Severity: major · Location: ``extensions/vscode/src/api.ts:449`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** Any runtime HTTP response whose body is very large (a bloated transcript/summary snapshot, a malformed or hostile runtime, or a proxy injecting data). Chunks are concatenated into `raw` with no byte ceiling until the socket closes, and only then is the whole string deserialized.

**Mechanism:** requestJson streams the response into the string `raw` via repeated concatenation with no Content-Length check and no running byte counter. The cap that does exist is temporal only — `timeout: options.timeoutMs` (line 438) plus the `request.on("timeout")` destroy handler (lines 459-461) — so a fast local runtime can still deliver an arbitrarily large body within the window.

**Impact:** A single oversized response allocates unbounded memory in the VS Code extension host and can OOM/kill it before the timeout ever fires. Users lose the extension session; the failure is not attributed to a size limit, so no actionable error is shown.

**Fix:** Add a MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES ceiling (mirror readJsonSafe's 8 MiB). In requestJson, reject early when `response.headers["content-length"]` exceeds it, track accumulated chunk byteLength on every "data" event, and on overflow call `request.destroy(...)` and reject with a clear size-limit error before any concatenation/parse.

### R21-L10-01 — install tmp rename without fsync

Severity: minor · Location: ``integrations/verifiers-codewhale/codewhale_harness/harness.py:336`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** A verifier run installs a pinned Codewhale version (no binary_path configured). The install publishes three binaries and its .sha256/.version receipt files via `mv -f` (rename) with no fsync of the staged bytes or of the containing `bin` directory.

**Mechanism:** The three binaries and the two receipt files (.sha256, .version) are each published with a plain `mv -f` rename. There is no `sync`/`fsync` of the temp file before rename and no fsync of `$install_dir/bin` after it, unlike the repository's durable-write primitive `writeFileDurable` (bridge-core/src/lib.mjs:32-67), which calls `handle.sync()` before rename and a best-effort directory `sync()` after.

**Impact:** On a verifier host that loses power mid-install, the next run's early-exit check at harness.py:311-314 (version match plus `sha256sum -c .sha256`) detects a mismatch and reinstalls, so the practical blast radius is one wasted install cycle and a transient inconsistent bin directory rather than silent data loss. This is the same mechanism sibling L10 cells reported as minor (#6555 "Durable writes not crash-atomic"); it is filed here because it is the only tmp+rename durability gap inside R21's owned files.

**Fix:** After writing each `$target.tmp.$$` and before its `mv -f`, flush the file (e.g. `sync "$install_dir/bin/$target.tmp.$$"` or an fsync via a small helper), and after the final rename fsync `$install_dir/bin`.

### R21-L11-01 — sync writefile in async handler

Severity: minor · Location: ``integrations/wecom-bridge/src/index.mjs:150`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** any inbound WeCom media message (image/video/file) carrying a valid downloadable URL; after the awaited download the full buffer is written synchronously.

**Mechanism:** `handleMediaMessage` is declared `async` (line 133) and is reached via `await handleMediaMessage(...)` from the message dispatcher (line 208). After an awaited network download it calls `mkdirSync` (line 146) and `writeFileSync(target, buffer)` (line 150), both blocking `node:fs` calls imported synchronously at line 2.

**Impact:** media files are explicitly anticipated in megabyte sizes — the success reply reports `buffer.length / 1048576` MB (line 153) — and no size cap appears in this path. Writing a multi-MB buffer with `writeFileSync` blocks the entire bridge event loop until the disk write finishes, so other conversations' messages, heartbeats, approval prompts and replies stall in that window.

**Fix:** Use the async fs API — e.g. `await mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })` and `await writeFile(target, buffer)` from `node:fs/promises`, or `await fs.open(...)` + `handle.writeFile(...)` as weixin-bridge does (index.mjs:1331-1332) — so the event loop stays free while the buffer is flushed.

### R21-L12-01 — raw slice splits surrogate in progress chunk

Severity: minor · Location: ``integrations/feishu-bridge/src/index.mjs:378`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** A streamed agent reply contains a non-BMP character (e.g. an emoji such as U+1F600 stored as two UTF-16 code units) whose surrogate pair straddles `config.maxReplyChars`, and more than 15 s have elapsed since the last progress send, so the progress flush at lines 377-380 fires exactly at that boundary.

**Mechanism:** `String.prototype.slice` and `.length` index UTF-16 code units, not Unicode scalar values. If `config.maxReplyChars` falls between the high and low surrogate of a non-BMP character, line 378 sends a string ending in a lone high surrogate and line 379 retains a string beginning with a lone low surrogate.

**Impact:** A Feishu user whose streamed reply contains an emoji near a chunk boundary sees a corrupted or replacement character at the seam of two progress messages, and the character is lost when the client re-encodes the unpaired surrogate as UTF-8. The effect is confined to progress messages during long streams (15 s cadence) and is cosmetic — no state or data is corrupted — but it is user-visible in a path that runs for any long reply containing emoji, which is common in chat.

**Fix:** Replace the two raw `responseText.slice(...)` calls in the progress-flush block with a code-point-aware split. Reuse the existing `splitMessage(responseText, config.maxReplyChars)` helper (or add an exported `splitAtCodePoint` if only the first chunk is needed): emit `chunks[0]` via `sendText`, set `responseText = chunks.slice(1).join("")`, and keep the existing `sentProgressAt` update.

### R21-L12-02 — utf16 slice breaks surrogate in code title

Severity: minor · Location: ``extensions/vscode/src/markdown.ts:109`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** A fenced code block in model output whose first line is longer than 80 UTF-16 code units and contains a non-BMP character (e.g. an emoji) at code-unit offset 79/80, so the 80-unit cutoff falls between its surrogate pair.

**Mechanism:** `firstLine.slice(0, 80)` truncates the first code line by UTF-16 code units. When the cutoff lands between the high and low surrogate of a non-BMP character, the resulting string has a lone surrogate.

**Impact:** The hover tooltip on a code block shows a replacement/garbled character at its tail when a model emits a long first line containing emoji near the 80-unit mark. The user can still read and copy the full code block (the `codeBlocks` array and `escapeHtml(code)` path are intact), so this is display polish with a narrow trigger, not data loss.

**Fix:** Replace `firstLine.slice(0, 80)` with a code-point-safe truncation, e.g. `Array.from(firstLine).slice(0, 80).join("")` (one line, stdlib), or use `Intl.Segmenter` if grapheme clusters (not just surrogate pairs) must be preserved.

issues.body:
# state, snapshot, memory, lane, cli, workflow*, skills, release: 10 verified defects from R19 (baseline bc58781ba)

## How to read this document (terms used below)

- **R<number>** — review unit, one area of the codebase; this document is about R19.
- **L<number>** — one of twelve review lenses (themes) applied to every unit; the table below names each lens.
- **P0 / P1 / P2** — priority rank: P0 highest, P2 lowest. It orders the work, not the severity of a finding.
- **Stage D** — the verification step: every cited line was opened at the baseline, the reachability was traced, and severity was re-scored. **Stage E** — the drafting step that produced this report.
- **Baseline `bc58781ba`** — the exact commit every quote refers to; re-check before acting if `main` has moved.
- **Confirmed** — a verifier opened the cited line, traced a reachable path and kept the finding; rejected and uncertain findings are not here.
- **Public** — this issue contains only findings cleared for a public report; security-class findings are handled through a separate private channel.
- **needs-test** — the written proof is static; a focused test named in the finding would settle the remaining question. No test was run in this audit.
- **Cell** — one audit cell: a review unit crossed with one lens; finding IDs keep the cell number, so a gap in numbering means a candidate was rejected, marked duplicate or routed to the private index.
- **NOT READ** — a scope marker in a cell: that region was not opened, so no claim is made about it.
- **not-applicable / sampled-rescan-passed** — negative-check outcomes: the lens did not apply to that cell, or a sampled rescan found no new signal.
- **Refs #N / UPSTREAM REFS** — existing tracked issues related to the theme or to the exact code site; they are cross-links, never a claim to close or fix those issues. A 500-issue open/closed sweep found no exact duplicate of these findings at the same file and line.
- **CALL PATH, TRIGGER, MECHANISM, IMPACT, EVIDENCE, FIX, REGRESSION CHECK** — copied verbatim from the verified finding file. CALL PATH = how a user reaches the code; TRIGGER = the condition that fires it; MECHANISM = what the code actually does; IMPACT = what the user sees; EVIDENCE = the supporting lines; FIX = recommended change; REGRESSION CHECK = the test that should be added.

Unit R19 (P2 — highest priority is P0, then P1, then P2), persistence, upgrade, release and install tooling. Confirmed unique findings: **10** — **10 public** in this draft and **0** withheld as private-advisory or held. Finding IDs keep their original cell numbers; a gap means the candidate was rejected, marked duplicate or routed to the private index.

No finding in this unit is withheld as a private security advisory or held item.


## Coverage

- Unit R19 at baseline `bc58781ba`. The full analysis, verbatim quotes and verification notes are in the following comments.
- 10 confirmed public findings. No test, build or product run happened in this audit.

## Findings (condensed)

The verbatim quote, full mechanism, evidence, verifier note and regression check for each finding are in the following comment(s).

### R19-L4-01 — swallow mark terminal error leaves lane pending

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/cli/src/lib.rs:1050`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** A lane start where backend.start fails and the subsequent mark_terminal_if_active also fails (registry reload/save or advisory-lock error), e.g. a transient disk I/O error while persisting the lane record.

**Mechanism:** On a failed `backend.start`, the reconciliation branch calls `mark_terminal_if_active` specifically to move the lane out of `pending`. That method returns `Result<bool>` (crates/lane/src/registry.rs:378-383), so its `Err` path — a failed lock acquire, live reload, or record save — is discarded by `let _ =`.

**Impact:** A failed lane start combined with a transient registry write or lock error leaves a stale `pending` lane that reconciliation will skip. `lane list` then advertises a lane that can never progress, and no stop/cleanup path acts on it; no log line explains the stuck state, so an operator reading logs sees only the start error.

**Fix:** Propagate or log the mark error with context, for example: ``` if let Err(mark) = reg.mark_terminal_if_active(&mut record, LaneStatus::Failed) { return Err(error.context(format!( "lane start failed; also failed to close lane as Failed: {mark:#}" ))); } ``` At minimum emit `tracing::warn!` with the lane id and `mark` so the stuck pending state leaves a durable trace.

### R19-L6-01 — shared staging check then use race

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/skills/src/mutation.rs:1511`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** two concurrent Codewhale skill-mutation invocations targeting the same skill name within the same skills dir (e.g. two terminals, or an agent install overlapping a user command).

**Mechanism:** `staging` is derived only from the skill `segment` and the shared `skills_dir`, so concurrent mutations of the same skill name resolve to the same `X.tmp` path. Lines 1512-1515 check whether that path exists and delete it; line 1516 then writes into it.

**Impact:** Concurrent installs of the same skill produce spurious failures, partial staging writes, or a wrong backup/replace decision; a user or agent sees an unexpected `skill ... failed` error or a skill replaced without its intended backup.

**Fix:** Give each mutation a unique staging directory (e.g. append process id + monotonic nonce as `place_package`'s caller does for memory probe files at `crates/memory/src/store.rs:49-55`) instead of the predictable `{segment}.tmp`; and re-evaluate destination existence inside `place_package` immediately before the backup/rename branch rather than trusting the caller's stale `dest_exists` bool.

### R19-L7-01 — cat file spawn without timeout hangs turn

Severity: major · Location: ``crates/snapshot/src/delta.rs:231`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** snapshot build over a repository whose object store sits on a wedged NFS/FUSE mount or a hung git hook; cat-file --batch never drains stdout

**Mechanism:** `git()` (delta.rs:63-71) builds a plain `std::process::Command` with no timeout wrapper; the child is spawned with piped stdin/stdout at 231-236 and the only wait is the blocking `child.wait()?` at 295. `wait_timeout::ChildExt` is not used here, no watchdog thread kills the child, and `std::process::Child` has no `kill_on_drop`.

**Impact:** A single stalled `cat-file --batch` blocks the turn pipeline indefinitely with no error and no timeout; the user sees a frozen request rather than the bounded error that every other git call in `repo.rs` produces.

**Fix:** Route `blob_facts`'s `cat-file --batch` through `codewhale_dependencies::run_bounded_git_with_timeout` or an equivalent bounded helper that drains both pipes, kills on timeout and reaps on a detached thread — the same mechanism repo.rs:2431-2447 uses — instead of the raw `spawn()`/`wait()` pair.

### R19-L7-02 — cat file error path kills without reap and detaches writer

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/snapshot/src/delta.rs:259`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** git cat-file --batch emits an unexpected header (corrupt/missing object, concurrent gc) or a read fails mid-blob; blob_facts returns early

**Mechanism:** The only success-path cleanup is `writer.join()??` at 292-294 and `child.wait()?` at 295, both reachable only after all blobs are read. On the header-mismatch branch at 259 `child.kill()` is called but `child.wait()` is skipped, so the killed child is never reaped.

**Impact:** Repeated failed snapshots (e.g. a repo with missing objects) leak a zombie per failure and can leave a live `cat-file` child consuming resources; the detached writer thread holds its stdin until git exits.

**Fix:** On every error exit, kill the child if still alive and join the writer and reap the child (or move all three into a small guard whose `Drop` kills, joins and waits) so no early return leaks a child or detaches the writer; ideally reuse the bounded helper from F-01 which already owns this cleanup.

### R19-L8-01 — skip unreadable recovery record deletes receipt

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/release/src/installs.rs:1325`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** A recovery folder older than RECOVERY_RETENTION_DAYS contains a record whose stored file still exists but whose symlink_metadata fails (e.g. permission change on the containing directory or a transient I/O error).

**Mechanism:** `complete` starts `true` (line 1319). A record whose `stored` path fails `symlink_metadata` is skipped with `continue` (1325-1327) and never sets `complete = false`; only explicit containment failure (1321) or a failed removal (1333) clear the flag.

**Impact:** A user inspecting recovery state after an expired-folder prune sees the folder removed from the reported `pruned` accounting and its manifest missing, while a stored file may remain on disk with no index explaining it. Post-hoc diagnosis cannot reconstruct what that file was or that a metadata failure caused the discrepancy — the #6559 "failure leaves no durable trace / receipt lies" class.

**Fix:** In the `symlink_metadata` failure arm, distinguish a missing file (`ErrorKind::NotFound` — safe to skip) from any other error: for other errors set `complete = false` and emit a `tracing::warn!` naming `record.stored`. Only delete `RECOVERY_MANIFEST` when every record was confirmed absent or successfully removed.

### R19-L8-02 — ignored decline persist result leaves no receipt

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/cli/src/update.rs:628`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** An unsigned-but-checksum-verified staged update is declined at the interactive prompt, and writing `staged.json` fails (e.g. read-only home, disk full, permission change).

**Mechanism:** The `declined` flag is set in memory, then `autoupdate::store_staged` — the only durable record of that decision — has its `Result` discarded via `let _ =`. The code then unconditionally prints a confirmation implying the decline was kept and returns success.

**Impact:** The user is told "Kept v{current}" and that they can update whenever they want, but the decline was never recorded. On the next startup the stale staged update is offered again, re-prompting for an already-answered consent decision with no durable receipt explaining why.

**Fix:** Replace `let _ = autoupdate::store_staged(&home, &staged);` with an explicit match: on `Err`, print a distinct warning and emit `tracing::warn!` naming the path — e.g. "decision not saved: could not record declined update at <staged.json>: <err> — you will be asked again" — rather than the unqualified "Kept v{current}" success line.

### R19-L9-01 — uncapped full file read workflow source before compile

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/cli/src/lib.rs:1522`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** `codewhale workflow run --source <path>` where `<path>` is a very large file (or a bare workflow name resolving to a large file in the workspace). No size guard exists at either resolve_workflow_source_path (1460-1479) or validate_workflow_source_file (1520-1534).

**Mechanism:** `validate_workflow_source_file` calls `std::fs::read_to_string` on the resolved source path with no `metadata()` length check and no `BufReader::take` ceiling, materialising the entire file into a `String`. Only after that full read does it inspect the content and hand the whole `source` string to the QuickJS-backed `compile_*_workflow` (crates/workflow/src/js_authoring.rs:26-40), which parses and allocates an interpreter over the materialised source.

**Impact:** A workflow source file of arbitrary size makes the CLI allocate and scan the whole file, then compile it, with no visible refusal. On a memory-constrained host this turns a bounded CLI validation into a stall or OOM that kills the process.

**Fix:** Before `read_to_string`, call `std::fs::metadata(path)` and return a visible `bail!` when `len()` exceeds a fixed ceiling (e.g. the 512 KiB skill/audit ceiling referenced by sibling #6554 findings, or the 1 MiB used by `memory import`).

### R19-L10-02 — atomic write helper rename without fsync

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/release/src/installs.rs:1400`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** An autoupdate stages the new binary, `STAGED_MANIFEST` and `STAGED_SIGNATURE` through `write_file_atomically`. A crash / power loss after the rename but before the staged bytes and the new directory entry are flushed can leave a staged file empty or missing even though the helper reported success — the installer then observes a valid-looking staged state and reports the update as ready.

**Mechanism:** `write_file_atomically` is named and used as an "atomic" publisher, but it writes the bytes with `std::fs::write` (line 1403), adds no `File::sync_all`, renames over the final name (1411), and returns success with neither the file data nor the destination directory entry flushed. Splitting write from rename only prevents readers from seeing a partially written file; it does not make the result crash-durable.

**Impact:** After such a crash, the autoupdate's staged directory can contain a truncated/incomplete binary plus manifest and signature. `load_staged` (autoupdate.rs:245) / `load_json` (227) deserialize these; a truncated JSON fails to parse (returns `None`, update silently discarded) and a truncated binary would be rejected by signature verification before install.

**Fix:** Replace `fs::write(&tmp, bytes)` with an explicit `OpenOptions` write followed by `file.sync_all()?` on the temp file; after `fs::rename`, fsync the containing directory (Unix: open `dir` and call `sync_all`, or reuse `sync_parent()` from crates/util/src/files.rs:722 behind `#[cfg(unix)]`). Apply the same to `rewrite_manifest` (1286-1307) which uses the identical write+rename pattern for the recovery manifest.

### R19-L10-03 — recovery manifest rewrite without fsync

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/release/src/installs.rs:1286`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** During recovery, each record is moved back and the manifest is rewritten with the still-remaining records. If the process crashes after the rename but before the manifest bytes and its directory entry are durable, the on-disk manifest can revert to the pre-rewrite list of records even though the corresponding files were already restored and moved back.

**Mechanism:** `rewrite_manifest` serializes the remaining recovery records into a `.tmp` file with `fs::write` (1305) — no `File::sync_all` — then renames it over `RECOVERY_MANIFEST` (1306) with no parent-directory fsync, and returns immediately. The manifest is the durable ledger that decides which future recovery attempts run.

**Impact:** A stale manifest makes recovery non-idempotent. On restart, records that were already restored are attempted again: `fs::rename(&record.stored, &record.original)` at 1247 fails with "move back failed" because the stored file no longer exists, pushing the record into `report.skipped` (1252-1259) — noisy false failures and a recovery that never converges on an empty manifest until the crash window is survived.

**Fix:** Write `text` through an `OpenOptions` handle, call `file.sync_all()?` before closing, then `fs::rename`, then fsync the parent directory (Unix: `File::open(dir)?.sync_all()?` / `sync_parent()` from crates/util/src/files.rs:722 behind `#[cfg(unix)]`). Since recovery is a retry loop, also make restoration itself idempotent: treat an already-absent `record.stored` whose `record.original` exists with a matching digest as success rather than pushing it to `skipped`.

### R19-L11-01 — sync fs inline in async skill mutation

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/skills/src/mutation.rs:816`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** Any skill install or update tool call issued through the async TUI handler or the async runtime API; the synchronous filesystem phase runs inline on the Tokio worker before/after the network await.

**Mechanism:** `install_remote` is an `async fn`, but its pre-network phase calls synchronous filesystem helpers directly with no `spawn_blocking` and no `tokio::fs`: `prepare_owned_target` (line 816) reaches `fs::canonicalize` at lines 244/246 and `create_owned_directory`/`fs::create_dir` at line 263; `installed_specs` (line 820) walks roots with `fs::read_to_string`/`fs::read_dir` at lines 637/686/774/781. The same async path calls `package_digest::compute_package_digest` at line 880 (a full-tree SHA-256 pass), and `update_skill` (line 1606) calls `ensure_remote_updatable`, `read_installed_marker` and `validate_owned_skill_path` synchronously before its own network await.

**Impact:** Each skill install/update blocks one Tokio worker for the duration of canonicalisation, directory walks and a package-hash pass — bounded by `ctx.max_size`, but potentially a large tree. Reached through the async UI handler at `handlers.rs:1473` and runtime API at `runtime_api.rs:6780/6821`, that worker cannot poll other tasks, so UI repaint, keystroke handling, cancellation and concurrent tool results stall for the window.

**Fix:** Move the synchronous filesystem phase of `install_remote`/`update_skill` (prepare/validate/spec scan/digest) into `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` (or convert the helpers to `tokio::fs`) so the Tokio worker is released before the network await. At minimum offload `installed_specs` and `compute_package_digest`, the two whole-tree passes.

Undated planning target approved November 5, 2026. Scope and data-loss semantics must be resolved before implementation; preserve accessibility, explicit cleanup controls and authoritative accounting. This milestone does not create a published release.

issues.body:
# tui/src/tui/ app, setup, approval, ambient, pet files: 12 verified defects from R18 (baseline bc58781ba)

## How to read this document (terms used below)

- **R<number>** — review unit, one area of the codebase; this document is about R18.
- **L<number>** — one of twelve review lenses (themes) applied to every unit; the table below names each lens.
- **P0 / P1 / P2** — priority rank: P0 highest, P2 lowest. It orders the work, not the severity of a finding.
- **Stage D** — the verification step: every cited line was opened at the baseline, the reachability was traced, and severity was re-scored. **Stage E** — the drafting step that produced this report.
- **Baseline `bc58781ba`** — the exact commit every quote refers to; re-check before acting if `main` has moved.
- **Confirmed** — a verifier opened the cited line, traced a reachable path and kept the finding; rejected and uncertain findings are not here.
- **Public** — this issue contains only findings cleared for a public report; security-class findings are handled through a separate private channel.
- **needs-test** — the written proof is static; a focused test named in the finding would settle the remaining question. No test was run in this audit.
- **Cell** — one audit cell: a review unit crossed with one lens; finding IDs keep the cell number, so a gap in numbering means a candidate was rejected, marked duplicate or routed to the private index.
- **NOT READ** — a scope marker in a cell: that region was not opened, so no claim is made about it.
- **not-applicable / sampled-rescan-passed** — negative-check outcomes: the lens did not apply to that cell, or a sampled rescan found no new signal.
- **Refs #N / UPSTREAM REFS** — existing tracked issues related to the theme or to the exact code site; they are cross-links, never a claim to close or fix those issues. A 500-issue open/closed sweep found no exact duplicate of these findings at the same file and line.
- **CALL PATH, TRIGGER, MECHANISM, IMPACT, EVIDENCE, FIX, REGRESSION CHECK** — copied verbatim from the verified finding file. CALL PATH = how a user reaches the code; TRIGGER = the condition that fires it; MECHANISM = what the code actually does; IMPACT = what the user sees; EVIDENCE = the supporting lines; FIX = recommended change; REGRESSION CHECK = the test that should be added.

Unit R18 (P2 — highest priority is P0, then P1, then P2), first run, approvals, ambient lifecycle, TUI entry. Confirmed unique findings: **13** — **12 public** in this draft and **1** withheld as private-advisory or held. Finding IDs keep their original cell numbers; a gap means the candidate was rejected, marked duplicate or routed to the private index.


## Coverage

- Unit R18 at baseline `bc58781ba`. The full analysis, verbatim quotes and verification notes are in the following comments.
- 12 confirmed public findings. No test, build or product run happened in this audit.

## Findings (condensed)

The verbatim quote, full mechanism, evidence, verifier note and regression check for each finding are in the following comment(s).

### R18-L4-01 — ok discards producer post error drops queued events

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/tui/pet_watch/live.rs:623`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** any io::Error from the /v1/producer POST (transient transport failure or non-2xx mapped to Err by Client::request) while one or more activity events are queued in Batch, with the pet companion visible.

**Mechanism:** `.ok()` at line 623 converts the `io::Result` from the producer POST into an `Option`, throwing away the error value with no log and no `Notice`. On failure `producer_seq` becomes `None`; on the next loop turn line 615 recomputes `seq = 0` and line 617 calls `events.clear()`, discarding every activity event queued since the last successful post.

**Impact:** A single transient POST failure silently drops the queued pet activity batch and resets the producer sequence. The companion/runtime projection loses those events (visual/activity glitches in the pet watch), and an operator reading notices or logs sees nothing — unlike the adjacent `/v1/action` POST at lines 589-607, whose errors are surfaced via a rate-limited `Notice::Message(e.to_string())`.

**Fix:** Match on the POST result instead of `.ok()`: on `Ok`, advance `producer_seq`, clear `events`, and update `last_produce` as today; on `Err(e)`, leave `producer_seq` and `events` intact for the next attempt and surface `e` through the same rate-limited `Notice::Message(e.to_string())` branch used for action errors (or a structured `tracing::warn!`). Do not compute `seq = 0` / clear `events` from a transport error.

### R18-L4-02 — map err unit erases hydration failure cause

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/tui/pet_watch/worker.rs:128`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** a session-scoped pet recording cannot be hydrated — corrupt/unreadable store file, concurrent lock, poisoned deadline mutex, or a QuickJS restore error.

**Mechanism:** The hydration closure is typed `Result<Store, ()>` (worker.rs:127), and every distinct failure is collapsed with `map_err(|_| ())` (lines 128, 129, 135; the same erasure is used at lines 126, 149). The `Err(())` branch can therefore only emit the fixed `Notice::StorageUnavailable` (line 151); the original `io::Error`/`rquickjs::Error` value is dropped and never logged, so no cause-bearing durable trace is produced for a failed load.

**Impact:** When a pet recording is corrupt, locked by another process, or the restore script fails, the user sees only a generic "storage unavailable" toast and logs carry no reason. An operator or support flow cannot distinguish disk I/O, decode failure, lock poisoning, or a JS error, and repeated failures produce the same indistinguishable notice — the failure leaves no structured receipt.

**Fix:** Change the hydration error type from `()` to a cause-preserving error (e.g. `Box<dyn std::error::Error>` / `anyhow::Error`), map failures with `map_err(|e| e.into())`, and on the failure branch emit a structured `tracing::warn!(error = %cause, "pet recording hydration failed")` alongside the existing `Notice::StorageUnavailable`.

### R18-L6-01 — clear event batch before delivery confirmed

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/tui/pet_watch/live.rs:623-624`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** A transient `client.post("/v1/producer", ...)` error (connection reset / timeout to the shared-pet server) while `events` holds one or more `Command::Observe` batches.

**Mechanism:** The producer advances its outbound position regardless of whether the effect happened. `producer_seq` is only set to `Some(seq)` when the POST succeeds (line 623: `.ok().map(|_| seq)` returns `None` on error), but `events.clear()` at line 624 runs unconditionally.

**Impact:** The shared-pet animation misses a batch of observed activity events after any transient network hiccup to the local pet server. This is cosmetic (pet reactions animate one turn behind / skip a beat); no user work or durable data is lost.

**Fix:** Clear the batch only on a confirmed send: `match client.post(...) { Ok(_) => { producer_seq = Some(seq); events.clear(); }, Err(_) => { producer_seq = None; /* keep events for the seq=0 restart */ } }`. If the server treats seq=0 as a fresh lease that would replay retained events, re-send the retained batch on the seq=0 restart instead of dropping it; if the server may have accepted the failed POST, dedup by (client, seq) before replaying.

### R18-L7-01 — detached stdin reader survives grace timeout

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/lib.rs:1135`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** `codewhale exec "<prompt>"` with a non-terminal stdin pipe whose first byte arrives after EXEC_STDIN_GRACE (2 s, lib.rs:1107), e.g. `tail -f app.log | codewhale exec "summarize"`; a tool subprocess spawned during the run also reads stdin.

**Mechanism:** `read_stdin_context` spawns a detached thread (lib.rs:1112) that takes `io::stdin().lock()` and blocks in `stdin.read()` (lib.rs:1113-1120) until the first byte or EOF. The `started_tx.send(())` that `recv_timeout` waits for happens only *after* that first read completes (lib.rs:1121).

**Impact:** With a slow pipe producer, a stdin reader outlives the 2 s window and competes with any tool subprocess the agent spawns for the same stdin bytes. When such a subprocess reads stdin (e.g.

**Fix:** Make the reader cancellable: share an `AtomicBool`/oneshot `CancellationToken` with the spawned thread; on the grace-expiry branch (lib.rs:1135-1136) set the cancel flag before returning so the thread stops polling stdin. Have the thread poll the flag between short non-blocking reads (or read a duplicated fd with `try_read`) so it exits without waiting for a byte.

### R18-L8-01 — clobber failed flag write with success notice

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/tui/app.rs:3528`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** Settings::transact_opt returns Err (e.g. settings.toml unwritable / read-only config dir) when the user first opens /fleet after onboarding with onboarding_needs_api_key == false and feature_intro_shown == false.

**Mechanism:** The Err arm writes a failure receipt into the single-slot `status_message` field (3528). Control then falls through the `match` and line 3532 assigns `status_message` again, unconditionally, to the localized "fleet is ready" notice.

**Impact:** A user whose settings.toml cannot be written (read-only home, full disk, permission change) is told only "Fleet ready"; the failure notice the code intended to show is never rendered. Post-hoc inspection cannot tell that `feature_intro_shown` failed to persist — the intro nudge simply reappears next launch with no explanation.

**Fix:** In the Err arm, emit the failure as a typed Error-level toast (`self.push_status_toast(err_receipt, StatusToastLevel::Error, None)`) and a `tracing::warn!` carrying the error, then set `status_message`/FleetReadyNotice for the nudge. Do not write the failure into the single `status_message` slot that line 3532 will overwrite.

### R18-L8-02 — onboard marker failure no durable receipt

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/tui/app.rs:3496`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** mark_onboarded() fails when finishing first run — e.g. Codewhale home not found (mark_onboarded returns io::ErrorKind::NotFound at onboarding/mod.rs:382-387) or the marker path is unwritable.

**Mechanism:** The only handling of a failed `.onboarded` marker write is an assignment to the single-slot `status_message` (3496). There is no `tracing` call in this function or in `mark_onboarded`/`mark_onboarded_at_path` (onboarding/mod.rs:381-403), and no `HistoryCell::System` receipt is added (contrast ui.rs:1126-1130, where the sibling "Failed to save constitution choice" failure is both a status message and a durable transcript cell).

**Impact:** The user is told of the failure only by a transient toast that is overwritten by the next status line. After a restart the `.onboarded` marker is still absent, so onboarding reappears with no log explaining why.

**Fix:** Add a `tracing::warn!(error = ?err, "onboarding marker not persisted")` in the Err arm and a durable `HistoryCell::System` receipt (as ui.rs:1127-1129 does), while keeping the toast. Only set `onboarding = OnboardingState::None` after the marker write succeeds, or record the failed state explicitly so the next launch can explain the repeat.

### R18-L9-01 — uncapped full file read before emptiness check

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/tui/setup/mod.rs:753`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** a large expert-override file is present at $CODEWHALE_HOME/<CONSTITUTION_OVERRIDE_FILE> when the guided setup screen computes SetupExpertOverrideState.

**Mechanism:** `load()` calls `std::fs::read_to_string(&path)` at :753 with no byte ceiling, materializing the entire override file into `raw` before it calls `raw.trim().is_empty()` at :754. There is no `metadata().len()` pre-check and no `BufReader::take()`; the whole file is allocated and copied only to classify it as Empty/Active/Disabled.

**Impact:** a large or hostile override file makes the guided-setup startup allocate and scan the whole file with no visible refusal, so on a memory-constrained host a bounded setup step becomes a stall or OOM before the UI is usable. The file is local and operator-controlled (path resolved under `codewhale_home()` at :5447-5451) and a workaround (remove/shrink the file) exists, hence minor rather than major.

**Fix:** before reading, call `std::fs::metadata(&path)` and return `Self::Unreadable` when `len()` exceeds a fixed ceiling (e.g. the 512 KiB ceiling used for skill/audit reads in sibling #6554 findings); otherwise read through `BufReader::take(ceiling + 1)` and treat `len() > ceiling` as oversize rather than allocating the whole file.

### R18-L9-02 — unbounded queued messages vecdeque

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/tui/app.rs:7489`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** many follow-up messages are queued during a single long-running turn, with no count cap on the queue.

**Mechanism:** `queue_message()` appends to `self.queued_messages` at :7489 with no length check. The field is declared as `VecDeque<QueuedMessage>` at :2530 and is only drained at end-of-turn; a class-wide grep over `crates/tui/src/tui` for `queued_messages`, `MAX_QUEUED` and `MAX_FOLLOW` found no count cap on the enqueue path (contrast `status_toasts`, which caps at 24 in app/status.rs:173).

**Impact:** every queued follow-up holds a display `String` plus optional attachments, so a long turn during which the user keeps pressing Enter grows the VecDeque without bound and raises the session's resident memory. The queue is human-driven, shown in a preview, and drained when the turn ends, so this is a narrow edge case with a workaround — minor, not major.

**Fix:** enforce a fixed cap in `queue_message()` (e.g. `MAX_QUEUED_MESSAGES`), dropping or coalescing the oldest non-restored follow-up and surfacing a toast, mirroring the bounded `status_toasts` pattern in app/status.rs:173-180.

### R18-L10-01 — onboarded marker fswrite no fsync

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/tui/onboarding/mod.rs:401`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** A user finishes first-run onboarding. The app sets OnboardingState::None and calls mark_onboarded(); mark_onboarded_at_path creates a zero-length marker with a plain std::fs::write and returns Ok(path).

**Mechanism:** mark_onboarded_at_path creates the "onboarded" marker with std::fs::write, which opens with truncate/create, writes zero bytes and closes. It issues no sync_all on the file and no fsync of the containing directory.

**Impact:** A crash or power loss immediately after onboarding completes can drop the marker. On the next launch is_onboarded() (line 377-379) checks only path.exists(), returns false, and the user is walked through onboarding again.

**Fix:** Publish the marker through the repository's durable atomic-write helper instead of a bare std::fs::write — e.g. replace line 401 with codewhale_util::utils::write_atomic(&path, b"") (or codewhale_config::persistence::atomic_write), which writes a temp file, fsyncs it, renames it and fsyncs the parent directory.

### R18-L11-01 — sync git gh subprocess inline in async run review

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/lib.rs:11963`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** `codewhale review --pr <N>` (or `--base <ref>`) on any supported platform; the network-bound `gh pr view` / `gh pr diff` and full-worktree `git diff` / `git log` run to completion inline before the async review loop at :12158 begins.

**Mechanism:** `run_review` at lib.rs:11943 is declared `async fn` and is polled on the multi-thread Tokio runtime built at lib.rs:2311 (`build_runtime(...).block_on(run_async_main_inner(...))`; `Review` is absent from `diagnostic_worker_count`, so it uses the default one-worker-per-CPU pool). At :11963 it calls `run_gh_pr_view` synchronously; that wrapper (lib.rs:12949) calls `review_pr::fetch_view`, which reaches `run_command` (review_pr.rs:458) and blocks on `child.wait_timeout(Duration::from_secs(60))` (review_pr.rs:487) with no `spawn_blocking`.

**Impact:** On `codewhale review --pr`, one Tokio worker is blocked for up to 60 seconds per `gh` call plus the full `git diff` / `git log` duration. Concurrent tasks scheduled on that worker (engine supervision, telemetry/plugin tasks already spawned by `run_async_main_inner`) are delayed, and cancellation/timeout responsiveness degrades.

**Fix:** In `run_review`, offload the three sync groups before the async loop: `let pr_view = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || run_gh_pr_view(number, repo)).await...?;`, `let diff = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || collect_diff(...)).await...?;`, and likewise for `collect_base_commit_messages`. Keep `GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS`/`GH_PROMPT_DISABLED` env scoping and the 60s child timeout inside the offloaded closure.

### R18-L12-01 — desktop shell name literal never matches image name

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/tui/window_control.rs:306`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** On Windows, when the parent-chain fallback resolves the host window, every ancestor process name is passed to is_desktop_shell; an ancestor whose image name is ShellExperienceHost.exe is not recognised as desktop shell chrome because the literal contains spaces.

**Mechanism:** process_entry reads the image name from PROCESSENTRY32W.szExeFile via String::from_utf16_lossy (:327-332), which yields the on-disk file name — for this Windows component "ShellExperienceHost.exe". is_desktop_shell lowercases it to "shellexperiencehost.exe" but compares against the literal "shell experience host.exe", which contains spaces.

**Impact:** On Windows the ancestor-window fallback (used in ConPTY hosts such as Windows Terminal / VS Code where GetConsoleWindow is skipped) evaluates ancestor processes to pick a pinnable window. Because the exclusion is dead, ShellExperienceHost would be treated as a candidate host and its visible top-level window could be resized / set topmost instead of being skipped.

**Fix:** Replace the literal "shell experience host.exe" with "shellexperiencehost.exe" (the lowercased image name) so the comparison can succeed. Prefer a small &[&str] table of excluded image names with a Windows-gated unit test feeding each name through is_desktop_shell.

### R18-L12-02 — hardcoded english jobs cancel status message

Severity: minor · Location: ``crates/tui/src/tui/ui.rs:1330`` · Upstream refs: none

**Trigger:** A user whose UI locale is not English opens the Tasks rail panel while live shell jobs are running and invokes the shortcut that prefills /jobs cancel-all; the status bar shows a fixed English sentence.

**Mechanism:** The function writes a fixed English sentence into `app.status_message`, the legacy status-bar sink. `App` carries `ui_locale` and this same unit routes other user-visible notices through the localization channel — window_control.rs:619-630 builds a toast with `app.tr(message)` and `codewhale_localization::MessageId`.

**Impact:** Minor locale drift: a non-English-locale user sees one untranslated status-bar sentence at the moment they are about to cancel all running commands. The prefilled command `/jobs cancel-all` is locale-neutral and Enter still submits, so there is no wrong action or data loss; the effect is an inconsistent English sentence inside an otherwise localized surface, contrary to the TUI contract.

**Fix:** Add a `MessageId` variant for "Press Enter to cancel all running commands", translate it into every shipped locale pack, and write `app.status_message = Some(app.tr(MessageId::<new>).into_owned())`. Better, follow the AGENTS.md toast rule and use `app.push_status_toast(app.tr(MessageId::<new>), StatusToastLevel::Info, ...)` instead of a new legacy-sink write.
