issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A warm bounded session read can lose the last inference model after an automation result or delivery mirror is appended, while a cold read of the same transcript retains it.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Seed a session with a real inference model change or assistant reply.
2. Read the bounded model context to warm the navigation cache.
3. Append a replayable automation result or delivery mirror, then enough ordinary entries to trim the earlier inference entry from the selectable window.
4. Compare the warm read with a cold read of the same saved transcript.

### Expected behavior

Warm and cold bounded reads retain the same real provider and model metadata. Automation and delivery entries remain in the transcript without becoming the inference model.

### Actual behavior

The cold projection retains `openai/synthetic-model`, but the warmed navigation path can omit that model after the artifact is appended. The artifact text remains present; the model identity is the part that differs.

### OpenClaw version

Source checkout `ab2da2bfe8c447acc8ec089ba3debcd1caffbcbc`

### Operating system

macOS arm64, Darwin 27.2.0

### Install method

Source checkout with an isolated in-memory SQLite fixture and the repository Vitest worker. No running Gateway was used.

### Model

`openai/synthetic-model` in a synthetic transcript fixture. No external model was called.

### Provider / routing chain

No external provider. The reproduction uses the real session navigation and projection modules over isolated SQLite rows.

### Logs

The independent owning-layer reproduction on the unmodified source:

```text
✖ seeding a bounded navigation snapshot keeps the inference state beside legacy artifacts
✖ append deltas cannot replace warmed inference state with an artifact
✖ a delivery mirror cannot erase the model supplied by an older inference reply
✔ a later actual model change still wins in a warm append
✔ a committed leaf switch reseeds the real ancestry before taking another warm read

tests 5
pass 2
fail 3
```

A regression added to the existing `session-model-context-compacted.test.ts` matrix also fails before the production repair:

```text
Test Files  1 failed (1)
Tests       1 failed | 15 passed (16)
```

### Impact and severity

Affected: bounded session context reads after replayable OpenClaw-authored artifacts.

Severity: incorrect model metadata in the reconstructed context. The reproduction does not show message loss or an external provider failure.

Frequency: edge case requiring a warmed bounded read and trimming of the earlier inference entry.

### Additional information

The cold projection already excludes transcript artifacts from model identity. The navigation cache used different predicates when seeding and advancing its cached model state. This report covers that warm/cold boundary only, not automation job/run provenance or session selection-source reporting.

issues.body:
A second OpenClaw installation that shares another installation's state directory can still take over its release slot through the local preparation paths, before any slot exists.

**Observed** (isolated npm installs on macOS, #203504 head 69f71652ac): installation A is installed and serving; installation C is the same build in another npm prefix with the same `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, config and port. From C, `openclaw update --tag <B> --yes --json`:

- `--tag` prepares locally and then sends `gateway.restart.request` (no `update.run`), so the Gateway's installation check never runs.
- `checkUpdateInstallationSlot` (`src/update/installation-identity.ts`) returns early because `<state>/git-install/openclaw` does not exist yet before the first conversion.
- C's preparation creates the slot pointing at C and writes C's launcher marker; A's Gateway restarts into C's release. Run `1eadd416` (trigger `cli`).

`--no-restart` from C has the same gap before the first conversion. Once a slot exists, both local paths refuse; the `update.run` path refuses through admission (#203504).

**Expected:** before local preparation, a CLI whose local Gateway serves another installation refuses with that installation's update command, as `update.run` does.

**Direction:** the local paths can ask the running local Gateway which installation it serves (its update status already reports the root) and compare identities with the same `updateInstallationMismatch` before preparing. No new state.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On Windows 10, openclaw 2026.11.5 aborts every config read with EACCES because the SQLite read-only worker cannot create its private snapshot staging directory, while 2026.9.5 on the same host with the same config and state DB exits 0.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install 2026.11.5 into an isolated prefix: `npm install --prefix <dir> openclaw@2026.11.5`.
2. Redirect HOME, USERPROFILE, LOCALAPPDATA, APPDATA and XDG_CACHE_HOME to an isolated tree.
3. Put a working 2026.9.5 `openclaw.json` at `<HOME>\.openclaw\openclaw.json`.
4. Put the 2026.9.5 state DB (`user_version=17`, 13,135,872 B) at `<HOME>\.openclaw\state\openclaw.sqlite`.
5. Run `<prefix>\node_modules\.bin\openclaw.cmd config validate` -> exit code 1 with the error below.
6. Remove the state DB and rerun -> exit code 0 (only `Unrecognized key: agents.defaults.heartbeat` warnings), so the state DB alone flips the result.

```
Config needs correction: ~\.openclaw\openclaw.json
  - <root>: read failed at <HOME>\.openclaw\openclaw.json: Error: filesystem did not
    enforce the private directory DACL; snapshot staging root <XDG_CACHE_HOME>\openclaw:
    check filesystem health and write permissions or set XDG_CACHE_HOME to a writable
    filesystem
Resolve the read error shown above, then retry.
```

### Expected behavior

`openclaw config validate` should read the existing config and report it as valid, as 2026.9.5 does on this host:

```
Config valid: ~\.openclaw\openclaw.json
(exit 0)
```

Same host, same `openclaw.json`, same state DB (`user_version=17`, 13,135,872 B), only the package version differs.

### Actual behavior

`config validate` exits 1 and never reaches the config content:

```
Error: filesystem did not enforce the private directory DACL; snapshot staging root
<XDG_CACHE_HOME>\openclaw: check filesystem health and write permissions or set
XDG_CACHE_HOME to a writable filesystem
```

`OPENCLAW_FS_SAFE_NATIVE_MODE=off` changes the wording, not the outcome (exit 1):

```
Error: private object security was not enforced; snapshot staging root <XDG_CACHE_HOME>\openclaw ...
[FS_SAFE_NATIVE_FALLBACK] FsSafeWarning: windows-private-directory is using its portable fallback
because native support is disabled by OPENCLAW_FS_SAFE_NATIVE_MODE (disabled).
Expected @openclaw/fs-safe-win32-x64-msvc@0.26.13. ...
```

Measured rule-outs on the failing host:

| Hypothesis | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Missing native module | files present under `<prefix>/node_modules/@openclaw/fs-safe-win32-x64-msvc` | still fails |
| Volume / filesystem | XDG_CACHE_HOME on C: and on D:, both NTFS | both fail |
| Loose inherited DACL | `icacls <root> /inheritance:r /grant SYSTEM:F Administrators:F <currentUser>:F` (SDDL becomes `O:...D:PAI(A;OICI;FA;;;SY)(A;OICI;FA;;;BA)(A;OICI;FA;;;LA)`) | still fails |
| Owner is a group, not the user | `icacls <root> /setowner <userSID>` + `Set-Acl` owner = user SID | still fails |
| Mode switch | `OPENCLAW_FS_SAFE_NATIVE_MODE=off` / `auto` | both fail, same exit code 1 |

Additional observations:
- After every failed run the staging root stays empty - no child directory is left behind, so creation aborts during its own verification step.
- The error string does not appear in `dist/*.mjs`; it is raised inside `@openclaw/fs-safe-win32-x64-msvc`.
- Hypothesis (not confirmed): on this machine the policy "System objects: Default owner for objects created by members of the Administrators group" is set to Administrators, so directories are owned by `BUILTIN\Administrators` unless ownership is set explicitly. If the fs-safe private-directory check requires owner == current user without SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege/SeRestorePrivilege, it cannot pass on this host.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.5 (npm @openclaw/openclaw 2026.11.5; regression vs 2026.9.5)

### Operating system

Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 10.0.19045, C: and D: both NTFS

### Install method

npm install --prefix <isolated dir> openclaw@2026.11.5, isolated HOME/USERPROFILE/LOCALAPPDATA/APPDATA/XDG_CACHE_HOME

### Model

N/A - config validate fails before any model is loaded

### Provider / routing chain

N/A - no gateway/provider in the path; failure occurs in local fs-safe private directory creation

### Additional provider/model setup details

None. This is not a provider/model issue. Native packages `@openclaw/fs-safe-win32-x64-msvc` and `@openclaw/proc-safe-win32-x64-msvc` are present; no gateway or provider is started by `config validate`.

### Logs

```shell
Version comparison on the same host, same config, same state DB:
- 2026.9.5 `config validate` -> `Config valid: ~\.openclaw\openclaw.json`, exit 0.
- 2026.11.5 `config validate` -> error above, exit 1.
- 2026.11.5 without the state DB -> exit 0.

Failure output (verbatim, 2026-11-18 23:12 local):

Config needs correction: ~\.openclaw\openclaw.json
  - <root>: read failed at <HOME>\.openclaw\openclaw.json: Error: filesystem did not
    enforce the private directory DACL; snapshot staging root <XDG_CACHE_HOME>\openclaw:
    check filesystem health and write permissions or set XDG_CACHE_HOME to a writable
    filesystem
Resolve the read error shown above, then retry.

`OPENCLAW_FS_SAFE_NATIVE_MODE=off` variant:

Error: private object security was not enforced; snapshot staging root <XDG_CACHE_HOME>\openclaw ...
[FS_SAFE_NATIVE_FALLBACK] FsSafeWarning: windows-private-directory is using its portable fallback
because native support is disabled by OPENCLAW_FS_SAFE_NATIVE_MODE (disabled).
Expected @openclaw/fs-safe-win32-x64-msvc@0.26.13. ... Private Windows directory creation launches
the packaged .NET helper for each check or creation.
(exit 1)

Staging root DACL before / after hardening (both still fail):

before: O:LAG:S-1-5-21-<...>-513D:(A;ID;FA;;;BA)(A;OICIIOID;GA;;;BA)(A;ID;FA;;;SY)(A;OICIIOID;GA;;;SY)(A;ID;0x1301bf;;;AU)...
after : O:LAG:S-1-5-21-<...>-513D:PAI(A;OICI;FA;;;SY)(A;OICI;FA;;;BA)(A;OICI;FA;;;LA)

Host: Windows 10 Pro 10.0.19045, node v24.21.0, npm 11.19.0, elevated Administrator.
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

- Affected: Windows hosts running 2026.11.x where objects created by Administrators are owned by `BUILTIN\Administrators` by default; observed on 1 host.
- Severity: blocks workflow.
- Frequency: always (every config-reading command fails while a state DB exists).
- Consequence: the 2026.9.5 -> 11.x upgrade cannot complete, because the first post-install `config validate` fails and the schema/state migration is never reached. Production stays on 2026.9.5.

### Additional information

- Regression bounds: last known good 2026.9.5, first known bad 2026.11.5 (both measured on this host).
- Non-blocking secondary finding: in 11.x `agents.defaults.heartbeat` is reported as `Unrecognized key` during validate (exit 0); 2026.9.5 accepts it.
- Related: #180892 (Windows Doctor rejects native capture for DELETE-self permission on a volume-root ancestor - same fs-safe Windows private-directory family, different check), #156985 (Kubernetes /tmp emptyDir lacks sticky protection required by fs-safe).
- Duplicate search on 2026-11-19: no existing issue matches this error text; `"private object security was not enforced"` returns 0 results.

issues.body:
We are seeing Node commands finish locally during a short connection outage while the Gateway has already settled the original invocation as disconnected. When the same Host reconnects and sends the result, it is ignored. The agent then has an uncertain outcome despite the side effects having occurred. Improving connection stability will help, but this failure can happen with any transport interruption.

I propose a negotiated extension that lets the original invocation retain its result owner briefly and attach to a freshly authenticated connection. The stale-socket protection in #78351 should remain: an old connection cannot clear replacement presence or complete replacement work. The new path would explicitly authorize recovery of one existing operation.

The essential checks would be:

- Match the authenticated device key, owner/profile scope and current persisted pairing generation, plus an opaque per-invocation resume token delivered on the original connection.
- Bind recovery to the original operation identity and immutable command/approval/audience fingerprint. A tool call can contain multiple operations, so each effect needs its own stable key.
- Atomically attach the operation to the new connection and fence the old attachment. Recheck current policy, cancellation and the existing completion/lifecycle owner before accepting output.
- Keep the original work deadline and consumed approval unchanged. Admit a separate fixed reporting budget at the start of the call; reconnect never grants more execution time or revives released authority. Increasing the existing invoke timeout alone would also increase the work budget forwarded to the Host.
- Acknowledge result acceptance explicitly, with an authenticated bounded terminal receipt for retries after the original waiter has settled. A successful transport RPC carrying `ignored` must not mean that the operation result reached its owner.

Current code distinguishes borrowed request continuation, approval-record retention and completion custody. The public invoke API has dispatch checks, while internal cleanup has its own completion callback. The first slice therefore needs an explicit original-caller completion handle at public admission, checked on attachment and first result commit. It also needs detached pairing/committed-policy validation: an absent Node must not be mistaken for revoked policy. Existing admission and pairing owners should retain those responsibilities; a reconnect must not re-admit a distinct operator continuation.

The smallest first slice would recover completed results without resending commands. That addresses the lost-answer path while avoiding execution replay. Safe redispatch can follow only with a Host ledger that records the operation before starting it, rejects a key/payload conflict and retains replay protection for the full recovery window. Host process loss or an expired grant yields an honest unknown outcome. We would promise at-most-once start within that process-lifetime contract and once-only terminal settlement; arbitrary external side effects across process crashes cannot be universally exactly once.

A three-minute maximum is the proposed first-version recovery/reporting grace, bounded by caller authority and reserved capacity, and subject to load qualification. Use a specific `invoke.resume.result.v1` capability with affirmative per-client selection and per-invocation opt-in. It would initially cover positively bounded direct `system.run` calls without input, stream-output consumers or pending interaction. Ledger-capable redispatch and duplex recovery would have separate feature contracts. Older peers would retain current behavior. Gateway process restart recovery is a separate problem.

I would like owner review of the explicit public completion handle, detached revocation contract and result-only negotiation before implementation. The design selects these semantics; source inspection is not implementation proof or security acceptance. The first fault-injection test should drop the socket immediately before completion, reconnect the same paired Host and prove one local execution plus delivery to the original waiting call. The same suite should include wrong-device/token rejection, unpair/re-pair, stale close/result races, caller/approval cancellation, temporary pairing-store unavailability, deadline expiry and an acknowledgement lost after the waiter has settled.

Who would be the right current Node/Gateway and approval-lifecycle reviewers for this extension? I can bring the client-side owner into the protocol review and prepare the narrow implementation against the agreed contract.

issues.body:
### Summary

Let the embedding cache lookup fall back to the vectors already stored in the published `memory_index_chunks`, so memory-core can stop retaining a second Float64 copy of each published chunk vector in `memory_embedding_cache`.

### Problem to solve

memory-core stores each chunk vector three times in the agent database:

| copy | table | encoding | bytes per 4096-dim vector |
|---|---|---|---:|
| canonical | `memory_index_chunks.embedding` | Float64LE BLOB | 32,768 |
| cache | `memory_embedding_cache.embedding` | Float64LE BLOB | 32,768 |
| search | `memory_index_chunks_vec` (vec0) | float32 | 16,384 |

The canonical column and vec0 are settled: the #153618 design record keeps Float64 BLOBs for "Memory chunks and embedding caches". This request leaves both untouched. It is about the cache copy. #131085 asked only for the canonical column's encoding ("Store `memory_index_chunks.embedding` as a **float32 BLOB**") and scoped the cache copy out as "a separate, larger win", so its resolution did not rule on the cache copy.

For memory files, the cache is the only place indexing looks for a reusable vector. A memory-file publication clears the file's chunk rows (`manager-source-index-kernel.ts:136-138`), and every chunk is resolved through the cache read, which selects only from `memory_embedding_cache` by `(provider, model, provider_key, hash)` and embeds every miss; for memory files it never consults `memory_index_chunks`. Session transcripts differ on main: since #103201 (merged 2026-10-10), a session delta keeps unchanged chunk rows in place by row id (`retainIndexedSessionChunks`, `manager-session-delta.ts:34-74`; `MemorySourceIndexKernel.replaceRows`, `manager-source-index-kernel.ts:129-183`). That stops unchanged session chunks from passing through the cache, but each newly embedded session chunk still writes a cache row that its published chunk row then duplicates. To avoid re-embedding unchanged chunks when a memory file is edited, the cache keeps its own copy of every published vector, and those copies count against the 50,000-row cap from #131121.

The two copies are not always bit-identical, because some providers are not bit-deterministic. On the store below, 35,529 of 35,702 chunk/cache pairs that share a hash are byte-identical. The other 173 (all `source = memory`) differ by at most 2.65e-4 per coordinate, with cosine similarity at least 0.999996. Within `memory_index_chunks`, 1,093 hashes appear on more than one chunk row; 105 of those carry more than one distinct vector, and these 105 are exactly the hashes where a cache row differs from some chunk row. Where all chunk rows of a hash agree, the cache row equals them in every case (31,713 of 31,713), and in all 105 disagreeing hashes the cache row equals one of the chunk variants. Any of these vectors is a valid embedding of its text; the proposal below never chooses between disagreeing vectors.

Measured on one agent database (`openai-compatible` provider, `text-embedding-q8_0`, 4096 dims, OpenClaw 2026.9.9, which predates #103201; 2026-10-10 17:29 -0700):

| measure | memory | sessions | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `memory_index_chunks` rows | 35,290 | 7,418 | 42,708 |
| distinct chunk hashes | 30,913 | 7,348 | 38,261 |
| cache rows whose hash a live chunk carries (live duplicates) | 28,982 | 2,836 | 31,818 |
| chunk/cache pairs sharing a hash | 32,825 | 2,877 | 35,702 |
| pairs byte-identical | 32,652 | 2,877 | 35,529 |
| pairs differing (max 2.65e-4 per coordinate, cosine at least 0.999996) | 173 | 0 | 173 |
| live duplicates equal to every chunk row carrying their hash | 28,877 | 2,836 | 31,713 |

No hash is carried by both sources, so memory files hold 91% of the live duplicates (28,982 of 31,818).

| measure | value |
|---|---:|
| agent database file | 4,543,901,696 B |
| freelist pages | 0 |
| `memory_embedding_cache` rows (at the cap) | 50,000 |
| cache rows no live chunk carries | 18,182 |
| `dbstat` bytes, `memory_embedding_cache` | 1,664,331,776 |
| `dbstat` bytes, `sqlite_autoindex_memory_embedding_cache_1` | 11,018,240 |
| `dbstat` bytes, `idx_memory_embedding_cache_updated_at` | 847,872 |
| `dbstat` bytes, `memory_index_chunks` | 1,487,114,240 |
| `dbstat` bytes, `memory_index_chunks_vec_vector_chunks00` | 1,145,348,096 |

The cache holds a single identity, `openai-compatible | text-embedding-q8_0 | 0a91e96d..b8e6` with 50,000 rows, equal to the provider, model and providerKey recorded in `memory_index_meta_v1`, and every chunk row has `model = text-embedding-q8_0`. A join on hash alone and a join on the full identity both return 31,818 rows, so the hash-only counts above are full-identity counts on this store.

Pro rata at 33,286.6 B of table pages per cache row (1,664,331,776 / 50,000), the 31,818 live duplicates occupy 1,059,114,169 B, 23.3% of the file, plus 7,551,119 B of the two cache indexes (11,866,112 B together). The 18,182 rows no live chunk carries occupy 605,217,607 B; that part is #164792's scope.

Most live duplicates were written in the 2026-10-06 and 2026-10-07 spikes (23,641 of 31,818), and ordinary syncs keep adding more:

| local day the cache row was written | rows written | still live duplicates |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2026-10-05 | 2,559 | 2,543 |
| 2026-10-06 | 20,112 | 13,399 |
| 2026-10-07 | 14,870 | 10,242 |
| 2026-10-08 | 3,589 | 398 |
| 2026-10-09 | 4,137 | 801 |
| 2026-10-10 (to 17:29) | 4,733 | 4,435 |

Of the rows written today, 4,435 of 4,733 (94%) are already duplicates of a published chunk. Rows written two days earlier mostly are not (398 of 3,589), because the chunks they were written for have since been replaced; those rows now sit in the cache as vectors of text that left the index.

The existing cleanup does not touch live duplicates. At the cap, rows are evicted on insert: the upsert reserves capacity before writing ("Reserve space before inserting vectors so even a transient overflow is impossible") and deletes as many of the oldest rows by `updated_at` as the batch needs, with no 100-row limit (`manager-embedding-cache.ts:174-193`; at bcfc888 `reserveMemoryEmbeddingCacheCapacity`, called from the upsert at `manager-embedding-cache.ts:173-181`). The prune is the backstop. On main, `pruneEmbeddingCacheIfNeeded` runs in the `finally` of every ordinary (non-full) sync, including no-op exits (`manager-sync-ops.ts:399-405`; commit bcfc888 `:392-398`), and after a successful full-rebuild publication (`:663`; bcfc888 `:620`). Both only enforce the row cap: the oldest rows by `updated_at` are deleted, at most 100 per call (`manager-embedding-cache.ts:102-128`; at bcfc888 the same oldest-first loop is `manager-embedding-ops.ts:355-380`, which produced this store). The post-publication call carries the comment "Cache-only rebuilds bypass insertion-time eviction; prune the canonical cache only after successful publication so failed rebuilds retain their work" (`manager-sync-ops.ts:661-662`). With the cache at the cap, about 4,700 writes a day evict about as many of the oldest rows through the reservation, whatever those rows hold.

### Proposed solution

A ladder, smallest step first. Step 1 is the request. Step 2 is deferred to the cache-budget decision on #114612.

**Step 1 (requested): read-through, and no new duplicates. No existing row is deleted.**

1a. Read-through. When the cache lookup leaves hashes unresolved, resolve them from the published database's `memory_index_chunks`, in the worker that serves the cache read today (`manager-publication.worker.ts:221-222` on main, `cache.read` calling `loadMemoryEmbeddingCache`; at commit bcfc888 the read is in-process, `manager-embedding-ops.ts:491`). Two scopes are possible, and the maintainer choice between them is part of the request:

| | 1a-scoped | 1a-global |
|---|---|---|
| lookup | hash, restricted to chunk rows of the same `(path, source)` being reindexed | hash, any chunk row |
| index | existing `idx_memory_index_chunks_path_source` | new `memory_index_chunks(hash)`, about 3.25 MB here (Additional information) |
| schema change | none | index only, no schema-version bump |
| precedent | extends #103201's per-source retention to memory files, by hash instead of row id | none |
| misses that 1a-global would serve | text copied or moved to another file; 992 of the 1,093 multi-row hashes here span more than one path | none |

Row id is not enough for memory files: a memory-file row id hashes `source:path:startLine:endLine:hash:model` (`manager-source-index-kernel.ts:80-82`; bcfc888 `:79-80`), so any edit above a chunk shifts its lines and changes its id. Only a hash lookup survives that edit, which is the common case the cache serves today.

The fallback, in either scope, runs only when all of these hold, and otherwise leaves the hash unresolved, so the existing path embeds it:

- `memory_index_meta_v1` records a `providerKey`. The field is optional (`MemoryIndexMeta.providerKey?: string`, `manager-reindex-state.ts:20`; bcfc888 `:19`), and identity validation skips it when `providerKeyKnown === false` (`:188-193`; bcfc888 `:182-187`). A meta without it is refused, never treated as a match.
- One of the requested identities equals `(meta.provider, meta.model, meta.providerKey)`. The requested list is the primary identity plus provider aliases from `resolveMemoryIndexProviderIdentities` (`manager-reindex-state.ts:40-73`; bcfc888 `:38-67`), passed as `providerIdentities` (`manager-embedding-cache-ops.ts:83`). Any entry may match, not only the first.
- The chunk row's `model` equals that identity's model, and `length(embedding)` equals `meta.vectorDims * 8`. `memory_index_chunks` has no `dims` column, so `meta.vectorDims` takes the place of the cache's `dims = length(embedding)/8` check (`manager-embedding-cache.ts:69-70`; bcfc888 `:71-72`).
- Tie-break: every chunk row carrying the hash within the lookup scope holds the same bytes (`count(distinct embedding) = 1`). When they disagree, the chunk table answers nothing for that hash; an existing cache row answers it, otherwise it is embedded again. The cache is read first, so a cache row always takes precedence, as today. On this store 105 hashes fall back under this rule.

Today the cache read runs only when the cache is enabled (`manager-embedding-cache-ops.ts:78-89`). The read-through should run whether or not `cache.enabled` is set: it reads only published rows and writes nothing, and #103201 already retains unchanged session rows "including when caching is disabled". An operator who disables the cache then still avoids re-embedding the unchanged chunks of an edited memory file.

1b. No new duplicates, after publication. Once a publication has committed, delete the cache rows that this sync generation itself wrote (identified by key and an `updated_at` at or after the generation start, through the existing `idx_memory_embedding_cache_updated_at`) whose bytes the published chunk rows within the 1a scope all hold exactly, under the generation's identity. It runs where the cap prune runs today, as a new worker command beside `cache.prune` (`manager-publication.worker.ts:262-270`), in transactions of at most 256 rows with a yield between them, the batch shape #164792 uses: in the ordinary-sync `finally` (`manager-sync-ops.ts:403`; bcfc888 `:396`) and after a successful full-rebuild `database.publish` (`manager-sync-ops.ts:663`, whose comment reads "prune the canonical cache only after successful publication so failed rebuilds retain their work"; bcfc888 `:620`). It follows the prune's gate (`manager-embedding-cache-ops.ts:45`), so a disabled cache keeps its rows as today.

1b adds no work to any publication transaction. That matters for full rebuilds: `publishMemoryDatabaseTables` already copies sources, chunks, recall metadata and provenance and rebuilds FTS and vec0 inside one `runSqliteImmediateTransactionSync` (`manager-db-kernel.ts:88-175`; bcfc888 `:108`), and #143640 (open, P1) reports that this transaction already reaches the 5 s busy timeout of concurrent agent writes: its body measures a 5.41 s publication of about 650 MB, at the edge of the budget (the concurrent writer succeeded after waiting 4.38 s), and records 18 overnight `step = begin` failures; its comments report 21 s and 44 s publications with concurrent writes failing. Inside that lock, 1b would have compared up to 1,253,736,448 B of cache blobs on a model-switch rebuild of this store.

The failed-run guarantee still holds without atomicity. Cache writes before publication are unchanged: `persistGeneratedEmbeddings` still stores each successful batch before index insertion (`manager-embedding-cache-ops.ts:190`, called from `manager-embedding-ops.ts:255` and `:343` on main; bcfc888 `upsertMemoryEmbeddingCache` at `manager-embedding-ops.ts:726`). A run that fails before publication never reaches 1b for a full rebuild, and on an ordinary sync 1b can delete only rows whose exact bytes are already published, so no unpublished vector is lost either way. A run interrupted between publication and 1b leaves harmless duplicates that step 2 or FIFO eviction later removes. Rows written before the generation started are left alone, and nothing is deleted when `providerKey` is missing. Concurrent writers (a second process, or another sync in the same one) are covered by the same byte check: a row another writer upserted with different bytes fails it and is kept, and a row with identical bytes stays resolvable through 1a.

**Step 2 (deferred to #114612): remove existing duplicates.** Delete cache rows that pass the same identity gate and whose bytes the published chunk rows within the 1a scope all hold exactly, at the same two sites and through the same worker command and batch shape as 1b, under the same `cache.enabled` gate. One sync drains the whole backlog in a loop, as `pruneEmbeddingCacheIfNeeded` does today (`manager-embedding-cache-ops.ts:54-56`). The pass is skipped when the index revision (`memory_index_state.revision`) and the cache row count are unchanged since its last pass in the process. Because ordinary syncs run it, step 2 does not wait for a full reindex and does not use #164792's collection point. It frees bytes at the cap, which is the question #114612 has open, so it should follow that decision rather than precede it.

Write-path cost on this store:

| work | runs | rows | cache bytes compared | transactions of at most 256 rows |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1b, ordinary sync | after its publications, in the sync's `finally` | rows that sync wrote; 4,733 on 2026-10-10 across all syncs; at most 678 for one memory file, 546 for one session | 32,768 per row | 1 to 3 per busy file |
| 1b, same-identity full rebuild | after `database.publish` | upper bound (today's misses): 7,006 here; under 1a these are read-through hits, so close to 0 | up to 229,572,608 | up to 28 |
| 1b, model-switch full rebuild | after `database.publish` | up to 38,261 | 1,253,736,448 | 150 |
| 1b inside any publication transaction | never | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| step 2, first ordinary sync after upgrade | in the sync's `finally`, one loop | 31,713 deleted | 1,039,171,584 | 124 |
| step 2, sync with no index or cache change | skipped | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| step 2, any other sync | candidate scan, then guard on the candidates | 50,000 scanned | candidates only | as needed |

Each compared cache row is read against its chunk rows, so chunk bytes are read in about the same amount again. For scale, without any hash index: the set-based hash-only candidate join over all 50,000 cache rows returned 31,818 candidates in 0.12 s, and the same join with the byte guard, which reads every candidate's blob on both sides, returned 31,713 in 7.23 s.

Effect on the store above:

| | step 1 | steps 1 and 2 |
|---|---:|---:|
| existing cache rows removed | 0 | 31,713 |
| table bytes freed (pro rata) | 0 | 1,055,619,072 |
| cache index bytes freed (pro rata) | 0 | 7,526,200 |
| cache writes retained per day (2026-10-10 rate) | about 298 of 4,733 | about 298 of 4,733 |
| oldest rows evicted per day at the cap | about 298 | 0 until the cache refills |

The 298 per day is a steady-state average, not a per-sync figure: the capacity reservation runs before 1b, so a sync with no headroom still evicts old rows before 1b deletes its new duplicates, and the headroom each 1b pass leaves absorbs the next sync's reservation.

Step 1 frees no space on a cache that is already at the cap. It stops 94% of new writes from being retained, so eviction slows from about 4,700 to about 298 rows per day and rows the index does not hold stay resident far longer. On caches below the cap it cuts growth by the same share. Step 2 frees about 1.06 GB here. Without step 2 the existing 31,713 rows leave only through FIFO eviction. Logical rows shrink immediately; the file shrinks only through the existing reclamation or Doctor `compact`, the same caveat #164792 documents.

With steps 1 and 2 in place, the cache stops being a store of every vector ever computed and holds only vectors that are not in the published index: batches from runs that have not published (pending or failed), rows of other provider identities, vectors whose bytes differ from the published chunk, and rows of text that has since left the index. Under step 1 alone this holds only for vectors first written after step 1: a cache hit writes nothing (`loadMemoryEmbeddingCache` is read-only and the upsert runs only for misses), so an older row that a sync hits and republishes stays as a duplicate that 1b never sees.

What is kept, what is lost, and what it costs:

| same-identity full rebuild with unchanged chunking | re-embeds the 7,006 chunk rows without a cache row | the rebuild reads the published database, so those chunks are read-through hits | same as global | same as global | today 7,006; step 1 about 0 |
| text copied or moved to another file (992 hashes span more than one path here) | cache hit while the row survives FIFO | read-through hit | miss once 1b or step 2 has removed the row | as the chosen step 1 scope | scoped: 1 per new copy; global: 0 |
| run fails or is interrupted before publication | every successful batch kept | kept: 1b runs only after publication and removes only published bytes | kept | kept | 0 |
| interrupted between publication and 1b | n/a | duplicates stay | duplicates stay | removed by the next pass | 0 |

The largest loss is the switch-back case on corpora well under the cap, where today's cache makes A to B to A free. ClawSweeper's review on #114612 says a cache budget "must preserve useful retry embeddings and account for re-embedding cost". Step 1 keeps retry reuse intact (third row) and spends the cap on vectors the index does not hold, so a cache at the cap keeps rows of replaced text longer than it does today. Its cost falls on the reverted-text, switch-back and downgrade rows, all for vectors that were published and then left the index, plus the cross-file row for the scoped variant.

### Alternatives considered

- Disable the cache (`memory.search.cache.enabled: false`). This is the existing operator workaround, and it frees nothing already written. On #114612, ctbritt first listed it as "~600 MB" of a 1,904 MB to 541 MB reduction made together with two other changes and a rebuild, on a pre-cap build with decimal-JSON vectors, and later retracted that on the same thread: "Setting `cache.enabled: false` does **not** help", because "a disabled cache never evicts what it already wrote". The space had come back because, on that build, "a full reindex clears the table (`manager-db.ts:225`)". On main a full rebuild keeps the cache, and both cleanups skip a disabled cache: the prune returns early (`manager-embedding-cache-ops.ts:45`), and so does #164792's collection (`collectOrphanedEmbeddingCache`, `manager-embedding-cache-ops.ts:73-75` at its head 03a9eb0c0a58; its contract row reads "Cache disabled | no collection"). Disabling the cache therefore stops new writes but frees none of the rows already written. Its cost is that every chunk of an edited memory file is re-embedded and all retry reuse is lost, since the cache read runs only when the cache is enabled (`manager-embedding-cache-ops.ts:78-89`). With 1a running regardless of `cache.enabled`, disabling the cache would keep unchanged-chunk reuse and lose only retry reuse.
- Byte-aware cache budget. This is the open maintainer-decision question on #114612: "Stage cache budgeting before age retention: First define a bounded cache budget that preserves retry reuse". It competes with step 2 for the same decision, and the two compose: a byte budget bounds the cost (at 4096 dims a 50,000-row cache is 1.66 GB, at 384 dims about 0.16 GB), while step 1 stops spending that budget on vectors `memory_index_chunks` already returns. Either can land first.
- Retain unchanged memory-file rows by row id, as #103201 does for sessions. Memory-file ids include `startLine` and `endLine` (`manager-source-index-kernel.ts:80-82`), so any edit above a chunk changes its id and the row is not retained; it also leaves the cache copy in place. 1a-scoped is the hash-keyed form of the same move.
- Demote on removal. When publication removes a chunk row, write its vector back into the cache under the published identity. This keeps today's reuse for reverted edits and makes A to B to A cheaper than today, at the price of one cache write per removed chunk row, up to the whole index inside a full-rebuild publication, which #143640 already finds too long.
- Evict live duplicates first. Keep the row cap and make eviction prefer rows the read-through can serve. It deletes nothing beyond what the cap already deletes and frees no bytes at the cap, but keeps more useful rows.
- Opt-in lossy cache encoding (float32 or int8 for cache rows only). Halves or quarters the cache, keeps two copies, and adds a precision question to a table #153618 keeps lossless. For this provider float32 would in fact be exact: 0 of 174,931,968 chunk coordinates and 0 of 204,800,000 cache coordinates change on a Float64 to float32 round trip. A conditional encoding is a separate idea and is not requested here.
- Skip the cache write when the vector is already in vec0. vec0 stores float32, so in general it cannot return the Float64 value the provider produced; `memory_index_chunks` can.

### Impact

Affected: every agent with memory search and the default cache enabled; the duplicate share grows with embedding width (32,768 B per row at 4096 dims, 12,288 B at 1536).
Severity: disk and write I/O, plus a row cap that evicts useful rows while duplicates hold 64% of it. The change trades this against re-embedding in the reverted-text, switch-back, downgrade and (scoped variant) cross-file cases above; with paid providers those re-embeds cost money. There is no functional failure.
Frequency: always. Every published chunk whose cache row has not been evicted has two Float64 copies (35,702 of 42,708 chunk rows here), and 94% of today's cache writes duplicate a published chunk. On main, #103201 reduces how often unchanged session chunks pass through the cache but leaves the copy written for each new chunk.
Consequence: on this store the agent database is 4.54 GB, of which 1.06 GB is cached copies of published vectors. Database size feeds the agent database read-only snapshot budget and update candidate validation time, as reported on #131085 and #114612.

- "which data is canonical, derived, reconstructible, retained, deleted, exported, or visible after restart": 1b and step 2 delete valid cache rows because the published chunk rows hold the same bytes, which makes `memory_index_chunks.embedding` the only retained copy of those vectors.
- "user-visible persistence semantics, including a second interpretation of existing durable data": `memory_index_chunks.embedding` becomes a reusable cache source in addition to the canonical index column.
- "upgrade, downgrade, rollback, retention, compaction, or corruption-recovery contracts": a build without the read-through finds fewer cache rows after a downgrade (table above), and 1b and step 2 change which valid cache rows are retained. The same page says "Changing which valid data is retained or deleted still needs acceptance."

Index owners (1a-global only). The chunk indexes are defined in three places, and the new index belongs in all three: the canonical agent schema (`src/state/openclaw-agent-schema.sql:871-875`), the memory-host SDK bootstrap (`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/memory-schema.ts:431-435`, run by the publication worker's `schema.admit` through `ensureMemoryIndexSchema`, `manager-publication.worker.ts:193-203`), and the storage-migration contract list (`memory-schema-storage-migration.ts:53-57`, `CHUNK_INDEXES`, passed as `allowedMissingIndexes` at `:136`) so legacy conversion accepts its absence. The direct precedent is the "Memory chunk path index retirement" entry in the same document, accepted on 2026-10-04: an index-only change on this table through the canonical schema and SDK bootstrap and, in its words, no "schema-version bump". This index needs no bump either. Its size, estimated by building it from this store's 42,708 hashes in a scratch database, is 3,190,784 B; the same build of the `id` index gives 3,588,096 B against the live 3,653,632 B, so the live hash index would be about 3.25 MB, close to the 3,059,712 B that the retired `idx_memory_index_chunks_path` still occupies on this 2026.9.9 store.

Update behavior. Upgrade needs no data conversion: with 1a-global the index is created, and existing rows stay under step 1. Step 2, if accepted, removes duplicates in bounded transactions on the first ordinary sync. Rollback opens the same tables: the schema contract rejects only unexpected unique indexes (`src/infra/sqlite-schema-contract.ts:151-157` at bcfc888; `:223-226` on main), so an older build accepts the extra non-unique index, and it re-embeds the chunks it no longer finds in the cache, at the cost in the downgrade rows above. No published vector, chunk text or provenance is deleted, and nothing is deleted when the identity gate cannot be evaluated.

Relation to #164792. Neither step uses #164792's collection point (after a successful full-reindex publication only; its contract lists "Incremental sync and other non-full paths | no collection"), though 1b borrows its batch shape ("in transactions of at most 256 rows through the existing publication worker"). The rows are disjoint: #164792 deletes rows no published chunk carries, while 1b and step 2 touch only rows the published chunks carry with identical bytes. With #164792 and steps 1 and 2 in place, a cache right after a full rebuild holds almost nothing: rows written after the rebuild started (which #164792 fences in), rows of other identities, and rows that differ from their chunk. With step 1 alone, rows that the rebuild hit and republished stay as duplicates.

Not a duplicate.

- PR #103201 (merged 2026-10-10) is the closest prior art: maintainers accepted reusing published chunk rows instead of re-embedding, for session deltas, keyed by row id within one source. This request extends the idea to memory files, keyed by hash because memory-file row ids change with line positions, and also stops retaining the cache copy, which #103201 does not touch. 1a-scoped is the direct extension.
- #131085 (closed completed 2026-10-07) is the origin of this request. Its requested change was the canonical column's encoding ("Store `memory_index_chunks.embedding` as a **float32 BLOB**"), and its body scoped the cache copy out: "Dropping the duplicate copy in `memory_embedding_cache` is a separate, larger win." It closed with #153683's encoding change as canonical, and its cluster lists no item for the cache copy. #156538's closing review lists #131085 as `partial_overlap` "with additional proposals about redundant vector copies". This issue is that remainder.
- #153618 (open design record, listed in #131085's closing review as the "Approved broader storage design") states "Memory chunks and embedding caches will store explicit little-endian Float64 BLOBs while preserving number-array provider/search interfaces and the canonical fallback independent of sqlite-vec." This request keeps both tables and that encoding; it changes which vectors the cache table retains.
- #114612 (open) is the canonical storage-policy issue. Its comments already record the triple storage (ctbritt: "The embedding is stored three times"; jzmudzinski: "with the vector held in the cache, in `memory_index_chunks` and in `vec0`"), and its maintainer-decision question is a byte-aware cache budget that preserves retry reuse. That question competes with step 2 (see Alternatives), which is why step 2 is deferred to it; #114612 does not propose resolving cache reads from the index. This issue can sit in the #114612 cluster as a separate decision.
- #143640 (open, P1) is about the length of the full-publication transaction. This request adds nothing to it: 1b and step 2 run after publication, in their own bounded transactions.
- #164792 (open PR) collects rows no published chunk carries; disjoint rows, see above.
- #131121 and #164083 (merged) own the row cap and its capacity reservation; the cap and eviction order are unchanged here.
- #95070 (closed by inactivity) proposed a float32 cache BLOB. #156538 (closed completed) counted duplicate cache rows by hash, which its review rejected without the full identity; the counts in this issue are shown equal under the full identity.

issues.body:
### Summary

Load the IP literal part of the `MEDIA:` remote host guard on demand, so the Control UI chat boot bundle no longer ships `ipaddr.js`.

### Problem to solve

Every cold load of the chat route downloads, parses and compiles `ipaddr.js` and `@openclaw/net-policy/ip` as part of the chat boot bundle, but first paint never uses them. They are only needed to classify an assistant `MEDIA:` line whose https host is an IP literal (for example `MEDIA:https://8.8.8.8/a.png`), which is rare in real transcripts. Hostname URLs never need the IP parser.

The import chain at `6e7ee204e1b1fef223c794dbbed42de069a2623e`:

- `ui/src/lib/chat/message-normalizer.ts:23` imports `splitMediaFromOutput` from `src/media/parse.ts`.
- `src/media/parse.ts:2` imports `splitMediaOutput` from `src/media/parse-output.ts`.
- `src/media/parse-output.ts:1-10` statically imports eight helpers from `@openclaw/net-policy/ip`, which wraps `ipaddr.js`. They are used only by `isBlockedRemoteMediaHostname` (`src/media/parse-output.ts:95-127`).
- `ui/config/control-ui-boot-modules.json` lists `node_modules/ipaddr.js/lib/ipaddr.js` and `packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts` in the chat boot set.

The chat boot bundle is also close to its gzip budget: 1,293,984 B against a limit of 1,294,735 B (751 B of headroom), so any small chat change can trip `pnpm ui:check-performance`.

Reproduce on the commit above:

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm ui:build
pnpm ui:check-performance
# chat boot JS: 20 requests, ... limits: 20 requests, 1294735 B gzip
grep -l ipaddr dist/control-ui/assets/control-ui-boot-chat-*.js
# prints the chat boot chunk
```

### Proposed solution

Split the remote host guard in two:

- A small module, used by the browser, that decides plain hostnames itself (they can never parse as an IP) and sends anything an IP parser could read to the full guard.
- The full IP literal guard, loaded as its own chunk. Until it is installed, those hosts are rejected (fail closed, never looser). The chunk loads the first time such a host appears, and chat items built before it loads are rebuilt once it is installed.

Server code keeps importing `src/media/parse-output.ts`, which installs the full guard at import, so the Gateway's decision stays synchronous and unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

- Keep the guard in the boot bundle: costs about 4.3 KB gzip on every chat cold load for a rare case.
- Reimplement IP literal parsing without `ipaddr.js`: duplicates a security-sensitive parser that `@openclaw/net-policy` already owns.
- Swap the module per build with a Vite alias: the browser and server would run different guard code under the same import path, and the unit tests would no longer cover what ships.
- Load the guard eagerly when the chat route starts: the boot manifest generator then counts it as boot code and puts `ipaddr.js` back in the chat boot set.
- Preload it at idle time after the chat route mounts: it then downloads on every cold load, and the lazy chunks (served without content encoding) cost more transfer than the boot bundle saves.

### Impact

- Affected: every Control UI user who cold loads the chat route.
- Severity: low. About 4.3 KB gzip (16 KB minified) of boot JS that first paint does not need, plus budget pressure on the chat boot bundle.
- Frequency: every cold load of the chat route.
- Consequence: extra boot bytes; on the base commit the chat boot bundle is 751 B under its gzip limit. A local cold-load benchmark did not show a timing difference beyond its A/A noise.

### Evidence/examples

`node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/check-control-ui-performance-base.mts 6e7ee204e1b1fef223c794dbbed42de069a2623e` with the proposed change applied:

```text
chat boot JS gzip vs base: 1293984 B -> 1289715 B (-4269 B); requests 20 -> 20
new boot JS gzip vs base: 800440 B -> 800493 B (+53 B); requests 15 -> 15
startup JS gzip vs base: 90484 B -> 90483 B (-1 B); requests 3 -> 3
```

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself. A PR is linked.

### Additional information

OpenClaw version: `6e7ee204e1b1fef223c794dbbed42de069a2623e` (main). No open issue or PR covers this (searched open issues and PRs for "ipaddr", "MEDIA host guard", "MEDIA IP literal", "chat boot bytes", "chat boot ipaddr", "control-ui boot chunk" and "parse-output").

issues.body:
### Summary

When a memory plugin runs beside the slot owner (#198445), let Active Memory's model recall use that plugin's declared recall tools by default, next to the owner's, instead of requiring each operator to list them in `toolsAllow`.

### Problem to solve

Active Memory builds its default `toolsAllow` from the slot owner's `recallToolNames` only (extensions/active-memory/index.ts `resolveSelectedRecallToolNames`, config.ts `resolveDefaultToolsAllow`). The registrar drops `recallToolNames` from every plugin that is not the slot owner (src/plugins/registry-registrars.ts), so a memory plugin running beside memory-core has no way to tell Active Memory which of its tools recall memory.

The result for an operator who runs memory-core plus a second memory plugin:

- Active Memory recalls from memory-core only, unless the operator finds the second plugin's tool names and writes a full `toolsAllow` list. That list then also replaces the owner's default, so a later change of owner tools is missed.
- The second plugin usually injects its own recall block before each prompt. The model then gets two memory blocks per turn, built from different stores, and pays for both.

With the second plugin's recall tools in Active Memory's default list, the operator can turn that plugin's own injection off and keep one memory summary per turn.

### Proposed solution

- The registrar keeps a non-owner's `recallToolNames` in a separate field of its registration (for example `supplementalRecallToolNames`) instead of dropping it. It never becomes part of the resolved owner capability, so the owner's recall grant, `deterministicRecallToolName` and private transcript recall are unchanged.
- Active Memory's default `toolsAllow` becomes the owner's recall tools followed by the supplemental ones, deduplicated and capped at the existing 32. An explicit `toolsAllow` still replaces the default.
- Only the model recall lane uses them. The deterministic trigger lane keeps using the slot owner's provider runtime.
- Tool policy is unchanged: each tool must still pass `toolAuthority.allows`.

### Alternatives considered

- **Operators list the tools in `toolsAllow` (works today).** It works, but every install must know the plugin's tool names and repeat the owner's defaults.
- **Let a non-owner drive the trigger lane.** The trigger lane runs the owner's provider runtime with a session authority; a second provider there needs its own authority and audience contract. Too large for this gap.
- **Have the second plugin call memory-core's search itself.** Plugins cannot reach another plugin's runtime, and it would still produce two injected blocks.

### Impact

- **Affected:** installs that run a memory plugin beside memory-core and use Active Memory.
- **Severity:** low to medium. A manual workaround exists.
- **Frequency:** every turn on those installs (double injection) until the operator configures `toolsAllow`.
- **Consequence:** extra prompt tokens and two partly overlapping memory blocks per turn, or Active Memory that never sees the second store.

### Evidence/examples

- extensions/active-memory/index.ts:64-71: default recall tools come from the registration whose `pluginId` equals `plugins.slots.memory`.
- extensions/active-memory/config.ts `resolveDefaultToolsAllow`: owner tools, else `memory_search`/`memory_get` (or `memory_recall` for memory-lancedb).
- extensions/active-memory/types.ts `ACTIVE_MEMORY_RESERVED_TOOLS_ALLOW`: plugin recall tools such as `hindsight_recall` are not reserved, so the `toolsAllow` workaround is accepted.
- src/plugins/registry-registrars.ts `registerMemoryCapability`: non-owner `recallToolNames` are dropped with "skipping its indexing runtime and recall registration".
- Related: #198445 (memory plugins beside the slot owner), #194673 (requester authority for corpus supplements).

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, after the sidecar issue has a direction; the change depends on it.

### Additional information

Use case: the Hindsight memory plugin running beside memory-core. In that mode it skips its own per-turn injection when Active Memory is enabled and its recall tool is in Active Memory's `toolsAllow`, so the turn carries one memory summary.

issues.body:
### Summary

Add an operator setting, `plugins.entries.<id>.memory.sidecar: true`, that loads a `kind: "memory"` plugin beside the plugin that owns `plugins.slots.memory` instead of disabling it.

### Problem to solve

A memory plugin can only run as the slot owner. When `plugins.slots.memory` names another plugin, the slot decision disables every single-kind memory plugin before `register()` runs. The only exceptions are dual-kind plugins and memory-core when it runs as the dreaming sidecar.

Operators who want memory-core's file memory (MEMORY.md, memory/*.md, `memory_search`, Active Memory) and also an external memory service have to choose one. Replacing memory-core means losing the file index, the Memory page and most of the memory CLI. Honcho avoids the problem by declaring no `kind` at all. A plugin that also wants to be a valid slot owner cannot do that, because the manifest kind is static.

The host already supports the runtime half. `registerMemoryCapability` from a plugin that is not the slot owner keeps only consolidation-safe fields: it drops `runtime`, `providerRuntime`, `recallToolNames`, `deterministicRecallToolName` and `supportsPrivateTranscriptRecall` (src/plugins/registry-registrars.ts). Memory learn contributions from non-owners are skipped. Corpus supplements, prompt supplements, hooks and tools have no ownership gate. Only the load decision is missing.

### Proposed solution

- A new operator setting `plugins.entries.<id>.memory.sidecar` (boolean, default unset). It sits beside the other per-entry grants (`hooks.allowPromptModification`, `subagent.allowModelOverride`).
- `resolveMemorySlotDecision` takes `sidecar`. When it is true and the slot names another plugin, the plugin is enabled and not selected. It never takes the slot, including when the slot is unset. With `plugins.slots.memory: "none"` it stays disabled.
- The four callers (runtime loader, config validation, CLI root descriptors, plugin root contributions) pass the normalized entry flag.
- `openclaw plugins enable <id>` keeps the current memory slot when the entry is a sidecar, instead of moving the slot to the enabled plugin.
- Nothing changes without the setting. Existing installs, the dreaming sidecar and dual-kind plugins behave as today.
- Conversation access stays governed by `plugins.entries.<id>.hooks.allowConversationAccess`, as for any other plugin.

### Alternatives considered

- **Drop `kind` from the plugin manifest (the Honcho approach).** The plugin can then never own the slot, so a plugin that offers both modes would need two packages with the same code.
- **Declare a second kind (`["memory", "context-engine"]`).** Dual-kind plugins stay enabled when they lose the memory slot, but `plugins enable` then also moves `plugins.slots.contextEngine`, and the plugin claims a role it does not implement.
- **A manifest field instead of an operator setting.** The plugin would decide that it runs beside the owner. Running two memory systems on every turn costs tokens and latency, so the operator should opt in per install. A manifest hint could be added later for doctor messages.
- **Generalize the dreaming sidecar.** That path is authorized by memory-core's dreaming config and is specific to consolidation.

### Impact

- **Affected:** operators who want memory-core plus an external memory plugin (Hindsight, LanceDB-style stores, other services).
- **Severity:** medium. Today the choice is all or nothing.
- **Frequency:** every install that adds an external memory plugin.
- **Consequence:** users either lose memory-core's file memory or skip the external plugin. Plugin authors ship kind-less variants that cannot own the slot.

### Evidence/examples

- src/plugins/config-activation-shared.ts `resolveMemorySlotDecisionShared`: a single-kind memory plugin returns `{ enabled: false, reason: 'memory slot set to "<owner>"' }`.
- src/plugins/registry-registrars.ts `registerMemoryCapability`: "Dreaming keeps an unselected sidecar active for consolidation. Strip its slot-owner fields so resolution cannot lend its runtime or recall grant."
- src/plugins/slots.ts `applyExclusiveSlotSelection`: enabling a plugin moves every slot implied by its kind.
- Checked on 2026.11.3 with an external memory plugin installed and enabled, and `plugins.slots.memory` set to `memory-core`: `openclaw plugins inspect <id>` reports `Status: disabled` and `Reason: memory slot set to "memory-core"`. `openclaw plugins list` shows the same entry as `enabled`, which reads as if the plugin runs.
- Related: #194673 (requester authority for corpus supplements), #141806 (unselected memory-core shadowed slot-owner recall tools; closed), #138366 (slot owner drives the Dreams page).

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I have a branch ready (feat/memory-sidecar-plugins).

### Additional information

The change is small: one config key, one decision parameter, four call sites and the enable path. Tests cover the decision table, normalization, the loader (sidecar loads and keeps its hooks, its recall grant is dropped, the unapproved case stays disabled) and the enable path.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On a POSIX Git install, `openclaw update` to any main commit from 5a7d1718aa5 (#198661) onward fails at `preflight-build` with `Declaration input escapes checkout`, because the updater builds the target in a worktree nested inside the install and the target's declaration build now refuses type files read from the install's own `node_modules`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Make a Git install at `v2026.11.4` (d843d6af39a4): `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm build && pnpm ui:build`. Plain macOS layout: no symlinked home, internal disk.
2. Stop the Gateway. Run `OPENCLAW_UPDATE_DEV_TARGET_REF=<target sha> node openclaw.mjs update --channel dev --yes --no-restart`.
3. Target 1c1814a0bf78 (parent of #198661): `preflight-build` passes.
4. Target 5a7d1718aa5 (#198661) or current main f947bdc9498: `preflight-build` fails and the install stays at d843d6af39a4.

### Expected behavior

The update builds the target and moves the install, as it does for 1c1814a0bf78 from the same install.

### Actual behavior

```
  ✓ preflight-deps-install (15.85s)
  ✗ preflight-build (23.11s)
    Failing check preflight-build (command-failed): Error: Declaration input escapes checkout: [redacted-path]
  ✓ preflight-cleanup (13.21s)
Failed: validating
```

The updater redacts the path. Building f947bdc9498 in the same nested layout by hand (`<install>/.artifacts/<dir>/worktree`) shows it:

```
Error: Declaration input escapes checkout: <install>/node_modules/undici/types/utility.d.ts -> <install>/node_modules/.pnpm/undici@8.12.2/node_modules/undici/types/utility.d.ts.
```

Cause:

- The updater puts its preflight worktree at `<realpath(install)>/.artifacts/.openclaw-update-preflight-XXXXXX/worktree` on POSIX (`src/infra/update-runner-git-commands.ts:104-113`, `src/infra/update-runner-git-preflight.ts:577,586`). That is three levels inside the install, whose root `node_modules` holds `undici`.
- `@anthropic-ai/sdk@0.137.0` `internal/types.d.mts` line 51 (also `openai` and `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk`) types `RequestInit` as a union of relative imports of `node_modules/undici` from 3 to 10 parent levels (`import("../../../node_modules/undici/...")` and longer). From the worktree's `.pnpm` layout, level 7 is the worktree's own `node_modules/undici` and level 10 is the install's.
- Since #198661, tsdown declarations come from one `tsgo -p <leaf> --listFiles` pass that reads the real filesystem, and every listed file must be inside the checkout (`scripts/lib/native-declaration-emitter.mts:377-386`, thrown at `scripts/lib/local-check-runtime.mts:166`). The API path it replaced denied reads outside the checkout, so the far union members did not resolve. #198661 lists this as intended ("Parent-install shadowing now fails loudly"), pinned by `fails closed when optional SDK relative imports reach a parent install` in `test/scripts/native-declaration-boundary.test.ts:239`. The updater's own nested worktree is a parent install in exactly that sense.

### OpenClaw version

From 2026.11.4 (d843d6af39a4) to main f947bdc9498. First bad target 5a7d1718aa5, last good 1c1814a0bf78.

### Operating system

macOS 27.2 (arm64)

### Install method

Git checkout (pnpm build), dev channel update

### Model

Not model related

### Provider / routing chain

Not provider related

### Impact and severity

- Affected: POSIX Git installs updating to a target that contains #198661. The preflight path does not depend on host layout; reproduced without a symlinked home or external disk. Windows builds in `C:\ocu` and was not tested.
- Severity: blocks the update. The install stays on its old commit and the Gateway starts on it again. No data risk seen.
- Frequency: 3 of 3 attempts from 2026.11.4 to main targets at or after 5a7d1718aa5 failed (5a7d1718aa5, 2516bca9fdb8, f947bdc9498). The update to 1c1814a0bf78 from the same build passed.
- Consequence: Git installs cannot reach current main. No release tag contains #198661 yet. A release cut after it would block Git installs on stable and beta the same way, since tag updates run the same preflight build.

### Additional information

Fix direction: keep declaration resolution inside the checkout when the checkout is nested in another install, for example by emitting through the bounded API filesystem when the command-line pass lists an input outside the checkout, instead of failing. Moving the preflight worktree out of the install would help only future updaters, since shipped updaters already pick the nested path.

issues.body:
### Summary

Let plugin session forks (`runForkedTurn`, `forkSession`) on a session whose model runs on a CLI runtime such as `claude-cli` branch the CLI's native session, instead of failing or calling the provider API.

### Problem to solve

On a session whose `anthropic/*` model runs through `agentRuntime: claude-cli`, plugin forks do not use the CLI:

- `api.runtime.subagent.runForkedTurn` always runs on the built-in runtime (`src/agents/session-fork-run.ts` sets `agentHarnessId` and `agentHarnessRuntimeOverride` to `"openclaw"`). With no Anthropic API key, every fork fails with `No API key found for provider "anthropic"`. With a key, the fork quietly bills the API instead of the subscription the session uses.
- `api.runtime.subagent.forkSession` fails closed with `Session forks are not supported for CLI runtime claude-cli.` (#170146).

So plugins built on forks do not work on Claude CLI setups. One example is the ClawHub plugin better-prompt, whose composer helper forks the chat with `read`, `ls` and `exec`. It fails on every Claude CLI chat without an API key.

The docs say "CLI runtimes are not supported" for session forks. #170146 explains why: a CLI runtime has no prepared provider request for the built-in runtime to replay.

### Proposed solution

Fork the native session on CLI backends that can branch it at a recorded reply. Claude CLI already supports this (`forkArg: --fork-session`, `resumeAtArg: --resume-session-at`), and `sessions.create` parent forks already use it.

- Each CLI reply in the transcript records its native session id and reply id. The fork resumes that native session in a new CLI process with `--fork-session --resume-session-at <reply>` and sends the fork prompt. The source transcript, the source native session and its binding stay unchanged. The branched session is not kept.
- Guarantees kept: only the requested tools run, through the Gateway's exact MCP grant, with Claude's native execution tools off. `read`, `ls` and `exec` keep the session's policy, the owner-only `exec` rule and "never ask for approval". The session's account boundary (auth profile and epoch) applies. Timeout, abort, plugin lane and attribution do not change. The final `before_model_request` policy runs as `side_question`.
- The fork fails before any CLI or provider I/O when it cannot branch cleanly: no recorded native reply at the anchor, or a reply from an older native session.
- Built-in runtime forks do not change.
- Plugin-owned tools (`runtimePluginToolGrant`, `toolContext.backgroundRun`) do not reach a CLI backend's MCP surface today. Forks that grant them keep the built-in runtime. Bundled Skill Workshop is one of these and is unchanged.

### Alternatives considered

- Make `runForkedTurn` fail closed on CLI runtimes, like `forkSession`. This matches today's docs, but plugin forks still do not work on Claude CLI setups, and CLI sessions that have an API key lose forks that run today.
- Run CLI forks as a fresh CLI process with the conversation pasted as text (like CLI `/btw`). This loses the native session's tool history and cache, and the prompt grows with every fork.

### Impact

Affected: plugins that fork sessions (`runForkedTurn`, `forkSession`) on agents whose model runs on `claude-cli`.
Severity: blocks the plugin feature on those agents.
Frequency: always, on every fork.
Consequence: errors on setups without an API key, or API spend on setups that use a subscription for chat.

### Evidence/examples

- `src/agents/session-fork-run.ts` forces `agentHarnessId: "openclaw"` and `agentHarnessRuntimeOverride: "openclaw"`.
- `src/agents/btw.ts` throws `Session forks are not supported for CLI runtime ${cliProvider}.` for `forkSession`.
- `extensions/anthropic/cli-backend.ts` declares `forkArg: "--fork-session"` and `resumeAtArg: "--resume-session-at"`.
- `docs/plugins/sdk-runtime.md`, "Session forks": "CLI runtimes are not supported."

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance

### Additional information

Related: #170146 (`forkSession`), #190950 (`runForkedTurn`), #200636 (fork `read`/`ls`/`exec`).

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A `config.patch` that moves `anthropic/claude-opus-4-6` from `agentRuntime: claude-cli` to `agentRuntime: openclaw` succeeds with no billing-route warning, although the model's primary and subagent consumers now bill through a metered API key instead of the Claude CLI's own credentials.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start an isolated Gateway (fresh `OPENCLAW_HOME` and `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`) with a fixture `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` set and this config. The reproduction also set the Anthropic `baseUrl` to a closed loopback port and kept the `claude` binary off PATH so no request left the host:
   ```json5
   {
     agents: {
       defaults: {
         model: "anthropic/claude-opus-4-6",
         models: { "anthropic/claude-opus-4-6": { agentRuntime: { id: "claude-cli" } } },
         subagents: { model: "anthropic/claude-opus-4-6" },
       },
       entries: { main: {} },
     },
   }
   ```
2. `openclaw gateway call config.get` and note `hash`.
3. `openclaw gateway call config.patch` with `raw: {"agents":{"defaults":{"models":{"anthropic/claude-opus-4-6":{"agentRuntime":{"id":"openclaw"}}}}}}` and that `baseHash`.
4. Read the response and the Gateway log.

### Expected behavior

Doctor already reports this class of change after its own migrations: "When model migrations change a configured consumer between subscription/OAuth and metered API-key billing, Doctor reports the consumer, model, and old and new routes" (`docs/gateway/doctor/config-migrations.md`). A Gateway config write that makes the same change should report it the same way, and `src/agents/AGENTS.md` says fallback to API-key billing "happens only where documented, never silently."

### Actual behavior

The response is `{"ok": true, "changedPaths": ["agents.defaults.models.anthropic/claude-opus-4-6.agentRuntime.id"]}`, with no warning in the response or the Gateway log. In the incident, subagents spawned after the write used the Anthropic Messages API (`[model-fetch] ... provider=anthropic api=anthropic-messages`).

Two things combine:

- `config.set`, `config.patch`, and `config.apply` never compare billing routes. Only Doctor calls `collectModelBillingRouteMigrationWarnings`.
- That comparator skips consumers without a catalog `selectedRoute` (`if (auth.availability !== true || !auth.selectedRoute) continue;` in `src/commands/doctor/shared/model-billing-route-migration.ts`). Only providers with catalog route rows (OpenAI) report `selectedRoute`, so Anthropic API-key vs token profiles and CLI-runtime native logins (`runtimeAuth.source === "native"`, no `selectedRoute`) are never compared, even by Doctor.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.9 (main @ 01a614821a3d)

### Operating system

macOS 27.2

### Install method

pnpm build from source; `openclaw gateway run` with isolated `OPENCLAW_HOME` / `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`

### Model

anthropic/claude-opus-4-6

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> claude-cli (before the write); openclaw -> anthropic-messages API with API key (after)

### Additional provider/model setup details

The incident config also had per-agent `anthropic/*` entries and a utility model on Anthropic. The write that switched `agentRuntime` from `claude-cli` to `openclaw` produced no warning. Overnight, about 1,960 calls went to the Anthropic API: about 1,930 from subagents, about 300 utility calls with `sessionKey unknown`, and 2 others. Credentials: an Anthropic API key in the environment plus the Claude CLI's own claude.ai login.

### Logs

```
# config.patch response (current main)
{ "ok": true, "changedPaths": ["agents.defaults.models.anthropic/claude-opus-4-6.agentRuntime.id"] }

# Gateway log after the write: no billing-route line

# incident, one line per call:
[provider-transport-fetch] [model-fetch] start provider=anthropic api=anthropic-messages ...
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Reproduced on an isolated Gateway with a fixture key and the Anthropic `baseUrl` pointed at a closed loopback port, so no request left the host.

### Impact and severity

- Affected: operators and agents that change `agentRuntime`, model refs, or auth profiles through `config.set` / `config.patch` / `config.apply` or `openclaw config set` while a Gateway runs.
- Severity: unexpected API spend (money).
- Frequency: reproduced on both attempts (2/2) with the steps above.
- Consequence: in the incident, about 1,960 metered calls in one night with no in-product signal.

### Additional information

Related, not duplicates: #145154 (Doctor migration rerouted Codex OAuth to an API key; origin of the Doctor warning), #148412 (claude-cli/anthropic credential selection falls back to `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`).

issues.body:
### Bug type

Bug (something is broken)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On a macOS app node, `exec host=node` with `timeoutSeconds: 0` ("0 disables" the process lifetime) is still cut off
after about 20 seconds. The node host reports `TIMEOUT: macOS app exec host response timed out; execution outcome is
unknown`, while the companion has started the command and runs it without a timer.

#172117 fixed the flat 20 s cap from #139706 for every finite timeout, and the fix shipped in 2026.10.6. This is the
one input it does not cover:
- The Gateway normalizes a `system.run` `timeoutMs` of `0` to `null` ("no expiry").
- The node host forwards `null` to the app.
- `requestExecHostViaSocket` exempts only `=== 0`, so `null` falls through to the 20 s default response deadline.

Source path on current main:
- `src/agents/exec-tool-timeout.ts` `resolveNodeExecTimeouts`: `timeoutSeconds: 0` yields `runTimeoutMs: 0` (program timer off).
- `src/gateway/node-registry.system-run.ts` `normalizeSystemRunTimeoutMs`: `timeoutMs <= 0` becomes `null`, "preserving null for no expiry".
- `src/node-host/invoke-system-run.ts`: the exec host request carries `timeoutMs: phase.timeoutMs ?? null`.
- `src/infra/exec-host.ts` `requestExecHostViaSocket`: `request.timeoutMs === 0 ? 0 : addTimerTimeoutGraceMs(...) ?? 20_000`, so `null` gets 20 s.
- `apps/macos/Sources/OpenClaw/ExecHostExecutor.swift`, `ShellExecutor.swift`: a nil timeout runs with no timer.

This error is produced on the node from the local socket call to the app and does not depend on the calling Gateway
client. For authority-level refusals see #166652 and #142874.

### Steps to reproduce

From source (no app needed):

1. Check out main and run `pnpm install`.
2. In `src/infra/exec-host.socket.test.ts`, add a case that calls `requestExecHostViaSocket` with `request.timeoutMs` set
   to `normalizeSystemRunInvokeParams({ command: "system.run", params: { timeoutMs: 0 } }).timeoutMs` (`null`). Advance
   fake timers by more than 20 s, then let the peer reply.
3. Run `pnpm test src/infra/exec-host.socket.test.ts`.

On a macOS app node (follows from the source path above; not re-run on a live node for this report):

1. Pair the OpenClaw.app node with an exec policy that allows the command.
2. From an agent, run `exec` with `host: "node"`, the app node, `timeoutSeconds: 0`, and a command that takes longer
   than 20 s, for example `sleep 45; echo done`.

### Expected behavior

With no expiry requested, the node host waits for the companion's reply. It is still bounded by the Gateway invoke
deadline and its `node.invoke.cancel`. The command returns `done`.

### Actual behavior

After about 20 s the call fails with `TIMEOUT: macOS app exec host response timed out; execution outcome is unknown`.
The node host closes the socket and the companion cancels its task, so the result is lost even when the command
completes.

On 2026.10.5 and earlier, every node exec over about 20 s failed this way, as
`COMPANION_APP_UNAVAILABLE: macOS app exec host unreachable` (#139706, fixed by #172117).

### OpenClaw version

Source-verified on v2026.10.6 (macOS app), v2026.10.7 (Gateway) and current main; not observed live on those builds.

### Operating system

macOS 27.0.1 (Apple Silicon)

### Install method

macOS app (node) plus Gateway

### Model

Not model-dependent.

### Provider / routing chain

Not provider-dependent: agent `exec` tool -> Gateway `node.invoke` `system.run` -> macOS app node host -> local exec host socket -> OpenClaw.app.

### Logs

Unit test from step 2 on main (excerpt, lines in log order):

```text
FAIL   infra  src/infra/exec-host.socket.test.ts > exec host real UDS boundary > waits past the 20 s fallback for a Gateway no-expiry run
AssertionError: expected "vi.fn()" to not be called at all, but actually been called 1 times
  "code": "TIMEOUT",
  "message": "TIMEOUT: macOS app exec host response timed out; execution outcome is unknown",
Tests  1 failed | 8 passed (9)
```

### Impact and severity

Long or unbounded commands on macOS app nodes (builds, polls, `ssh` sessions) return an unknown outcome after 20 s
even though no timeout was requested. Callers cannot tell success from failure and may re-run non-idempotent work.

Related: #139706 #163978 #162789 #135272 #166652 #142874

Draft PR #163978 (written before #172117 landed) also covered nonpositive timeouts as part of a broader rework; current
main still has the gap.
