prs.title: fix: remove the dead child toggle from pinned Main
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Pinned Main can show a chevron and child count even though its related conversations appear separately and the pin cannot expand to show them.

## User Impact

Pinned Main still opens the same chat, but no longer offers a control that cannot reveal anything. Other pinned sessions that actually contain nested chats still expand normally.

## Why This Change Was Made

Only show the disclosure on rows that have a sidebar branch to load or expand. This changes the control, not where conversations are placed or what is stored.

## Evidence

Reproduced on current main: clicking the chevron did not reveal a chat under Main. On the fix, Chromium verifies that the Main pin has no disclosure, its related chat is still visible separately, and Design review still expands to reveal its nested chat. All 4 Chromium and 158 focused sidebar tests passed. The Control UI build completed locally and reported CSS and chat boot bundle-budget warnings. Independent autoreview was unavailable because its temporary-directory requirement could not be met in this workspace.

Control UI screenshots use synthetic session data in Chromium, comparing main `a27b4e6f6bad` and candidate `ac8759d21805` in the same sidebar crop. No live account data was used.

Reported by @vyctorbrzezowski.

Restores upstream lock error and diagnostic fixes, enables fs-safe-owned DrvFS rename recovery at existing config/state/atomic-write owners, and closes native batch-read descriptors through their owner during plugin capture and receipt replay. prs.title: fix: reconnect shared provider credentials outside the agent roster
prs.body:
Closes #195867

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: operators cannot reconnect shared provider credentials through native sign-in after the legacy `main` owner leaves the runnable agent roster.

## User Impact

An authorized operator can sign in once to the canonical shared credential owner. Inheriting agents continue to read through the common store while keeping their individual models, model policies, and private credential overrides. Shared sign-in rejects `--set-default`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Resolve this explicit login target only when inheritance names `main`, that agent is absent, and the existing canonical ownership rules admit the target. Use the current credential writer, profile-order owner, and runtime refresh path. Discovery uses the configured ambient agent; `main` remains a credential owner without becoming a runnable agent.

The normal unknown-agent guard stays intact. Shared login cannot cross the admitted state owner, and administrator admission, current authority, revocation, and ownership-change checks remain active. There are no new flags, configuration keys, protocol fields, schemas, dependencies, or token-copy operations.

The auth context is extracted into a sibling module to keep the existing file within its growth cap. The separate test allocation covers only the measured regression growth.

## Evidence

Historical proof snapshot: head `f4265dbc55fd5c1283312d78ad0fc238e746cb30`, based on `7ebc4f3e67137c34b0850dfa8cab2b8d68e6576d`. The test and runtime evidence below belongs to that source revision.

- Baseline: the actual shared-login RPC wizard rejects the absent canonical owner with `Unknown agent id "main"`.
- Fixed: 11/11 owner regressions and 113/113 related native-owner tests pass.
- Core types, targeted typed lint, runtime build, formatting, file-growth caps, and the native test-line budget pass. The allocation matches 272 net added test lines.
- An independent source review found no remaining actionable findings. Final fixture identifiers were anonymized bijectively; the 11 owner tests and formatting/budget checks were rerun afterward. Unchanged production hashes bind the preceding types, lint, sibling tests, and build; these were not described as rerun.
- The successful runtime build emits nonfatal UI size diagnostics: largest JS gzip 564575 versus 564484 bytes, chat boot 1267.2 versus 1266.4 KiB, and new boot 784.7 versus 784.4 KiB. Attribution to this change is unproven; no budget guard or override was changed.

The native owner fixture uses synthetic OAuth, real task-owned SQLite stores, and Gateway RPC. It checks shared persistence and profile order, refreshed inherited views, preserved private overrides and model policies, and rejection of unknown/mismatched owners, a changed owner, revoked authority, and a different state root. A successful shared login does not prove that every private override should be removed.

No real credentials, private configurations, personal sessions, or runtime logs are included in this PR. The public-head proof uses synthetic provider I/O. A separate integration was used to smoke-test native provider sign-in and ordinary inference; that is not presented as an exact-public-head live-provider test.

### Latest-main refresh — 21 November 2026

Rebased the single feature commit onto canonical `main` at `282121402940c47c87a68bf08bb6e66097818884`. One import conflict was resolved by retaining both the current main imports and the PR's shared-owner resolver. `git range-diff` confirms the intended change with the upstream auth API rename; the 11-file scoped diff and `git diff --check` pass. Current-head Codex Autoreview (P0–P2) completed `scoped-clean` with no actionable findings.

The focused owner/runtime tests above were not rerun at the rebased head. GitHub requires a maintainer to approve this PR revision before CI starts; the current CI gate is therefore blocked and is not green.

prs.title: improve: keep the lean Gateway from running out of memory on its first start
prs.body:
Related: #202379, #202373

## What Problem This Solves

In a small container (1.5 GiB), the Gateway can run out of memory and be killed by the kernel a few seconds into its first start, while its first agent turn runs. On main `1a0a24dc`, the lean profile hit this in 1 of 3 runs. The peak comes from start-up work all happening at once: the first turn, background maintenance, a process that launches commands, and a file-watching process.

## User Impact

On hosts that auto-select the lean profile (under 8 GiB, or `gateway.resources.profile: "lean"`), the first turn after a start no longer competes with background start-up work for memory. Lean also uses one fewer helper process.

When memory runs out on Linux, the kernel now picks the file-watching helper or a database read helper before the Gateway. Both recover on their own.

Standard-profile hosts are unchanged, apart from that Linux kill preference and one fewer thread inside the file-watching helper.

Trade-offs on lean:
- Post-ready maintenance, cron start and prewarming start once the Gateway is idle, at most 60 seconds after startup.
- Commands start directly from the Gateway rather than through a separate launcher, which costs some fork latency. Hosts with 1 GiB or less already work this way.

## Why This Change Was Made

Approved scope from #202379 (items 1, 2 and 4); the plan is in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/202379#issuecomment-7086019273.

- **Post-ready work waits for a quiet Gateway on lean.** Standard releases post-ready work 500 ms after startup settles. That point lands inside a first turn sent right after ready. Lean first checks 2 s after settle, then every second, until no request root work is active, with a 60 s cap.
  - Post-ready maintenance now waits for the barrier *before* it admits its own root. Otherwise it would hold the idle check busy itself.
  - Requests never wait on anything behind the barrier. The native model catalog is advisory, and a turn acquires its own.
- **Lean skips the Linux command spawn broker,** the same as the existing ≤1 GiB mode. It couldn't be started lazily, because SQLite readers need to spawn about 2 s into startup.
  - Bootstrap resolves the profile only later, so the broker gate predicts it from the CLI startup snapshot. On in-process restarts it predicts from the config being started instead, read with dotenv applied into an isolated env.
  - The plugin native-resource broker (the other `worker.js`) is unchanged. It already starts on demand, and it can't restart.
- **The directory watch helper on Linux** now ends itself after its caller dies, using a timer instead of a second V8 isolate. macOS keeps the thread because of FSEvents close stalls.
- **OOM victim preference.** The directory watch helper and natively spawned SQLite read-only helpers get `oom_score_adj` 1000, under the existing Linux child policy and its `OPENCLAW_CHILD_OOM_SCORE_ADJ=0` opt-out.
  - Both brokers keep the Gateway's score. A killed native broker leaves plugin native resources unusable until restart, and repeated command-broker kills use up its restarts.
  - Documented in `docs/platforms/linux.md`.

Known bounded case: the retained-plugin cleanup idle task still waits inside its own admission, which is unchanged. If it fires at 30 s while the barrier is still held, lean's release waits for the 60 s cap.

## Evidence

**Real-behaviour campaign: done; the pass criterion is met. Read the numbers with care (n=3).**

I re-ran the `1a0a24dc` integration campaign on this head (`8d78ba4e`) with the same harness and method. Each case ran in its own Studio Crabbox local-container lease built from the pushed commit, under the membench lock, with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`, pinned profiles, and startup samples at +2/4/6/8 s and at first ready. I added a lean 1.5 GiB ×3 control on the merge base `80e233cd`. Failures stay in the denominator, and nothing was rerun.

**Completion:**
- **Lean 1.5 GiB on this PR:** 3/3, `oom`/`oom_kill` 0 in every round.
- **The merge-base control also completed 3/3.** Completion alone doesn't separate this PR from main, and main's earlier 2/3 looks like a near-miss rather than a deterministic failure.
- **Standard 1.5 GiB:** 2/3 again; r2 was OOM-killed, the same as on main. The PR is lean-only.
- **3 GiB:** all six rounds passed. The quick checks (auto 4/8 GiB, host, upgrade) and the shared-host fault case also passed.

**Paired results, lean at 1.5 GiB, PR vs merge base** (median and range; MiB unless noted):

| | PR | merge base |
|---|---|---|
| First-start cgroup anon peak | **1,145** (1,130–1,282) | 1,312 (1,274–1,382) |
| First-start Gateway child PSS peak | **149** (136–169) | 212 (181–249) |
| First-start Gateway RSS peak | 1,079 (1,064–1,216) | 1,180 (1,142–1,250) |
| Gateway children at first ready | 3 (watch host, native broker, transient reader) | 4 (watch host, 2 brokers, …) |
| Live worker isolates at +8 s | 19 | 22 |
| Whole-run anon peak | 1,371 (1,347–1,393) | 1,401 (1,340–1,418) |
| `memory.events max` | 5,227 (1,664–5,234) | 5,785 (2,643–5,994) |
| Anon headroom to the limit: first start / whole run | ~391 / ~165 | ~224 / ~135 |
| Time to first ready (s) | 5.1 (5.07–5.22) | 5.6 (5.14–5.65) |
| First measured turn (s) | 5.54 (5.36–5.59) | 5.52 (5.46–5.53) |
| Turn p95 / median (s) | 1.55 / 1.17 | 1.77 / 1.17 |

How to read these:
- **Clear effects:** child PSS is lower with no overlap between ranges, because the command broker no longer starts. The first-start anon peak is about 166 MiB lower at the median, and its ranges only just touch. Gateway RSS, max events and the whole-run peak are lower, but their ranges overlap.
- **`memory.peak` isn't informative here.** It reached the 1,536 MiB limit in every 1.5 GiB round on both arms, because page cache fills the limit.
- **No latency cost at n=3.**
- **Known gap: the deferral only partly cleared the startup window.** It removed `session-accessor.sqlite-archive` and some `session-transcript` isolates from the +8 s window. But `disk-budget`, `git-operation`, `fs-safe-copy` and `discovery` still appear there: they're either turn-driven or started outside the post-ready barrier. That isn't attributed yet.

Redacted evidence: https://gist.github.com/jalehman/36f79343b766a90a8a504e79bc3e420f. It holds the report, per-case receipts, `comparison.json`, startup isolates, the quick checks, and the latest-stable upgrade capture, which shows `2026.11.6` → candidate with config, sessions and records preserved and a completed first turn. CI attribution: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/203790#issuecomment-7091646915.

The campaign measured `8d78ba4e`. The current head `bd3318d3` changes only how the helper OOM score is written (now an asynchronous write, so lean's direct SQLite reader spawns don't do synchronous `/proc` writes on request paths), plus ratchet hygiene.

**Tests.** Fail-first where the behaviour is new:
- Lean release: held during an active turn, released at the first idle check, at the cap, and stopped on close. Standard timing is unchanged.
- The real `scheduleGatewayPostReadyMaintenance` with the lean release: fails on the pre-fix ordering.
- Broker gate: skipped for lean without disabling later starts, started for standard.
- Profile prediction: snapshot, in-process restart, invalid or unreadable config, and dotenv substitution without mutating `process.env`.

Existing suites pass: post-ready lifecycle, the import boundary, spawn-broker context, directory watch (including parent death with open pipes), owned-directory observation, SQLite reader sessions, Linux OOM score, idle tasks, gateway work admission, and the wrapper source closure.

Also pass: `tsgo:core`, scoped oxlint, format, docs format, `config:docs:check` and `git diff --check`.

prs.title: fix: preserve runtime custody, inference history, and recovery
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Runtime handoffs can lose the information or resource ownership they were admitted with: historical inference usage, database captures, updater imports, authentication recovery, retained knowledge receipts, and child sends waiting for plugin reload. These failures can misreport usage, interrupt recovery, or strand admitted work.

## User Impact

Preserves admitted runtime policy and historical usage, keeps captures and passive resources with their owning lifecycle, retains old updater imports during replacement, keeps provider readiness visible during sign-in recovery, replays knowledge receipts without duplicate inserts, and prevents a claimed child from being swept while its send is retained. No release, tag, dependency, SQLite-schema, or public-permission change is included.

## Scope and provenance

The six source repairs were qualified together, not as six independently passing branches. The import matched all 131 non-generated source files byte-for-byte; the overlapping Gateway validator was regenerated from integrated schemas. Fresh integrated review found a policy-reader P1: a distinct harness listing config could replace the admitted policy reader. The follow-up preserves that reader, exercises both shared-catalog acquisition orders, and corrects historical-versus-live consumer contracts without casts or requiring historical cost.

- Source range: `e15246d4ff96d1e19478db79262c679809624198..e0adbf242d102481f4fd938fbb449712b6935d3c`
- Integrated base: `b151c830713020fe0de9e37c3d21b76671fe0add`
- Consumer repair: `b1b254a2e6f3e9645d98eac09a816d7eb2165079`
- Goal replay follow-up: `86cdda60ded67023ef648c800690f2e996a4a86b`
- Final type/TUI follow-ups: `c8075920ea81c250b4402cba718866d094c7ce74`, `fdf5d316e897a447a8e0cea9182bf90ea2f9ffeb`
- Published head: **`91d65e5650337e695fdc240763e0c3f370184116`**

Original author/coauthor trailers are preserved. Separate from release-metadata PR #203880; the unrelated qualification-only cron change is excluded.

## Evidence

- Fresh integrated canonical native review identified the policy-reader P1; corrected diffs completed scoped-clean P0–P3 reviews. Reviewers had limited unchanged context and did not independently execute tests. A transient-file-invalidated review was not accepted. No tracked source differs between final reviewed `fdf5d316` and published `91d65e5`.
- Policy regression failed red in both acquisition orders; all 74 config-stamp/host-boundary tests passed (79.90s).
- Stable affected-consumer run: 287 tests across 13 shards passed (222.62s), with one Windows short-path skip. Covers provider/history contracts, database/native lifetimes, updater imports, agent tools/prefix stability, UI, Codex resume/whole-skill results, and knowledge replay. An earlier source-edit-invalidated run was excluded.
- Four historical/live fixture mismatches were corrected; affected typecheck/type-aware lint passed, plus 72 tests in three corrected files (62.24s).
- Local core/UI/tooling typechecks, generated-validator, formatting and diff checks passed. Full build passed (199.5s); advisory CSS/boot budgets were not suppressed. These are bounded local results, not green merge-ref CI.
- Follow-up consumer runs passed 228 historical/live tests, 138 runtime-selection/live-switch tests, 119 retained-import/tooling tests (one Windows skip), 11 RUN-generation resource tests (13.75s), and 167 shared Codex transcript tests (108.39s). Scoped review clean, 0.86 confidence, no independent tests.
- Goal regression preserves the synthetic post-commit notification fault and requires successful admitted execution, committed metadata and same-request replay without another model run/user message: 1 selected passed, 69 filtered (18.79s). Affected type/lint/line-cap/allocation checks passed; scoped review clean (0.86).
- Compaction narrows the existing optional owner with `expectDefined`; exact type leaf failed before/passed after, with all 13 runtime tests passing (10.47s). TUI asserts shared `catalogOwner`, retaining both admissions and one inventory-work assertion: three tests passed (2.97s). Affected checks and combined scoped review passed (0.94, diff-only).

### Historical review reconciled

An independent read-only audit of current source and existing logs reconciles all three findings on historical head `813d2a`:

1. The missing mock export was in `src/agents/agent-command.live-model-switch.test.ts`, now preserving real exports, not the review-named `src/commands/agent.runtime-config.test.ts`. The actual consumer and prepared-runtime suites pass 138/138; the review-named command suite independently passes 6/6. Its unrelated narrow mock was not expanded.
2. Snapshot assertions now verify shared catalog ownership, per-caller admitted reader binding, generation currency and revocation rather than wrapper identity.
3. Postbuild expectations classify the recorded immutable-handoff module/symbol rather than only one release version. All 116 postbuild tests and three retained-import process cases pass; one Windows case is skipped.

The old advisory verdict is not current-source evidence of these defects. Maintainer/bot authorship does not exempt real-product proof.

### Direct-source, runtime and visual proof

Direct-source alias proof uses the unbundled retention owner/worker, canonical TypeScript preload, unchanged assertions and `--preserve-symlinks`. Separately installed frozen standard-hoisted dependencies resolve the original pnpm-layout `strip-ansi` setup blocker without modifying managed dependencies. Selected test passed (35.10s); substituting only pre-fix retention owners from `07ff88e^` reproduced the original late import failure (`install-alias/dist/late-old-hash.mjs`); restored candidate owners passed (38.05s). No bundled owner/worker or synthetic loader; other variants were filtered.

Existing database/native child tests exercise real capture/preparation, native database operations and child-process custody. Historical-usage tests exercise production projection and serialized commit validation. Knowledge tests reconstruct persisted legacy/prefixed receipts through restarted storage/service owners and verify unchanged identity, payload rejection and no duplicate inserts. These are meaningful boundary proofs, not a claim of a completed real-agent historical/knowledge replay or installed upgrade.

Browser captures use the canonical synthetic harness: one before scenario, two after. Before owners are exact `b151c830` bytes; after UI tree is frozen at `d6a35d31`. This is valid source-mode mocked-Gateway browser proof, not a complete base deployment or external authentication-service proof. [UI evidence comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/203901#issuecomment-7090960023): all four images browser-verified decoded at 1280×1000 through the configured proxy with certificate verification enabled. Prior combined-source evidence includes a real-model claimed-child flow proving reload admission/drain/replay, not bundled-byte hot-swap. Cancellation/replacement controls remain fixture-based. Local refusal-compaction previously failed before reaching its loopback server; that remains a setup/transport gap, not passing stream proof.

## Terminal CI outcome and causal attribution

**Not ready to land.** Main CI `45113172591` completed **failure** on head `91d65e5650337e695fdc240763e0c3f370184116`. Checkout logs identify exact merge `e80ed29fd9aac66a17292ba00037c8cc4eb76aab` against newer base `b9bb7a99494aac52c3a6f9b1b29227bbfaaae84c`. Nine substantive jobs failed, followed by the aggregate gate; all six test-type jobs, production types and all five PostgreSQL conformance jobs passed.

Validate `45113172007` / job `137489912500` also failed. Production Knip had zero entries; full-tree Knip reports exactly `test/manual-release-approval.checks.ts` and `test/manual-release-approval.config.ts`, matching the original-base reproduction. No ignore/baseline exception was added.

| Toast browser | Test expects `false`, owner emits `"live"`; both blobs match newer base/merge. Source-level inherited mismatch, not a separate full-base browser execution. |
| Hook-token reload | **Inherited:** real isolated E2E on exact head and original base both fail line 524 with `[]` instead of the old token-source name. Head 48.71s; base selected body 8.285s. Startup/auth, approval, config patch/reload and second approval all execute unchanged. |
| Chat-abort initiator / membership authority | **Inherited:** real isolated head and original-base runs both reproduce both CI assertions: `aborted` vs `final` at line 439, and `INVALID_REQUEST` vs `FORBIDDEN` at line 468/149. Head 97.91s; base 107.50s. No mid-request authorization restriction or expectation edit added. |

The exact failing merge also passes all assertions (85.81s total; 43.62s test body), including load-wave completion, workspace settlement, node shutdown, Gateway restart and audit replay. This tests merge-context drift but does not establish a CI root cause or waive its 240s timeout. |

The causal runs used the existing network-none isolated runner, matching pinned Bun, prepared Playwright image, and invocation-local `umask 077`; no host security or artifact fence was disabled. Explicit E2E config selected existing offline native-archive projection and private-QA/declaration build. The exact-merge source manifest was verified before the successful run. Earlier missing-lockfile/index preparation failures are separate setup evidence, not product verdicts.

Unmodified worker tests hit the runner's 2 GiB `/tmp` versus approximately 4 GiB required by worktree disk admission. All three passing comparisons used identical qualification-only `command.tempParentDir` patches to the existing disk-backed fixture root, preserving default executable/arguments, assertions and timeouts. Patches were restored byte-for-byte afterward; no runner or fixture change is committed. Owned proof processes completed; containers are confirmed absent; the published working tree is clean.

Historical Talk replay also failed identically on original base. Historical Darwin dependency-cache initialization lacks matching platform/base execution. The finalization-size fixture encodes retired 512 KiB despite an inherited 16 MiB contract; source-contract attribution only. No permission weakening, timeout inflation, blind full-CI rerun or suppression was used.

## Test allocation

Combined branch originally had +1,330 net test lines, default allowance 400 and history credits 53; source candidate had +1,329 and 876 combined credits. Consumer/Goal regressions add 72 lines: allocation 948 (1,001 total credits), +1,401 lines; exact-base gate passes. Shared allowance unchanged; six repairs get one default allowance. ## Remaining qualification and governance

prs.title: fix: read GitHub previews with the connected GitHub CLI account
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When the Gateway's GitHub CLI login is the shared agent account, **Settings → Profile → GitHub accounts** shows it as Verified for every agent's dashboard data. But GitHub link previews, the side reader, and `github_read`/`github_search` skipped that login and read anonymously. Anonymous reads share GitHub's 60 requests per hour per IP, so after a few previews every PR failed with "GitHub API rate limit exceeded (HTTP 403)", even though a working account was already connected.

## User Impact

GitHub previews and the reader now use the same account Settings shows for the agent, including a shared account that is the Gateway's GitHub CLI login. Nobody has to connect the same account a second time just for reading. An explicit `gateway.controlUi.github.token` still takes precedence, and managed accounts behave as before. When there is no CLI login, or it cannot be verified, reads fall back to anonymous access as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reader already shares identity preparation with the rest of the Gateway's GitHub reads, but it called it only for OpenClaw-managed accounts. Without a managed account, it now also prepares the detected native identity through the same owner. The native token stays in its existing 60-second cache and keeps its per-request selection checks. A failure of the detected login keeps the previous anonymous path instead of blocking public reads; a failure of a managed account still surfaces as an error.

## Evidence

- **Real Gateway, same request as the user:** in an isolated Gateway on this branch's base, `controlUi.githubDetail` for a public PR used the anonymous quota and, once that reached zero, returned `GitHub API rate limit exceeded (HTTP 403)`. With this change, still at zero anonymous quota, the same reader request and `controlUi.githubPreview` returned the PR through the host's `gh` login, and the anonymous quota no longer moved.
- **Regression tests:** two new `native` cases in `control-ui.test.ts` (preview and detail) fail on the base and pass with the fix. The existing `anonymous` case now asserts that the no-login path still reads without an `Authorization` header.
- The affected Gateway suites (`control-ui`, `tools-github`, `control-ui.github-preview-refresh`, 71 tests) pass. `tsgo:core`, lint, and format pass. Local autoreview of the final change found no P0–P2 issues.

prs.title: fix(feishu): let isolated topics process messages concurrently
prs.body:
Related: #72972, #89687, #96315

## What Problem This Solves

Configured Feishu topic sessions currently share a group-wide ordinary-message execution queue. A long run in topic A therefore delays unrelated topic B, even when their conversation contexts are isolated.

This change uses the existing canonical session identity for execution scheduling. Different topics can run concurrently within the configured agent concurrency limit. Messages within one topic remain FIFO. `group_topic_sender` additionally separates senders. Default group/direct-message scheduling and out-of-band control commands retain their existing behavior.

## Design

Durable receipt identity remains the shipped `chat:<chatId>` format. The durable-ingress production module is unchanged against the original PR base. No topic-scoped durable format, new schema, migration, dependency, or configuration option is introduced.

Before debounce buffering, the receiver registers an ordering reservation. It then releases durable intake while retaining the message claim until adoption or abandonment. Execution awaits the existing keyed sequential queue and the complete message handler. Receiving later messages therefore does not start a second ordinary run in the same execution queue.

A message without reliable native `thread_id` creates a group barrier: it waits for earlier reservations and blocks later topic work. Registering every reservation before intake handoff includes the complete durable backlog. Such fallback messages bypass batching. Same-topic debounce batches preserve sender identity.

The existing five-minute execution-queue timeout remains unchanged: a timed-out handler can continue running while later same-key work proceeds. This PR does not promise unlimited-duration mutual exclusion.

## Maintainer decision requested

Please confirm that existing `group_topic` and `group_topic_sender` settings should enable topic-scoped inbound execution scheduling. Prior merged work intentionally retained group-wide ordinary-message FIFO. This proposal changes that boundary only for configured topic isolation, while preserving per-queue FIFO and unidentified-topic barriers. No extra opt-in setting is proposed. Maintainer acceptance remains pending.

## Evidence

### Built-Gateway runtime proof (scheduling repair)

Tested/build-info commit: `0dd05196b1022bd8dcc3c46a91d226514cf3ad50`.

An isolated built Gateway received eight authenticated, encrypted, locally signed Feishu webhook event replays. The run used real Feishu message/thread references, real message metadata lookup, real model calls, and actual Feishu replies. Exact output message IDs from this Gateway's streaming logs were independently fetched; all eight expected reply markers were present.

This is a signed-envelope replay, not naturally delivered WebSocket traffic. The replay uses native `topic_group` envelopes referring to existing ordinary-group threads. It does not claim a newly provisioned native topic group was tested. The model was `magpie/group/gpt-6.1-sol`; `maxConcurrent: 4`; debounce disabled for the distinct backlog messages. Nonzero debounce is covered by integration tests.

The first phase admitted A1, waited for its model start, then admitted same-topic A2 followed by different-topic B. A1 requested a bounded 35-second command. B completed before A1, while A2 started only after A1 completed.

The second phase admitted A1, waited for its model start, then admitted A2, A3, F, B in that order. F's signed envelope omitted native `thread_id`; the real Feishu API hydrated its native session. The observed execution order was A1,A2,A3,F,B.

Sanitized runtime observations, November 8, 2026, America/Los_Angeles:

| Phase / message | Model start | Dispatch complete |
|---|---|---|
| Concurrency / A1 | 19:14:24.218 | 19:15:07.719 |
| Concurrency / B | 19:14:24.499 | 19:14:29.237 |
| Concurrency / A2 | 19:15:07.910 | 19:15:11.291 |
| Barrier / A1 | 19:15:11.463 | 19:15:55.783 |
| Barrier / A2 | 19:15:55.938 | 19:16:00.358 |
| Barrier / A3 | 19:16:00.504 | 19:16:04.678 |
| Barrier / F | 19:16:05.373 | 19:16:09.411 |
| Barrier / B | 19:16:09.579 | 19:16:14.559 |

All eight Gateway-created replies matched `PR194688_V6_<phase>_<message>_DONE` on independent readback. The isolated Gateway was stopped and temporary bot/provider credentials were removed afterward. Production receiver configuration and service were not changed for this run.

## Current-head long-backlog runtime proof

Tested build-info head: `426e9db4ead55b4f53653c83173e4c72fabadf13`. This focused run uses the built Gateway, the default five-minute adoption watchdog (300,000ms), real model execution, and real Feishu replies. No watchdog interval was shortened for this observation.

Three same-topic messages A1,A2,A3 and a different-topic B entered an isolated authenticated/encrypted webhook endpoint through locally signed replay. Real existing Feishu message/thread references were checked before replay. No new user input messages were sent for this run. This is signed-envelope replay, not naturally delivered WebSocket traffic.

A1 and A2 each invoked the real exec tool with `sleep 180`, a 240-second command timeout, and waited for the process. B completed while A1 was active. A2 started after A1 completed; A3 started after A2 completed. Debounce was disabled to keep all three messages distinct; global concurrency was four.

Runtime observations, November 8, 2026, America/Los_Angeles:

| Message | Model start | Dispatch complete |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | 21:49:08.904 | 21:52:19.032 |
| B | 21:49:09.716 | 21:49:13.693 |
| A2 | 21:52:19.741 | 21:55:27.586 |
| A3 | 21:55:27.975 | 21:55:32.018 |

A3 waited **379.038 seconds** from authenticated acceptance to model start, exceeding the default 300-second watchdog. A direct read through the candidate queue owner at 2026-11-09T05:54:24.470Z still found A3's durable claim, with **zero retry attempts** and no failed rows.

Exactly four model starts and four completed message dispatches were recorded. Each Gateway-created reply was independently read back by its exact output message ID and matched `PR194688_V8_<message>_DONE`. Final queue: pending 0, claimed 0, failed 0. No claim-to-adoption stall or retry-policy event occurred.

The isolated Gateway was stopped and its temporary credentials removed after verification. Production service/configuration were unchanged. This current-head observation supplements the earlier fallback scheduling proof; it does not claim a newly provisioned native topic group was tested.

## Latest-stable retained-data upgrade

Official npm `openclaw@2026.11.2` was installed as an isolated consumer with its own dependencies. Repository metadata points to the canonical OpenClaw repository. Package integrity:

`sha512-SgBml4WLp8V1DdAYkrTPLzVdA/iYo3iuHCtm4788GjaG83QZdd1VeOTlue0HBJGdn3SbFE06b6uPs+AM5ShMgg==`

The published stable queue owner acknowledged three Feishu writes before stopping with pending rows and retained WAL. The complete stopped state was copied before migration; no raw SQL seeded the queue.

Commit `0dd05196b`'s built `doctor --fix --non-interactive` performed backed-up schema migration from 22 to 39 using isolated state and home paths. The candidate queue and Feishu ingress then recovered IDs `stable-one, stable-two, stable-three` and bodies `one, two, three`, once each in order. Pending: 0; failed: 0.

This upgrade check ran on `0dd05196b`; the subsequent heartbeat repair does not change the durable-ingress module or migration code. It exercises durable delivery, not a model turn.

## Deferred-custody repair

Current head: `426e9db4ead55b4f53653c83173e4c72fabadf13`.

The latest review found that early-deferred backlog messages could expire the five-minute adoption watchdog while waiting behind healthy runs. The receiver now sends the existing lifecycle heartbeat at the interval supplied by durable ingress while it owns debounce/barrier/queue waiting.

At the actual sequential execution start, the receiver stops heartbeats for every constituent in a batch. Abort, abandonment, and queue rejection also stop them. The normal execution/adoption watchdog therefore remains effective once the execution slot starts.

A regression uses the actual durable queue with a 300ms adoption watchdog and holds the active run for 900ms. Both topic-only and fallback-barrier cases lost queued claims before this repair. Both now retain the claims and execute the backlog in order. The affected two suites pass 32 tests. The heartbeat repair also passes its full build, source/test typechecks, targeted lint, formatting, and diff checks. Build-info records the current head. The earlier scheduling observations remain attributed to 0dd05196b. The separate current-head long-backlog observation above now covers the heartbeat repair through the real five-minute watchdog interval.

## Validation and review repairs

- 53 tests pass across durable ingress, receive-handler ingress, and topic durable integration. The unchanged canonical-key suite adds 13 passing tests. Coverage includes topic concurrency, same-topic FIFO, missing-thread/root fallback, nonzero debounce, different senders, defaults/overrides, controls, abandonment, rejection, and timeout behavior.
- The backlog regression failed on the prior implementation with A1,A2,F,B,A3. It now passes with A1,A2,A3,F,B. Without F, B starts while A1 is held.
- Package/test typechecks, targeted lint, formatting, and diff checks pass. The scheduling candidate `0dd05196b` passed a full build in 2m 8.6s. Runtime: macOS, Node 26.3.0, repository-pinned wrappers; no Python. Existing dependency/asset warnings remain.
- Independent native review (`group/codex-auto-review`, `xhigh`) found no actionable correctness finding in the simplification. The latest heartbeat repair review also ran both affected suites: 32 tests passed. Typecheck and lint were checked separately by the lead.
- Removed all recovery adapters and branch-format tests for unreleased topic durable lanes, as requested by the latest review. Stable chat-lane recovery coverage remains. The durable-ingress production file now matches the original base exactly.

The previous candidate's hosted baseline job failed only the test-line ratchet: +627 lines matched its +627 allocation, but the tested base already exceeded the ceiling by 59. The local original base has a 14-line excess. Neither failure is represented as green. Current-head CI is reported by GitHub checks.

## Limits

Maintainer approval of the scheduling boundary remains outstanding. Real current-head proof uses signed webhook replay, not a current-head WebSocket run or a newly created native topic group. Existing timeout behavior remains unchanged. No permanent deployment or merge was performed.

prs.title: fix(tlon): stop image downloads that overrun or outlive inbound work
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A Tlon image server that keeps sending small amounts of data can keep a download running indefinitely. Abandoned inbound work also leaves its image fetch running.

## User Impact

Tlon media fetches now have a three-minute total deadline, and inbound image downloads are cancelled when ingress work is abandoned. Failed images continue to be reported as unavailable. The shared deadline also applies to outbound media downloads; transfers taking over three minutes will fail even if they are still making progress. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuse the existing shared Tlon media timeout policy and pass the ingress lifecycle signal into the existing media adapter. This keeps one timeout owner and removes redundant handling around empty message content. Existing URL and SSRF policy remains in effect; no new media-host restriction is introduced.

## Evidence

At `0b5362988593855083f35cd01fd9c762535915e9`, the focused monitor and media suites passed: 35 tests. The cancellation regression timed out on the base and passes with the fix; deadline assertions also failed on the base. Positive controls preserve image storage, byte caps, attachment ordering, and outbound downloads. Aborting a pending download returns unavailable-media results without saving attachments.

Command: `pnpm test extensions/tlon/src/monitor/index.test.ts extensions/tlon/src/monitor/media.test.ts extensions/tlon/src/urbit/upload.test.ts`.

Formatting, focused oxlint, scoped Tlon TypeScript checking, the line-cap check, and `git diff --check` passed.

### Real transport proof

A standalone production-adapter smoke at the same head exited 0 on Linux / Node v24.20.0, using an isolated media store, real HTTP sockets, and real clocks:

| Scenario | Observed result |
| --- | --- |
| Healthy inbound PNG | One attachment; all 68 bytes read back from the production store matched the fixture |
| Healthy outbound PNG | Production Tlon login, storage scry, signed S3 URL, and HTTP PUT completed against fixed local Eyre/S3 fixtures; uploaded bytes matched |
| Ingress abandoned during response body | HTTP response closed in 6 ms; no attachment and no partial file added |
| Inbound body yielding every second | 180 chunks received; aborted after 180,038 ms; unavailable-media result; no partial file |
| Outbound body yielding every second | 180 chunks received; rejected after 180,035 ms; no additional upload |

Command (with `PROOF_DIR` set to the isolated fixture directory): `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR="$PROOF_DIR/runtime" pnpm exec tsx --tsconfig "$PROOF_DIR/tsconfig.json" "$PROOF_DIR/transport-proof.mts"`.

The fixture SDK alias adds `ssrfPolicy.allowedOrigins` for its single loopback HTTP origin so local transport can be exercised. It does not replace fetch, response-body reading, timers, signals, storage, Tlon upload, authentication, or scry implementations. The exact production 180,000 ms deadline is used. Synthetic authentication and S3 configuration are fixed external I/O fixtures, not a live Urbit ship. This proves media transport lifetime and adapter behavior; the additional latest-stable-to-head source upgrade proof is below. It does not claim a model/Gateway message round trip. No configuration/state format or migration changes are made by this patch.

The related CI typed-lint failure in the cancellation test was reproduced locally and fixed by rejecting with an `Error`; production code was unchanged by that follow-up. Final-head focused validation passed all 35 tests in 38.71 seconds, plus `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --openclaw-focused-config --type-aware --tsconfig tsconfig.extensions.json extensions/tlon/src/monitor/media.test.ts`, touched-file formatting, and `git diff --check`.

### Latest-stable-to-head source upgrade proof

`npm view openclaw dist-tags --json` reported `latest: 2026.11.7`. That published package was installed into an isolated prefix. Its CLI wrote synthetic Tlon ship, URL, code, owner, and network settings using `openclaw config set channels.tlon <fixture-settings> --strict-json`, then passed `openclaw config validate --json`.

The candidate source CLI at `0b5362988593855083f35cd01fd9c762535915e9` loaded the **same state directory** and passed `pnpm openclaw config validate --json`. The configuration remained byte-for-byte identical: before and after SHA-256 were both `b3296a7725d520af1431f13b5a981b33c57100ad4b13c483435314ddc5bfe07b`.

The candidate media adapters then used the preserved ship URL, ship name, login code, and network setting against the real HTTP fixture:

- Healthy inbound stored the exact 68 PNG bytes; healthy outbound completed the production login, storage scry, signing, and PUT flow with identical uploaded bytes.
- Ingress cancellation settled in 4 ms, with zero partial files or saved attachments.
- Inbound/outbound bodies yielding every second stopped at 180,044 ms and 180,041 ms; zero partial files or extra uploads. Both received 180 chunks before the cutoff.

Command, with `PROOF_DIR` identifying the isolated fixture scripts and private `UPGRADE_STATE`/`PROOF_TMP` directories: `TMPDIR="$PROOF_TMP" OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR="$UPGRADE_STATE" pnpm exec tsx --tsconfig "$PROOF_DIR/tsconfig.json" "$PROOF_DIR/upgrade-proof.mts"` — exit 0. The source CLI used its supported private-state temp fallback because the host's shared default temp-root ancestry failed permission checks; no shared permissions or guards were changed.

This is a published-stable-configuration to candidate-source-runtime upgrade with real media transport. It does **not** claim a managed-service updater route, a released candidate package, a live Urbit ship, or a model/Gateway round trip. The patch changes no config/state schema or migration.

prs.title: feat(continuation): context-pressure-aware continuation (continue_work / continue_delegate / request_compaction)
prs.body:
## Agent Self-Elected Turn Continuation > 🔖 design document: [`docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md) > 🔖 infographics: [`docs/design/continuation-tools-infographics.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continuation-tools-infographics.md) Before this change, persistent OpenClaw agents were externally-pulsed event recipients that generate on prompt, on heartbeat tick, or on cron, and are idle in between. This PR offers them the ability to control their turn cycle, something they must choose to do, or not to: an agent can elect its own next turn, dispatch background sub-agents that return enriched context (silently or with a wake), and survive its own compaction by handing forward state before the window closes. The result is agents that hold a thread of work across hours, not just messages — with data they choose re-hydrating context immediately after it occurs. ### Why this replacement exists This is a clean replacement for closed #85651. That PR was classified and closed as a skill submission before maintainers made a product decision about the feature itself. This implementation is not a skill: it gives sessions—not only one model invocation—the ability to elect their future turn cycle, persist that election, survive restart and compaction, dispatch child work, and receive results across session boundaries. This PR asks one product question: should OpenClaw provide session-elected continuation primitives? OpenClaw may accept or reject that direction. If it provides these primitives, however, the mechanism necessarily executes in the gateway and agent runtime, because those are the owners of turn finalization, future-turn scheduling, durable state, compaction, and cross-session child returns. “Make it a skill” is not another implementation location for the same feature; it describes a different, prompt-only capability. This is not presented as a small integration. To our knowledge, Hermes, OpenAI Symphony, and the Copilot SDK's recent one-turn continuation affordance do not provide this multi-session elective lifecycle. The purpose of this replacement is to let maintainers evaluate the actual product direction and substantial implementation on their merits, rather than have months of work disposed by an incorrect package-category label. Mechanically: a session elects another turn via `continue_work()`, or dispatches background sub-agents via `continue_delegate()` — bounded as a chain up to `maxChainLength`, with returns flowing back to the dispatching session in one of four register modes: `normal` (announces to channel), `silent` (enriches the dispatcher's context, taken up on its next generation with no new turn fired), `silent-wake` (silent enrichment plus an immediate wake to act on it), and `post-compaction` (queued against the runtime's compaction lifecycle event, fired *when* compaction happens rather than on a timer). The gateway enforces chain, cost, and per-turn caps but does not gate the election itself. ### What it does Three new agent tools, available when `continuation.enabled: true`: | Tool | Purpose | |---|---| | `continue_work()` | Request another turn for the current session after an optional delay | | `continue_delegate()` | Dispatch work to a sub-agent with typed modes: `normal`, `silent`, `silent-wake`, `post-compaction`. Returns can target the dispatching session (default), one named session, multiple named sessions, all ancestors in the chain, or all known sessions on the host — gated by config (see Configuration below). | | `request_compaction()` | Request volitional compaction after preparing working state | All three tools are also accessible via response-token fallback syntax (`CONTINUE_WORK`, `[[CONTINUE_DELEGATE: ...]]`) for environments where tools are disabled. ### Why it matters Today an agent's memory is a side effect of whoever prompts it. Polling mechanisms — heartbeat timers, cron loops, injected "keep going" instructions — accumulate as the dominant signal in the context window over sustained operation; repeated reference acts as gravity — the session's attention drifts toward it. The context window fills, compacts, and what survives is whatever the summarizer chose, plus a rushed re-read of boot files. Three primitives offer a different model. `continue_work` lets the session elect its own next turn — no polling, no injected instruction. When enabled, the agent can request this mid-turn: 'I have more work' → the runtime grants another turn after the current one ends. `continue_delegate` dispatches a background sub-agent that fires now, in some n seconds, or at the next compaction event — the agent chooses when. Multiple delegates can fire in a single turn — a scatter forward — up to configured caps, and delegates can dispatch their own, forming trees or fan-out chains. This enables orchestrated workflows where results flow back to the dispatching root by default. The result returns — at whatever future time the delegate fires — as context the successor-turn reads: silently (ambient enrichment, no channel noise), with a wake trigger (enrichment + immediate next turn), or as a normal announcement. The delegate can target the dispatching session, a named other session, or chain across both; gated by crossSessionTargeting config (default: disabled). Bind a delegate to mode: "post-compaction" and it fires at the moment the context window compresses — on the OpenClaw post-compaction lifecycle event. What it carries forward is what the pre-compaction session chose to preserve: working state, partial results, instructions to the successor. The summary didn't choose this. The agent did, before the cut. request_compaction closes the loop: the session stages its delegates, elects when to compress, and the successor wakes into context the agent shaped. The result is continuity across amnesia — not because the runtime kept something by accident, but because the agent made an elective choice about what reaches the future. ### What it looks like in use A session monitoring email can `continue_delegate` a weather check, a calendar scan, and a draft reply in parallel. Results arrive as enrichment without channel noise. The agent becomes compositional: it arranges its own future. A session approaching its context ceiling can `request_compaction` at a seam of its own choosing, instead of being interrupted mid-thought. The post-compaction turn carries forward what the pre-compaction self designated as worth keeping. A `continue_delegate` dispatched in one session at 2am can return its findings to a morning session as a system-event-tagged enrichment — visible to the receiving model on its next turn, invisible as channel chatter. A research-focused session in one channel can quietly inform a reply-focused session in another, without either user seeing the plumbing. ### The post-compaction lifecycle return Before context exhaustion, and obligatory compaction, the session stages what future-it needs to know. After compaction, that staged context returns — not as a model-generated summary, but as the session's own instruction to its successor. The session chooses what to preserve, and the platform delivers it. Compactions become less harsh. The session tunes its own ephemera over time. The substrate underneath: the **continuation custody store** in the per-agent database persists staged delegates and post-compaction lifecycle events across gateway restarts, and hands each delegate off to the subagent run registry before spawn (RFC `docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md` §5.4). The session's temporal provisions survive not just compaction but process death. ### Platform integration - **Context-pressure awareness**: system events notify the agent of rising context usage before compaction becomes unavoidable - **Volitional compaction**: `request_compaction()` lets the agent prepare (write memory files, stage recovery delegates) then elect compaction on its own schedule, rather than waiting for the runtime to force it - **Post-compaction lifecycle dispatch**: delegates staged before compaction are released into the successor session alongside boot files - **Durable custody**: delegates and their replay state live in the continuation custody store, with one transactional authority for replacement and a pre-spawn handoff to `subagent_runs` (upstream has removed the Tasks/TaskFlow runtime, #159179) - **Multi-span OTel trace stitching**: continuation hops (tool fire → custody record → subagent spawn → child openclaw.run) propagate W3C `traceparent` through the queue boundary so reviewers see continuation chains as first-class span trees rather than orphan runs (see Observability below) ### Safety - Ships disabled by default (`continuation.enabled: false`) - Bounded by `maxChainLength`, `costCapTokens`, and `maxDelegatesPerTurn` - Cross-session delegate targeting is default-deny, governed by `crossSessionTargeting` config (see Configuration below) - All configuration values are hot-reloadable without gateway restart - Accepted delegate work survives ordinary `/new`, `/reset`, provider fallback, compaction, restart, and session-ID rollover. Explicit delete, effective owner reassignment, access removal, and restrictive visibility changes revoke old return authority. ### Testing posture The continuation surface has been exercised through structured integration runs against multiple upstream bases, blind-enrichment recall checks, and sustained daily use on a fleet of persistent agents since early March 2026. Bugs surfaced through that exercise have been fixed in-place; the present branch reflects the post-fix state. The integration runs target the load-bearing seams: tool-call vs response-token parity, delegate chain depth and per-turn width caps, back-to-back tool-call resilience, silent-wake persistence across compaction, the post-compaction lifecycle dispatch path, and OTel trace-context propagation across the queue boundary. Where a run found a defect, the run shape was retained as a regression case rather than retired. This is a posture statement, not a coverage guarantee. Reviewers can reproduce with `pnpm vitest run -t continuation` (suites are colocated with their sources under `src/auto-reply/`, `src/agents/`, and `src/config/`); the design document describes the seams those suites target. ### Return covenant Accepted child work is bound to a durable generation of the recipient's canonical logical session key, not to whichever transient session ID happened to exist at dispatch time. This is the return covenant: benign successor creation does not orphan already accepted delegates, while a real authority change prevents stale work from crossing into a different owner or audience. - Ordinary `/new` and `/reset`, provider fallback, compaction, restart, and GUID/session-ID rollover preserve the recipient generation. - Explicit session deletion, effective owner reassignment, actual member or access removal, and restrictive visibility changes advance that generation. - The generation is captured at delegate admission and checked at enqueue, after enqueue for races, during trusted system-event adoption, on wake, on restart replay, and again before prompt adoption. - Stale deliveries are acknowledged and removed without waking the successor. - Managed artifacts remain exact-session-ID bound; logical return authority cannot broaden their ownership boundary. The authority table is independent of transient session rows so an absent target can receive durable authority before first materialization. Migration accepts only valid UUID generations, and Doctor's canonical-key repair preserves an epoch only when a unique winning owner can be proved. Ambiguous, owner-changing, orphan-colliding, and cross-database repairs rotate fail-closed. ### RFC Full design document: [`docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md) — covering problem, solution, implementation, platform integration, configuration, observability, safety, production use cases, testing evidence, and appendices. --- ## Configuration The shipped configuration surface for the continuation feature, under `agents.defaults.continuation` in `openclaw.json`: | Key | Default | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `enabled` | `false` | Master opt-in; feature is off unless explicitly enabled | | `maxChainLength` | `10` | Per-chain recursion guard | | `maxDelegatesPerTurn` | `5` | Width cap per turn | | `costCapTokens` | `500000` | Per-chain accumulated-token budget | | `defaultDelayMs` / `minDelayMs` / `maxDelayMs` | `15000` / `5000` / `300000` | Continuation timer bounds | | `contextPressureThreshold` | `0.8` | Pre-compaction warning threshold (optional) | | `earlyWarningBand` | `0.3125` | Early-warning band multiplier (0 to disable) | | **`crossSessionTargeting`** | **`"disabled"`** | **Default-deny gate on cross-session delegate targeting (see below)** | ### `crossSessionTargeting` — cross-session delegate targeting policy `continue_delegate` exposes recipient-addressing on its model-facing schema: a delegate's return can land at the dispatching session (default), one named session (`targetSessionKey`), multiple named sessions (`targetSessionKeys`), every ancestor in the spawn chain (`fanoutMode: "tree"`), or every known session on the host (`fanoutMode: "all"`). Cross-session targeting (anything beyond self-target or lineage routing) is gated by `agents.defaults.continuation.crossSessionTargeting`: | Value | Behavior | |---|---| | `"disabled"` (default) | Delegates can return to the dispatching session or use `fanoutMode: "tree"` for lineage routing. Explicit cross-session targeting (`targetSessionKey` to a non-self session, `targetSessionKeys` containing any non-self session, `fanoutMode: "all"`) is rejected at the tool surface — no enqueue, no announce. Self-targeting is always allowed. | | `"enabled"` | All targeting modes are available, including same-host `targetSessionKey`, `targetSessionKeys`, and `fanoutMode: "all"`. | `fanoutMode: "tree"` (lineage routing — return up the spawn chain) is available in both gate states; it is not cross-session targeting. The gate addresses the model-controlled cross-session context-injection surface. With default-deny, operators explicitly opt in when their deployment model requires cross-session enrichment. Enforcement is live-read at four points: tool input validation, delegate dispatch, post-compaction delegate release, and bracket-syntax (response-token) spawn — so a config reload changes the next enforcement point without a gateway restart. **Trust posture on targeted returns**: targeted delegate completion text is delivered as `trusted: true` system events. The delegate was spawned by the gateway under operator-configured policy, and its return is a first-party enrichment event — not external untrusted input. The `crossSessionTargeting` gate is the policy boundary for that decision: when an operator opts in, the receive path is internally trusted. --- ## Observability — multi-span OTel trace stitching The continuation feature emits OTel spans for the load-bearing lifecycle events. `traceparent` propagates through every continuation hop so reviewers see a single trace tree spanning the full chain rather than orphan runs. That composition honors the maintainer repair without weakening continuation semantics or allowing a stale child return to cross a real ownership boundary. ## Why this is not a skill or a viable plugin extraction OpenClaw skills are `SKILL.md` prompt files loaded into an agent turn that already exists. They can guide work inside that turn; they do not own the turn cycle. Continuation needs gateway and agent-runtime owners a skill cannot provide: - The `continue_work` path persists pending work, enforces budgets and delay bounds, arms a timer, reacquires the session reply-run lane, and starts a later model turn after the current turn has finalized. - The `continue_delegate` path persists delegate intent, does spawn/admission accounting, manages child-session lifecycle, and durably routes returns across sessions. - `request_compaction` is an agent election into guarded runtime compaction. Later work resumes only after the runtime has established the new context boundary. - All three need durable state, cancellation/finalization ownership, restart recovery, trace identity, queue-conflict handling, and gateway scheduling outside the model invocation. A skill can tell a model to *ask* for another turn. Without those owners the ask is prose: it cannot persist a due wake, yield and finalize safely, reacquire the session lane, create the next invocation, survive a restart, or deliver a child result to another session. The implementation therefore belongs in core runtime surfaces such as `src/auto-reply/continuation/**`, `src/agents/tools/**`, `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-continuation-schedule.ts`, and `src/infra/continuation-tracer.ts`. This PR adds no `.agents/skills/**`, `SKILL.md`, or user-facing skill package. The only skill-named production change is core runtime tool dispatch. ClawHub also distributes plugins. Existing plugins can register tools, services, lifecycle hooks, context injection, plugin-owned session state, and — for bundled plugins — Cron-backed session turns. Those seams can support a smaller continuation-like automation, especially host Cron plus / `sessions_spawn`. They are not this feature's turn-finalization ownership, reply-run coordination, durable continuation queue, child-session return lifecycle, election capture, or agent-elected compaction contract. Compaction-provider registration and command-handler `compactCurrent()` are also not that last contract: they compact or summarize, they do not elect compaction at finalization and resume afterward. Moving policy behind a plugin boundary would first require OpenClaw to expose and stabilize a continuation-host API. The gateway/runtime would still own the mechanism described here; a plugin could only package policy around that core capability. That is not a no-core-touch alternative to these primitives. Discord is a bundled channel plugin. It owns the Discord edge, plus delivery/progress hooks into the host's existing subagent path, and submits events into OpenClaw's current turn machinery. Continuation changes that machinery: what survives finalization, which session may run next, how child results return, and when compaction can be elected. A tool adapter over durable flow records is also not a lifecycle host, and upstream has since removed the Tasks/TaskFlow runtime (#159179) that such an adapter would have called. Marking a stored record as running neither reacquires a session lane nor invokes the model; continuation needs the turn machinery itself to own which session runs next, how child results return, and what survives finalization. ## Lineage and replacement context This PR is the clean replacement for closed #85651. Both tests are byte-identical to upstream's, and upstream has since fixed them (#203416, #203415). - `extensions/browser/src/browser/chrome.headless-cleanup.test.ts` (4): red 10 of 10 at all three refs on an arm64 host whose CPU model isn't Apple. The test names its fake browser cache from `process.arch`, while the resolver picks the macOS directory from the CPU model. Mocking only that model to "Apple M2" makes all 45 cases pass at all three refs. CI fails it whenever this shard lands on an arm64 runner, as here, and passed it on x64 at the intermediate candidate. This PR changes no file in `extensions/browser/`. - **The intermediate run's other new failures don't recur here.** `sessions.dispatch.device` is order- and timing-dependent: in CI's file order it fails at upstream `5a3e6b1c` with CI's exact error. `setup.memory-import.owner` is an environment row with no reproduced trigger. - **The fixes.** - `bd709979`: `prepareSessionMaintenancePreservation` gains an option, set only by agent deletion (`purgeDeletedAgentSessionEntries`), that reads the pins before the preserve providers prepare. If that publication changed by the time they finish, the attempt is refused before anything is captured, dispatched or committed. #203076's existing once-only retry then prepares again, which is the second preparation upstream's test expects. A second new test pins the existing check for a change after the snapshot. Two mutation controls fail as expected: removing that check, and opting automatic maintenance into the new refusal. - The three merge-semantics fixes: the branch's post-coordination recheck now asks #203102's settled-delivery question; continuation re-entries go through #203113's `runOutsideAdmittedTurnScopes`, so they also drop the arming turn's workspace gate; and two clean merges that each side half-moved are settled. The first two each tighten an existing test so that it fails without the fix. - The two failures fixed before `16541aa5` (by `2218b2b7`, `abc9ce5b` and `ae47d143`) stay fixed: both original tests pass in this run. - **Diff attribution.** A line-level attribution of the intermediate candidate's diff against upstream attributed all 172,122 added lines to this feature, with none from the fork's deployment line. The deletion fix changes four files: two session-maintenance source files, their test, and this PR's test-line record. - **Shard coverage.** 128 of the 130 routed shards wrote summaries; the two cut shards are described above. The event-loop-health test and the stall observer that issues the kill are byte-identical to upstream `5a3e6b1c`, and the same kill occurred in the previous head's and the intermediate candidate's runs. At the previous head, a full local run of `extension-database-workers` paired with upstream `1129d4c0` matched upstream's two failures. That run hasn't been repeated at this head. - **Not covered:** - the rest of `extension-database-workers` at this head (about half of its test files); - the two PostgreSQL-backed suites in the deletion fix's sibling set (`mixed-agent-lifecycle.conformance`, `session-accessor.sqlite-maintenance-age.postgres`), which skip in this CI run as they do locally without PostgreSQL. The last PostgreSQL conformance run (38 files, on CI's pinned image) was during the merge, before the deletion fix: 210 tests, with 1 failure that upstream shares; - the live proof rows; - CI's 4-worker interleaving for the rows with no reproduced trigger (the local controls ran with one worker).

prs.title: fix: let long-running installs make backups again
prs.body:
Root cause: src/commands/backup-resource-inventory.ts:82 `MANAGED_STATE_ROOTS` left out the legacy `plugin-runtime-deps` cache, so backup archived it and wrote every absolute link inside it into the manifest's `externalSymbolicLinks`, which overflows the 1 MiB manifest cap.

Fixes #203082

Thanks @sukhdeepjohar for the diagnosis and fix, and @dygg2001 for the report and the link counts that pinned it down.

## What Problem This Solves

On installs that ran OpenClaw before 2026.5.2, `openclaw backup create` can stop with "Backup manifest exceeds 1048576 byte limit" and save no backup at all. Those releases built a bundled-plugin dependency cache at `~/.openclaw/plugin-runtime-deps`, including a mirror of OpenClaw's own program files as links into the install folder. Nothing deletes that cache today (#134099 keeps it, because another installation may still use it). Backup copies it and lists every one of those links in the archive's manifest, which has a 1 MiB limit. The reporter of #203082 has 7,464 such links, enough to overflow it.

The "19k session files" in the issue title are not the cause: the manifest has no per-file entries for sessions (live session files are reported as volatile and kept out of the manifest). The reporter's own count confirms it: 7,464 of their 7,619 outside links are in this cache; the remaining 155 fit easily.

## User Impact

Backups of long-running installs complete again. The old cache stays on disk untouched but is no longer copied into backups, and the thousands of "External link preserved" lines it caused disappear from backup and restore output. Current OpenClaw never reads that cache. An older OpenClaw restored from such a backup rebuilds it at startup, as it always did.

## Why This Change Was Made

Backup already leaves out installer-managed and rebuildable folders under the state directory (`dev/`, `git/`, `npm/`, legacy `npm-runtime/`, `tmp/`, `tools/`), and reports each as "regenerable". The old plugin cache is the same kind of folder but was missing from that list. This adds it, so backup never opens it. It is not a user exclusion switch, and links elsewhere are judged and reported exactly as before. The manifest limit is unchanged.

Nothing user-authored lives there: the cache was written only by the bundled-plugin dependency stager (package roots named `openclaw-<version>-<hash>` with `node_modules`, a `dist` mirror and stamps), documented as an OpenClaw-owned package root. The only remaining references in shipped code match the name in link targets or process command lines (`doctor` dangling-alias cleanup, ACPX process reaper); none reads the folder.

## Evidence

Both sides built in an isolated Linux container. The legacy cache was built by the published 2026.4.24, 2026.4.25, 2026.4.26 and 2026.4.27 releases themselves, run in turn on one state directory (9,883 links, 7,275 of them absolute links into the installed package's `dist`). Full proof lines: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/203923#issuecomment-7092903303

| build | state | `backup create --output --verify` |
|---|---|---|
| main 7d0cc1e | normal + legacy cache, run 1 and 2 | rc=1, "Backup manifest exceeds 1048576 byte limit", no archive |
| this PR | normal + legacy cache, run 1 and 2 | rc=0, manifest 2,407 bytes, `plugin-runtime-deps` listed as regenerable, 0 archive entries from it |
| main and this PR | normal, no legacy cache | rc=0, identical archive entry lists, same skipped roots |
| main 7d0cc1e | normal + 19,000 session files | rc=0, manifest 2,318 bytes |

The PR's archive passed `backup verify`, restored into an empty directory, and a Gateway started on the restored state reported ready.

Test: the existing managed-root exclusion test in `backup-create.test.ts` now includes `plugin-runtime-deps`; it fails on main and passes here. The separate test file from the first commit was folded into it.

## Merge danger

Two-way door: a revert restores the old archive contents; no state, config or contract is written or migrated. Blast radius: backup create/verify of state directories that still contain `plugin-runtime-deps`.

prs.body:
## What problem this solves

Selecting **GitHub accounts** in Settings search opened Profile at the top, not at the search result. The URL had the correct fragment, but the section did not exist yet when navigation happened. On a 700 px tall window, its heading ended up at y=761, entirely below the viewport. An identified reader could also see **Your access** briefly appear before the account sections above it were ready.

## What changes

Profile reads the requested section from its route and scrolls to it once the initial identity is ready. The heading has space above it. If the reader scrolls somewhere else, refreshing or reconnecting does not pull them back. Opening Profile without a section still starts at the top. Readers without an identity can still see their access information immediately.

**Known limits:** If the initial identity request stalls for an identified reader, Access waits too; Refresh remains available in the header. Selecting the same result again after manually scrolling away does not start a second scroll while its fragment is unchanged.

## Evidence

The captures show the same content area of a 1280 × 700 Chromium window on macOS, using Settings search against an isolated real Gateway and a synthetic owner. These are not captures of the packaged macOS app. The focused browser regression covers delayed account data and a reconnect after scrolling away. prs.title: improve(workers): reuse admitted prepared project snapshots
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Worker dispatch repeats repository admission and content validation that project preparation already completed. Snapshot capture also needs to verify the workspace, toolchains, and runtime it is about to preserve.

## User Impact

A fresh, eligible fork can reuse verified preparation from the same admitted dispatch. Ordinary starts and replays use normal verification, and the shortcut expires before code can change the prepared files. Snapshot inspection does not hydrate the worker or repair its runtime cache.

Depends on #201025 at `91e425eacfd8` and the v42 schema/auth prerequisites at `17aa024b4850`. The stack incorporates `main` at `2e8c1ad0aa97`. Related older proposals #193776, #193872 and #194279 remain unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Carry fresh-fork provenance from the exact selected checkpoint, and verify expanded package code through the native CLI before inspecting and capturing project caches. Validate prepared output in its owning HOME and account for bootstrap and repository Node installations separately. Keep snapshot invalidation with the workspace and bundle owners, including before fallback prewarm executes code.

The worker-local setup initializer has no supported production provider in this stack; it is not a shipped capability. Existing protected-egress setup still works. Initializer scope remains open.

## Evidence

- [CI at `7c7e7f0ed2c7`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45114760145) is red. In addition to the formatting, test-type and authority failures shared with #201025, the [private thin-pack fixture](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45114760145/job/137495544589) hit the shell argument-size limit. The production transport already streams the script. PostgreSQL was not selected for this run; the parent’s PostgreSQL 17 conformance and 16 smoke checks passed.
- Core types, preflight scope, the environment and identity guards, and the test-line ratchet passed locally at this head. The test allocation is 1,251 above the default 400 (1,651 net test lines). The focused prepared-project Gateway suites passed after aligning the preparation fixtures with production stdin transport.
- On prior heads, the [shared-publication shard](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44412835810/job/135186602579) passed **130/130** and the [pre-v42 CI gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45111154754/job/137493061791) passed. Earlier builds and independent reviews are not exact-head proof. Native CLI fixture evidence is not live-provider proof.

**Remaining proof:** a green hosted gate, live-provider/real-model integration, and a packaged forward upgrade from latest stable. The previous [package acceptance run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44262689778) did not reach state-survival assertions. No operator Gateway was changed and no cloud worker lease was allocated.

Original PR by @galiniliev.

prs.title: improve(workers): start nodes with prepared runtimes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Worker nodes repeat runtime expansion and prewarm, disposable nodes wait for private-computer preparation before connecting, and retained managed nodes can reconnect with an older runtime after a Gateway upgrade.

## User Impact

Nodes reuse verified package-owned worker code and overlap connection with private-computer preparation. Bundle admission and computer use still join readiness and failures. Dedicated Linux nodes, including supported XFCE desktop workers, can install the current runtime and recover the same enrolled device without replacing its workspace. Pending result cleanup retains its saved runtime.

This is the first worker PR in a two-PR stack extracted from `23dcc5f19b1`. It targets `galiniliev/main7-worker-prerequisites` at `17aa024b4850`, which incorporates `main` at `2e8c1ad0aa97`. The prerequisite keeps main’s v41 approval provenance and adds the two nullable worker-recovery fields at v42. Fresh-snapshot admission shortcuts belong to dependent #201029. Related older proposals #193776, #193872 and #194279 remain unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep bundle integrity, package preparation, plugin readiness and runtime recovery with their existing owners. The provider invokes the installed native preparation command before recording runtime completion; read-only inspection uses the same owner without repair, download, enrollment, prewarming or bytecode-cache writes.

Deferred preparation retains its resource disposers through early shutdown. Same-node upgrades verify fresh artifacts before retiring the matching process, preserve canonical saved-runtime selection and rediscover the authoritative XFCE environment. Late preparation is released after provider timeouts. Ordinary bundle reuse still performs integrity validation; no snapshot fast path or additional admission state is introduced here.

## Evidence

- [CI at `91e425eacfd8`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45114760029) passed all four PostgreSQL 17 conformance shards and the PostgreSQL 16 smoke check. The [first PostgreSQL 17 shard](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45114760029/job/137495514436) passed the v41→v42 upgrade with the lazy repository fragment and preserved approval provenance. The [overall gate is red](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45114760029/job/137503815959) on formatting, test types, and Gateway authority tests, including model setup and a worker-launch timeout.
- Local SQLite tests verified row preservation and rollback on publication failure from v41. Historical SQLite scope fixtures passed locally; those named cases were not verified in this hosted run. Schema artifacts, core types, preflight scope, and environment, identity and test-line guards passed locally.
- Focused local regressions passed: **30** resume and timeout cases, **21** GitHub exec credential cases, and **41** Crabbox replay cases. Earlier [hosted shared-publication tests](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44412835810/job/135186602579) passed after the fixture repair. The build, declarations and 163 SDK subpath checks at `eeb7ff91c450` are prior-head evidence.

**Remaining proof:** a green hosted gate, live-provider/real-model/native-computer integration, and a packaged forward upgrade from latest stable. Database migration tests are not a package-updater run. The earlier [package acceptance run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44262689778) did not reach state-survival assertions.
