prs.title: fix(signal): unblock approvals while the requesting turn is waiting
prs.body:
Closes #194029

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Signal approval responses wait behind the turn they need to release. Once dispatched, UUID approvers can be rejected after command normalization, and a typed approval confirmation can cancel the waiting turn with a transcript conflict.

## User Impact

An authorized owner can approve a waiting command from Signal using `/approve` or a supported reaction. Ordinary messages and session-mutating commands retain their conversation ordering. Existing access, exact-target approval checks, and durable audit records remain enforced.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Route the existing narrow set of Signal controls and canonical approval-reaction candidates through a conversation-scoped control lane. Previously stored controls can move only from their exact original conversation lane to that conversation's control lane.
- Supply text-command facts for core active-run admission.
- Preserve UUIDs through Signal command/allowlist normalization instead of stripping their letters into phone-number-like values.
- Keep fast `/approve` exchanges visible in history but outside model context, using the existing context-free recorder contract. Their confirmations must not invalidate the transcript snapshot of the turn waiting for approval; the decision still reaches the model through the tool result.

The lifecycle type lives in the existing leaf types module, removing the review's import cycle. The existing routing helper moves unchanged into the context sibling to respect the oversized handler's growth guard. No schema, dependency, public SDK surface, or configuration option is added.

Related reviews: #175345 does not change Signal ingress; #191787 concerns native-approval capability metadata; merged #153829 supplies the Telegram control-lane precedent. The final recorder fix follows the existing context-free status mechanism from #192585.

## Conflict refresh — 2026-11-22

Merged upstream `5e371a0b7799801eb738b993ae3b9687f78dd636` into the existing branch. Updated head: `9a127a4edc681600339ba441ccdd6459aa567e48`.

The sole conflict was in the slash-command guide. The resolution documents both the context-free fast `/approve` exchange and upstream's deferred recording of other command exchanges during an active turn. The TypeScript patch introduced by this PR is identical to the previous revision.

- **152 focused tests passed across 10 files** on the merged tree. Coverage includes Signal approval scheduling, replay, UUID handling, mentions, view-once attachment handling, and command history during an active turn, including late `/stop` delivery.
- Scoped review found no issue in the manual resolution or the overlapping automatic merges. Targeted lint, formatting, diff checks, the test-line budget, pre-commit, and the import-cycle check passed.
- The earlier live Signal/model, upgrade, and authorization tests below remain evidence for their recorded revision. GitHub CI on the refreshed head is tracked separately in the PR checks.

## Conflict refresh — 2026-11-17

Merged upstream `edbc5bcea9b605a826cc722d298c784c6a8fef78` into the existing branch, preserving its four original commits. Updated head: `8ce7760f3ebe8ea065b5f00099fbc6c0448fafab`.

The only textual conflict was in Signal's inbound context helper: this branch relocates the existing routing helper, while upstream #200058 renders native mentions in quoted messages. The resolution retains both. Automatically merged changes preserve upstream response-prefix handling and restart tests alongside the approval fixes. The introduced PR diff remains 15 files, +269/-70.

- **176 focused cases pass in 10 files** on the resolved tree: 81 Signal cases (including upstream quoted-mention and group-mention tests), and 95 shared command/transcript cases. Signal wrapper wall time: 120.55 seconds; shared wrapper wall time: 98.78 seconds, including compilation.
- Production core and Signal package type checks, focused regression-test types, targeted lint, formatting, diff checks, pre-commit guard, and import-cycle check pass (0 runtime value cycles). The current test-line budget passes: +138 test lines, 400 allowance, 138 existing allocation credit; no baseline or allocation changes.
- Fresh independent read-only review of the public conflict-resolution bundle found no actionable merge regression. The initial agy review timed out without a result; the completed fallback review covered the manual resolution and overlapping automatic merges.
- The first sandboxed test attempt was stopped after process-identity/loopback restrictions caused fixture failures. The completed run used the required local process and loopback permissions. One type-check attempt overlapped lint's artifact ownership; it was rerun successfully after lint completed.
- Live Signal/model, stable-upgrade, and final-effect authorization receipts below remain evidence for the explicitly pinned earlier head `d24bc8ab8ccbd869accc368c9b6a595016e65055`; those external/live checks were not repeated for this conflict refresh. New-head GitHub CI is separate from the earlier passing runs. [CI run 43902495410](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43902495410) currently reports `action_required` with zero jobs; no new-head CI pass is claimed. GitHub reports the updated PR mergeable; maintainer review and the workflow action remain pending.

## Evidence from the earlier tested head

- Base used for local proof: `8b023da72a1a595450b3071782ec1d4940bd459f`. Previously live-tested candidate: `d24bc8ab8ccbd869accc368c9b6a595016e65055`.
- Red before repair: DM/group queue controls do not dispatch; command context is `normal` rather than `text-slash`; three UUID formats fail approval authorization after command formatting; the fast-approval recording boundary omits `contextFreeCommand`. Corresponding regressions pass after repair.
- **206 relevant cases pass across 11 test files**: 113 Signal cases and 93 shared command/transcript cases. The final consolidated fixture was also verified by rerunning its 74-case lifecycle suite. Signal validation took 63.80 seconds; shared validation took 103.85 seconds, including compilation. Existing authorization, wrong-target, ordinary FIFO, replay, and routing controls remain covered.
- Official production-core and extension type checks, focused changed-test type checks, type-aware lint, formatting, diff and pre-commit checks pass. Temporary test configurations extend the repository configuration; no compiler settings were committed.
- Final clean Linux CLI-startup build passed in **2m 10.7s**. This is the startup profile, not a full release/package/declaration build. Local architecture check reports **0 cycles**.
- Independent reviews of the cycle repair, UUID repair, and final recorder diff returned scoped-clean. The test fixture stays in its existing suite and shrinks by consolidating repeated values.

### Live Signal and model proof

Verified the exact clean candidate with a real agent, configured OpenAI model, and the registered Signal account through Signal Desktop. Approval mode remained gated; only allow-once decisions were used.

```text
candidate: d24bc8ab8ccbd869accc368c9b6a595016e65055
whoami request: pending
/status during the wait: replied; displayed d24bc8a
/approve <redacted> allow-once: allowed via channel policy
whoami final reply: stdout openclaw
separate printf signal-final-ok request: pending
thumbs-up on its native prompt: allowed via channel policy
final reply: signal-final-ok
ingress after both cases: completed=20, pending=0, claimed=0, failed=0
```

These checks exposed and reproduced both the UUID normalization refusal and the typed-confirmation transcript conflict before their repairs. The final run completed without those failures. Only sanitized decision metadata and receipts are included here; no private transcript, account identifier, credential, or screenshot is published.

### Actual stable upgrade

The installed stable core and official Signal plugin, both 2026.11.1, accepted real Signal events into a separate state directory. The stable journal contained an ordinary completion, a claimed typed approval, and a pending reaction in the original direct-conversation lane. After stopping stable, applying the supported offline Doctor migration to the test copy, and starting the candidate, all three records were completed, with the pending reaction reconciled to the control lane; no pending or failed ingress remained.

Account, account UUID, owner allowlist, agent/session filters, default model, and exec/elevated/filesystem policies were checked against the verified native backup and retained. The fixture uses a separate workspace and disables scheduled jobs. Native reaction tests explicitly use forwarding mode `session` with the existing private-session filter; `targets` alone does not start Signal's native approval handler. This demonstrates real packaged-state transport replay, not continuation of an already terminated process's exec call.

### Final-effect authorization proof

The follow-up security review requested rejection at the actual decision owner, beyond the identity helper. On the same exact built head, a separate credential-free Gateway loaded the real Signal plugin and approval capability. Its real exec tool requested a harmless file-marker command; no approval or execution callback was mocked.

For each public resolver used by Signal—legacy `exec.approval.resolve` for typed commands and canonical `approval.resolve` for reactions—both checks passed:

| Resolver | Refused actor | Approval after refusal | Decision waiter released | Command ran before current approval | Same command ran after current approval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `exec.approval.resolve` | Unlisted UUID | pending; no decision | no | no | yes |
| `exec.approval.resolve` | Queued, then revoked UUID | pending; no decision | no | no | yes |
| `approval.resolve` | Unlisted UUID | pending; no decision | no | no | yes |
| `approval.resolve` | Queued, then revoked UUID | pending; no decision | no | no | yes |

The unlisted UUID differs from the listed UUID only in letters, retaining the same numeric projection. In each revocation case, the old actor's control was first persisted with the real SQLite channel-ingress queue, and its pending row was checked. The Gateway's runtime configuration publisher then replaced the Signal approver policy while the original exec request remained alive. Only after publication was the unchanged queued control claimed and submitted to the real resolver. It was refused with `APPROVAL_NOT_FOUND`; `approval.get` still showed pending without a decision, the real decision waiter remained blocked, and the command's marker did not exist. A current listed actor then approved that exact request; the waiter returned allow-once and the real command created its marker. This positive control was repeated for all four cases.

This is an owner-boundary integration proof with synthetic identities and a test-controlled dispatch barrier, not another live Signal-network/model run. It deliberately submits to the final resolver rather than relying on earlier channel rejection. Runtime policy publication isolates the custody guard from file-reload scheduling; no authorization checks or process guards were bypassed. Separately, an attempted public `config.patch` policy reload was observed deferring Signal reload until active Gateway requests finish, so that timed-out attempt is **not** counted as revocation proof. The earlier exact-head live Signal/model proof remains the transport/user-flow evidence. The final isolated Gateway closed cleanly. No production source change was needed for this additional proof.

### Check boundaries

The local test-line guard against the historical base remains **25 lines over due to inherited debt**: base 6,533,876/6,533,851; candidate 6,534,014/6,533,989. The patch adds 138 counted regression lines and exactly 138 allocation credit. The shared baseline and unrelated tests were not changed.

The SQLite and HTTP fixtures were run on a qualified host with process-owner and loopback access. The exact candidate's [CI gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42223925652/job/127915523030) and [architecture guard](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42223925652/job/127913150828) pass.

The candidate was used for bounded tests, and the normal stable service was restored. No permanent deployment or merge has been performed. Maintainer/security review remains required.

## What Problem This Solves

The release skills directed operators toward fresh qualification when same-parent continuation could not restore its execution plan, without making the dedicated receipt-backed recovery route easy to discover. ## User Impact

Documentation only. Release operators can distinguish same-parent continuation from receipt-backed aggregate recovery and assess the latter before restarting a drained FRV. No runtime behavior, qualification policy, or publication gate changes.

- Link the route from maintainer phase selection, validation guidance, and existing continuation limitations.
- Preserve original admission, C/Q, receipts, artifact identities, and raw waived failures; require authenticated recovery and normal publication verification.
- Make clear that recovery creates a separate aggregate and never changes the failed original parent to green.

## Evidence

- Formatter check passed for all three changed Markdown files.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Recovery links and target anchors verified in all three changed files.
- Commands and constraints checked against the canonical receipt-backed recovery documentation and dispatch implementation.
- Runtime tests not run: this change only updates release skill documentation.

prs.title: fix: preserve chat participant recording after SQLite upgrades
prs.body:
Related: #186529 (startup repair for a different column on the same table) and #181875 (database-port compatibility with missing first-use columns).

## What Problem This Solves

An upgraded SQLite store can report the current shared-state schema version while its profile identity table still lacks `verified_email_json`. Chat can continue even though participant recording fails when the identity reader selects that column before any profile write has run.

## User Impact

Participant attribution can read existing profiles on affected upgraded stores without waiting for a profile edit. Existing roles, identity links, and display metadata are preserved. Fresh installs still create profile tables only when needed. Offline SQLite port inspection and migration continue to accept these stores without modifying the source.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use the existing startup repair path to add this already-canonical nullable column to an existing identity table. The offline port uses the same column definition in its compatibility list, both for source inspection and to fill it in the private working copy. No version bump, new table, read-time schema write, or access-policy change.

## Evidence

- **Isolated WebChat upgrade passed on `9f47764cb`.** Started the latest stable package (`v2026.11.6`) on synthetic state and completed a WebChat turn. With stable stopped, seeded the absent-column shape and an existing account link, then ran the candidate's real maintenance preparation (shared state 36 → 41, agent state 38 → 43). On the source-mode candidate Gateway, a second signed WebChat turn completed through loopback inference. The same owner and the prior session stayed readable. After shutdown the candidate turn had a durable profile participant row, the account link and config bytes were unchanged, the column was present, and SQLite `quick_check` returned `ok`. The owner is deliberately hidden from the RPC's participant summary when shown separately as owner, so the test verified the persisted row.
- Reproduced `no such column: "verified_email_json"` through the real profile identity selector on upstream main before the change. All 46 focused state tests pass on the corrected revision, covering affected and healthy current-version stores, role and account-link preservation, display metadata, and reopening.
- Reproduced ClawSweeper’s offline port finding on the previous PR head (`641f6037f`): the existing state-port regression refused the incomplete source schema. All 20 port-command tests pass on `9f47764cb`. The state case checks the existing role and identity link, a `NULL` value in the added column on the private copy, and an unchanged SHA-256 for the source.
- The 27 Gateway chat-method tests passed on the first revision, including authenticated participant recording. The follow-up changes port compatibility and its test without changing the startup classification. Targeted no-emit typecheck for state and infra, oxlint, formatting, and `git diff --check` passed on the corrected revision.
- **Still pending:** a packaged-candidate run with a real model. The stable side used the shipped package; the candidate ran under the repository’s isolated source-mode Gateway harness. Inference used a synthetic loopback provider; no production state or credentials were used.

<details>
<summary>Terminal evidence: stable-to-source WebChat upgrade</summary>

Selected output from the isolated test at `9f47764cb95194ff70351df614a1f0a1de6e20e9`. Terminal color codes removed; no raw logs, connection addresses, credentials, or profile identifiers included. The second JSON line was emitted only after the Gateway shut down and the persisted participant row and copied database were checked.

prs.title: docs: say which sessions get no memory audience
prs.body:
Closes #203820

## What Problem This Solves

Some sessions get no memory audience, and the docs do not say which ones. A new `openclaw agent --session-id <id>` session, or the agent's main session when only the `agent` method has run turns there, records no chat type. Memory providers that scope memory by audience then return nothing in that session, including when they run as a backend under a fusion slot owner. Operators see empty or partial results and a provider warning, with no docs to explain it.

## User Impact

User impact: operators and memory plugin authors can find out from the docs which sessions get no memory audience, how to spot it in the Gateway log, and how to give a session an audience.

## Why This Change Was Made

Docs only. The Memory audience section now names the sessions the Gateway `agent` method creates without a chat type, the log reason, and the repair. It also lists the main session among the sessions that `sessions.create` does not stamp `direct`. The Memory backends section says a backend has no audience of its own, so a session without one gets nothing from audience-scoped backends, and that the owner should report that as a warning with partial coverage. The `openclaw agent --session-id` docs link to the audience section.

## Evidence

The text matches the code on main:

- `src/plugins/memory-audience.ts:407`: a root session with no `chatType` is denied with "has no durable chat type".
- `src/gateway/server-methods/agent-session-patch.ts:244`: the row the `agent` method writes sets no `chatType`.
- `src/gateway/session-create-inheritance.ts:50`: the operator-root stamp skips the agent's main session.
- `src/commands/agent-exec.ts:275`: only `openclaw agent exec` passes `operatorDirectRoot`, so its new root records `direct`.
- `src/auto-reply/reply/session.ts:648`: a message turn records `direct` when the row has no chat type.
- `src/plugins/memory-provider-open.ts:92`: `backends.open(id)` reuses the owner's caller authority, so a backend sees the same missing audience.

Observed on an isolated Gateway with a native audience-scoped provider as a backend under a fusion slot owner: in sessions from `openclaw agent --session-id` and in plain `agent:main:main`, that provider returned a warning that the session has no memory audience and the owner reported partial coverage. A legacy `memory-core` backend still returned its hits.

Checks against a fresh `main`: `pnpm check:changed` (docs-only lanes) passes, and `git diff --check` is clean. `pnpm docs:check-links:anchors` reports 7 existing broken links, none in the files this PR changes.

Local ClawSweeper review (`--local-range` against `origin/main`, head `4a03578952c`): complete, checkout verified, patch is correct, no findings, security cleared.

prs.title: fix: recover the Processes panel after session access changes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The conversation’s Details and Processes panels can get stuck on an access warning. If a session change arrives while the process list is loading and that request is then denied, the panels drop the queued refresh. The warning can remain after access is available again, until the user clicks Retry or another change arrives.

## User Impact

User impact: The process list can recover without a conversation reload when an already-queued session change restores access. If the new request is still denied, process output stays hidden and polling does not restart.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared process reader now honors a queued session change with one fresh read even when the previous request was denied. The Gateway still checks access for each read. Stop requests are not replayed. No new state, timers, or permission changes are introduced.

## Evidence

- A focused Control UI regression reproduced the stuck Details warning on the base. With the fix, multiple overlapping change events produce one fresh read, old rows remain hidden while that read is pending, and both panels show the new result after it succeeds.
- All 27 tests in the two focused suites passed, including the persistent-denial check. The UI typecheck, scoped lint, formatting, and production UI build passed. The build printed advisory CSS size and chat boot request budget warnings.
- The regression controls Gateway response ordering in a UI fixture; it does not establish what caused the original live denial. Independent local review did not run: its isolation check rejected workspace-local temporary storage. No broad CI was run for this draft.

Reported by @vyctorbrzezowski.

prs.title: fix: retry the primary after a local dispatch failure
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A 30-second primary-model recovery probe exists to check whether a cooldowned provider has recovered. A worker failure before provider handoff consumes that probe today, so immediate turns remain on fallback even though no provider request was made.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The worker-turn launcher marks `WorkerRunnerUnavailableError` only when it knows the provider handoff never happened. Harness preflight failures also happen before dispatch.
- The fallback runner releases only the exact reservation for those known pre-dispatch failures. It keeps the throttle after provider outcomes and after coordination errors that may happen after a request.
- Probe reservation now happens synchronously with the cooldown decision, before the async observer can let a concurrent turn pass the same decision.
- The broader `isNonProviderRuntimeCoordinationError()` classification still prevents unsafe provider fallback. It does not prove that no provider request started.

## User Impact

After a local worker dispatch failure, the primary model can be tried again immediately. Failures after provider dispatch keep the existing 30-second throttle.

Closes #127649

## Evidence

The committed runner `node src/gateway/worker-environments/repro-cooldown-probe.mjs` exercises the production worker-turn launcher, `runWithModelFallback()`, and `runEmbeddedAgent()` against a localhost OpenAI-compatible provider with isolated synthetic auth state. No external provider or credential was used.

Before-fix comparison used pinned validation base `b8a55ae92072dac7ec0c456a04831f7284e22170` and the committed regression copied into a temporary base worktree. The base-only copy omitted the assertion for `providerDispatchStarted`, introduced by this change; the retry and provider-request assertions were unchanged.

```text
before: base b8a55ae92072dac7ec0c456a04831f7284e22170
$ OPENCLAW_EXPECT_PROBE_RETRY=false node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/worker-environments/worker-turn-launcher-failure-recovery.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 --reporter=dot --disableConsoleIntercept -t "proves cooldown behavior at worker and loopback provider boundaries"
[probe-proof] pre-dispatch=WorkerRunnerUnavailableError handoff=false retry=throttled provider_requests=0
[probe-proof] post-dispatch=loopback-429 then transcript-coordination retry=throttled provider_requests=1

after: head e8fe0d284f80805e0bf9d8e7371170fef0fc48ce
$ OPENCLAW_EXPECT_PROBE_RETRY=true node src/gateway/worker-environments/repro-cooldown-probe.mjs
[probe-proof] pre-dispatch=WorkerRunnerUnavailableError handoff=false retry=started provider_requests=1
[probe-proof] post-dispatch=loopback-429 then transcript-coordination retry=throttled provider_requests=2
negative-control: the immediate retry after the loopback 429 and injected transcript-coordination error remained throttled; no extra provider request was sent
```

The post-dispatch negative control uses an actual loopback HTTP 429, then injects `SessionTranscriptWriterClaimReboundError` after the provider call. The error is injected by the test callback, rather than produced by the transcript writer itself.

The full `worker-turn-launcher-failure-recovery.test.ts` suite passed (18/18), and `model-fallback.personal-cooldown.test.ts` passed (11/11), including preflight release, post-dispatch retention, and concurrent reservation coverage.

prs.title: fix: slow macOS dashboard reconnects when the app keeps refusing native sign-in
prs.body:
Related: #168743 ## What Problem This Solves When the macOS app keeps refusing native sign-in for an open Dashboard page, that page reconnects to the Gateway every 9 to 15 seconds for as long as it stays open. On 2026.11.5, which already includes #185963, one Mac still produced hundreds of `code=4008 reason=native authorization unavailable` closes overnight. #185963 stops closed and replaced pages; a page that is still open has no limit. ## User Impact A native Dashboard or chat page that the app keeps refusing now retries quickly about ten times, then about once every five minutes. Coming back to the window (focus, or the window becoming visible again) still retries at once, but it no longer starts a new fast series. The page still connects by itself as soon as the app grants it again, and short refusals recover exactly as before. ## Why This Change Was Made The Control UI client marks every native refusal as retryable, and its reconnect loop has no attempt limit, so the 15 second backoff ceiling repeats forever. The page's native auth adapter now counts consecutive refusals. From the tenth one, the refusal carries a five minute retry floor, which the shared reconnect loop already honors for retryable errors (300 to 360 seconds with jitter). Any native grant resets the count. The count lives in the native auth adapter, which is created once per page, not in the connection client. Page activation (focus, visibility, Retry) replaces the client. With the count on the client (the first commit, `2d4b7f498c1`), every activation started a new fast series, and the packaged app still logged 38 closes in 600 seconds. Recovery is not removed: no stop, no new state, no new setting, and the page activation recovery is unchanged. This bounds the retry side for every native page. In the app runs below, hiding the app, restarting its SSH tunnel and showing it again leaves the visible Dashboard page refused until the Dashboard is reopened. Whether that is the path on the reporter's Mac is not known (the window state was not recorded). The app-side cause is a separate fix and is not part of this change. Maintainer decision: the issue carries `needs-product-decision` because ending retries would change the recovery contract from #159860. This change keeps that contract (retries never stop) and only lowers the pace after ten consecutive refusals. ## Evidence - Packaged macOS app (release 2026.11.5, its own WKWebView and native auth bridge), Dashboard served by a test Gateway with the Control UI of the commit under test, 600 seconds of a refused, visible page: - main `9ebaece1079`: 66 closes, steady to the end. - first commit `2d4b7f498c1`: 38 closes, with new fast bursts after the window became visible again. - this branch `1426dc12ce3`: 12 closes. After the first ten refusals: one scheduled attempt (308 seconds after the previous one) and one attempt for each of the two times the window became visible again. Activating the app afterwards gave exactly one refusal. Reopening the Dashboard connected about 1.2 seconds later. - Real Gateway and headless Chromium with a refusing native bridge stub, 420 seconds: main made 35 attempts, one every 12.5 to 14.6 seconds; this branch made 11 (ten fast, then one at +378.2 seconds). A focus event gave 3 attempts within 3 seconds on main and 1 on this branch. - Regression test `slows reconnects after ten consecutive native refusals until a grant` in `ui/src/app/native-gateway-auth.node.test.ts` (real `GatewayBrowserClient` and application gateway store, fake native bridge). It checks ten fast refusals, one immediate attempt on page activation without a new fast series, the five minute floor, recovery on a grant, and fast backoff again after the grant. It fails on main (13 sockets after a minute and one activation, expected 11) and on the first commit alone (19 sockets five minutes after the activation, expected 11), and passes on this branch. - Mutation checks: reverting the second commit's source fails the same way as the first commit (19, expected 11); removing only the grant reset fails the last step (13 sockets, expected 14). - Related suites pass on `1426dc12ce3`: `native-gateway-auth.node.test.ts`, all of `ui/src/api`, `gateway-page-activation.test.ts`, `gateway-store.auth.test.ts`, `local-error-copy.test.ts` (16 files, 284 tests). The third commit `cf98d246e5b` changes no behavior: the same suites give the same results at `1426dc12ce3` and `cf98d246e5b` on one host, and the regression test fails again with the source change reverted (13 sockets, expected 11). - Control UI performance (`pnpm ui:check-performance:base`): on base `17f71647045`, `1426dc12ce3` grew chat boot JS gzip by 67 B (1333280 B against 1333277 B allowed while that base is over its cap). The third commit `cf98d246e5b` only reshapes the same code: 59 B on `17f71647045`, and 57 B on `95449145a82` (pass). - `pnpm check:changed` at `cf98d246e5b` against a freshly fetched `origin/main` (merge base `9ebaece1079`): format, lint, UI and core test typechecks, i18n and the ratchets pass. The dead export scan fails the same way on `9ebaece1079` without this change (two unused exports in `src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-spawn.authority.test-support.ts`). - Local review: ClawSweeper `--local-range` (Claude runner), base `origin/main`, head `cf98d246e5b`, full committed range, complete and checkout access verified; outcome: patch is correct, no findings, rating C (proof D, patch B); remaining findings: none. prs.title: fix(catalog): recommend canonical deepseek-flash in model seeds
prs.body:
Related: #194819

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `deepseek/deepseek-flash` is not recommended in model pickers and gets collapsed under "All models" because `scripts/lib/recommended-models.json` omits the canonical `deepseek-flash` key.

## User Impact

Users selecting DeepSeek models see `deepseek/deepseek-flash` directly as a recommended option in `/models` and model pickers without having to expand "All models".

## Why This Change Was Made

The DeepSeek provider manifest declares the canonical model id as `deepseek-flash` with display name `DeepSeek V4.1 Flash`. In `scripts/lib/recommended-models.json`, versioned aliases (`deepseek-v4.1-flash`, `deepseek-v4-flash`, `deepseek-v4-pro`) were present, but `deepseek-flash` was missing. Because canonical key recovery distinguishes `deepseek-flash` from versioned display names, the published catalog projection could not match the native Flash row.

This change adds `deepseek-flash` to `scripts/lib/recommended-models.json` while preserving existing valid keys declared by other providers (such as OpenCode Go).

## Evidence

### Unit & Ratchet Validation
- Verified reproduction failure on baseline: `publish-model-catalog-v2.test.ts` failed on `upstream/main` when projecting DeepSeek recommendations:
  ```
  AssertionError: expected [ 'deepseek-v4-pro' ] to deeply equal [ 'deepseek-flash', 'deepseek-v4-pro' ]
  ```
- Added regression test `projects canonical deepseek-flash from the recommended seed` in `test/scripts/publish-model-catalog-v2.test.ts`.
- Budgeted test lines in `config/test-lines-allocations/194819-deepseek-flash.txt`: exactly 12 lines for the 12-line test addition, verified with `node scripts/check-test-lines-ratchet.mts --base upstream/main --no-merge-base`.
- Passed full test suite:
  ```bash
  pnpm test test/scripts/publish-model-catalog-v2.test.ts src/tui/components/selectors.test.ts
  ```
  Result: 2 Vitest shards passed (24/24 tests in `publish-model-catalog-v2.test.ts`, 1/1 tests in `selectors.test.ts`).
- Passed typecheck:
  ```bash
  node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.root.tooling.json --incremental
  ```
- Passed format and lint:
  ```bash
  pnpm exec oxlint scripts/lib/recommended-models.json test/scripts/publish-model-catalog-v2.test.ts
  git diff --check
  ```
- CI Status: `openclaw/ci-gate` passed (run 42462396646, all applicable checks green including `checks-fast-baseline-ratchets`).

prs.title: fix: line up questions with their answers on the summary page
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On a tablet or desktop, a completed question page centered each prompt even though its answer label started at the left edge of the summary. With several questions, it was hard to tell which answer belonged to which prompt.

## User Impact

Each prompt now starts directly above its answer label, including when the text wraps. The status heading stays centered. The phone layout and questions inside Chat do not change.

## Why This Change Was Made

prs.title: fix(update): preserve plugin consent and target the invoking installation
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw update --accept-capabilities` loses consent when a running Gateway performs the update, so plugins requesting additional capabilities remain withheld. A CLI started from another checkout can also update the Gateway's installation instead of its own, or replace the shared launcher target with `--no-restart`.

## User Impact

Plugin capability consent reaches updates through the running Gateway. An update requested through the running Gateway (`update.run`) from the wrong checkout refuses before an update run or release switch, identifies the installation in use, and gives its update command; so do the local preparation paths (`--tag`, `--no-restart`) once the state directory has a release slot. Git identity follows the common repository directory, so release worktrees remain the same installation.

Not covered (#203807): before the first conversion creates the release slot, `--tag` and `--no-restart` from a second installation prepare locally without asking the Gateway which installation it serves, so they can still take over the shared slot. Observed in this PR's end-to-end run; `main` has no check on any of these routes.

Older Gateways still receive their existing request. When consent is requested, the CLI follows that first update before applying consent through the replacement Gateway; if support remains absent after a downgrade, it fails visibly rather than claiming consent was applied. That first update through an older Gateway cannot prove checkout identity and can still reach the wrong installation. This affects Gateways from be5f7fad9d until this fix and shipped Gateways using the legacy update route.

The installation check runs in update admission, before any owner takes the request, so a Gateway whose updates an OCM manager owns also refuses a checkout from another installation. OCM cannot carry capability consent, so `--accept-capabilities` through an OCM-owned Gateway is refused ("OCM owns this update and cannot apply capability consent…") instead of being dropped, as an explicit Git target already is.

Accepted edge case: `update.run` reads the saved channel, so `--channel` is written before the Gateway can refuse a checkout from another installation. The refusal then says that only `update.channel` was saved and how to restore it. Carrying the channel in the request would be a protocol addition.

## Why This Change Was Made

An advertised capability gates additive, optional consent and installation-identity fields; the protocol version and existing clients remain unchanged. Gateway and local preparation share the installation comparison instead of relying on a release directory's changing path.

## Evidence

Focused source tests passed across 57 cases: capability-gated request compatibility and older-Gateway ordering, refusal before any Gateway run is recorded, shared Git identity across release worktrees, the local launcher-slot refusal, and forwarding `--accept-capabilities` to plugin maintenance. Generated protocol validators were regenerated successfully.

After merging `main`: `tsgo:core` and the gateway-methods test project clean; `cli.test.ts` 17/17, `update-run.test.ts` 12/12, `update.ocm.test.ts` and the protocol schema tests pass; `gateway:validators:check` passes on the regenerated predicates. New regression: a forwarding installation whose launcher marker names a symlinked state path keeps the managed identity (fails before the realpath fix).

End to end at this head (macOS, isolated npm installs built from `69f71652ac`, installation A serving its Gateway, installation C a second npm prefix sharing A's state directory, authenticated CLIs):
- From C, `openclaw update --yes --json` reaches `update.run` and is refused with `installation-mismatch`, naming A and its update command; no update run is recorded and A keeps serving.
- From C with `--channel beta`: the same refusal, plus "Only the requested update channel was saved…"; the config shows `update.channel=beta`.
- Not proven end to end: consent through the Gateway. A's own request reached `update.run` and was refused safely by the schema preflight because the Gateway resolved a public beta instead of the fixture (harness: the Gateway process had no local-registry env and the channel was `beta` from the previous case). Consent forwarding is covered by the focused tests above.
- Harness note: `OPENCLAW_UPDATE_PACKAGE_SPEC` (set by the isolated npm harness) turns into an explicit tag and sends updates down the local preparation route; it was unset for these cases.

Core production and test typechecks, a full build with declarations, tarball checks, and an isolated npm install followed by the packed CLI's version/help commands passed. The repository's unused-export scan also reports existing exports in unchanged files; those are not removed by this update fix.

Merge danger: two-way door. The protocol fields are optional and capability-gated; a revert removes their use without a data migration. Blast radius: update CLI transport, Gateway update admission, and plugin maintenance consent.

prs.title: fix: start compatible MOV attachments faster in chat
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When someone presses Play on a QuickTime recording in chat, OpenClaw can re-encode the whole clip even when the video and audio are already browser-compatible. The inline player waits for polling and shows “Preparing playback…” before it knows whether the file needs more time.

## User Impact

User impact: Compatible MOV attachments can start playing inline sooner without losing quality or changing the original download. Recordings that still need a full conversion retain the existing fallback.

## Why This Change Was Made

Copy compatible streams into a streamable MP4 first and give the first playback check up to 500 ms to pick up the result. Reuse the same job across requests and fall back to encoding if the copy fails. The inline player shows preparation only after the server reports the rendition is still pending; audio and the lightbox keep their existing loading behavior.

## Evidence

- In a Chromium replay with a synthetic 7.77-second H.264/AAC MOV, a mock Gateway, and the real conversion code, playback started in 2.3 s on a patched run versus 8.1 s on the deployed baseline. The patched first check returned ready on that run; the playback copy preserved the original 1842 × 1200 resolution. This is a fixture replay, not a production benchmark or a guarantee that every remux finishes within 500 ms.
- 45 focused media, staging, and Gateway tests and 33 focused video/audio player tests passed. One conversion pipeline still owns staging, validation, caching, and fallback; the patch adds 94 net lines including 60 lines of regression tests. The UI bundle built, but its size and boot-request budget checks reported violations. Full CI and independent review are not claimed.
- [Clean and annotated before/after screenshots](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/203688#issuecomment-7085562813). The before image uses the deployed baseline, not a fresh build of `main`.

prs.title: fix: let Docker config and channel commands work while the Gateway runs
prs.body:
Fixes #202040

## What Problem This Solves

With the shipped Docker Compose file, `openclaw-cli` cannot change config or add a channel once the Gateway is running. Before a write, the CLI checks that the running Gateway owns the shared state, and `openclaw-cli` runs in a different PID namespace from the Gateway, so the check cannot verify the owner and the write is refused. The documented `docker compose run --rm openclaw-cli channels add ...` step hits this. So does `./scripts/docker/setup.sh`, which writes config through `openclaw-cli` after starting the Gateway: it can print `WARNING: Failed to reset agents.defaults.sandbox.mode to off`, and with `OPENCLAW_SANDBOX=1` it cannot turn sandbox mode on.

## User Impact

User impact: with the default Compose stack, `openclaw-cli` config commands and `channels add` reach the running Gateway instead of being refused, and `setup.sh` applies its sandbox settings.

### Upgrade notes

- Update the Compose file, not just the image. Pulling a new image leaves an existing `docker-compose.yml` as it was, and without the new `pid` line on `openclaw-cli` these commands stay refused while the Gateway runs. Take the Compose file from the release you are upgrading to (`git pull` in a source checkout). If you maintain your own `openclaw-cli` service, set both `network_mode` and `pid` to `service:openclaw-gateway` and drop `init: true`.
- Stopping or recreating the Gateway container now also ends any open `openclaw-cli` session or TUI. Start it again once the Gateway is back.

## Why This Change Was Made

`openclaw-cli` already shared the Gateway's network, and with it the hostname, so the PID namespace was the only part of the ownership check that could not match. The service now sets `pid: "service:openclaw-gateway"`, the line the Compose operations guide used to suggest as an override. The decision to make PID sharing the default is recorded in [this comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202288#issuecomment-7051833433).

The CLI service also drops `init: true`. In the shared namespace the Gateway's docker-init is PID 1 and reaps orphaned processes. A second docker-init would not be PID 1 and would print a warning on every command.

Once the CLI can see the Gateway as the owner, its writes go to the Gateway's listener. `setup.sh` issued them right after `docker compose up -d`, before the listener accepts connections. It now runs the image's own health check through `docker compose exec` and waits up to 180 seconds before those writes. If the Gateway never reports healthy, it prints a warning with the logs command and continues, so a slow Gateway does not abort setup.

The Docker docs describe the shared PID namespace, and the security note says the CLI container can see and signal Gateway processes; it already receives the same Gateway token and state mounts. The `compose-setup` Docker E2E gains a config write through `openclaw-cli` while the Gateway runs, read back from inside the Gateway.

Compose has resolved `pid: service:<name>` since v2.1.0. The file's `env_file` `required:` entries already need a later Compose release, so this adds no new version requirement.

## Evidence

Real Docker Compose runs:

- Config write while the Gateway runs, on Linux arm64 under Colima (Docker 29.5.2, Compose 5.5.1), with the same source-built image on both sides. On the base, `openclaw-cli config set agents.defaults.sandbox.mode off` was refused with `cannot verify Gateway ownership from this process` and exited 1, and the Gateway still read back `non-main`. With this change it printed `Updated agents.defaults.sandbox.mode. Change will apply without restarting the gateway.`, exited 0, and the Gateway read back `off`. Screenshots are in [this comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202288#issuecomment-7048270977).
- The shipped `scripts/docker/setup.sh --offline` on this head, on Linux arm64 (Docker Engine 29.10.0, Compose 5.7.1). Plain setup reached `Waiting for gateway health...`, the Gateway became healthy, and `sandbox.mode` changed from `non-main` to `off`. With sandbox enabled, setup exited 0 and the recreated, healthy Gateway read back `mode=non-main`, `scope=agent` and `workspaceAccess=none`. Details are in [this comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202288#issuecomment-7050521450).
- An upgrade from the published v2026.11.6 image over the same state. This head still reports 2026.11.5, so the candidate stopped at the older-binary guard as designed, and the saved credential record and workspace bytes were unchanged. With the same patch applied to a 2026.11.6 `main`, the candidate Gateway became healthy and kept a custom setting, the saved credential record and the workspace bytes (same comment).

Local checks, without a Docker daemon:

- `test/scripts/docker-setup.test.ts` passes 27 of 27 with this patch on current `main`, where none of the six changed files differ from this head. The new test, "waits for Gateway health before runtime CLI config writes", fails against `main`'s `setup.sh` (the health-wait index is `-1`) and passes with this change in about 1.8 s. The five sandbox-path tests bind a Unix socket to stand in for the Docker socket, which my environment refuses, so they ran from a copy that links an existing socket instead, with the assertions unchanged.
- `docker compose config` resolves `openclaw-cli` with `pid: service:openclaw-gateway` and no `init`.
- `bash -n` and `shellcheck -S warning` are clean on `scripts/docker/setup.sh` and `scripts/e2e/compose-setup.sh`. oxlint is clean on the test file. `oxfmt --check`, docs markdownlint with the repo config and `git diff --check` pass.
- Local autoreview was not available in my environment. ClawSweeper reviewed this head and reported no findings.

Not run: `channels add` with real channel credentials (it goes through the same ownership check as `config set`), `pnpm test:docker:compose-setup`, and Docker Desktop on macOS or Windows.

prs.title: fix: keep model identity in warm session reads
prs.body:
Closes #203801

## What Problem This Solves

A warm bounded session read can lose the last inference model after an automation result or delivery mirror is appended. A cold read of the same saved transcript keeps the real model, so reopening or reusing the navigation cache can produce different model metadata.

## User Impact

Warm and cold bounded reads now retain the same real provider and model. Automation results and delivery mirrors keep their existing transcript behavior without replacing the inference model.

## Why This Change Was Made

The cold projection already excluded OpenClaw-authored transcript artifacts from model identity. The navigation cache used different predicates when seeding and advancing its cached model state. This change uses one predicate at all three sites. Pending and placed background results remain owned by the existing placement logic, and no stored format, configuration, or migration changes.

## Evidence

Base: `ab2da2bfe8c447acc8ec089ba3debcd1caffbcbc`
Head: `5281910dc9f8493b05882cb14955ac91e606c5b6`

Before the repair, the independent SQLite reproduction failed three cases and passed two controls: warm seeding, append deltas, and delivery mirrors lost the real model. The new case in the existing compacted worker matrix failed against the unmodified production files, with 1 failure and 15 passing controls.

On the exact head:

- The independent reproduction passes all five cases, including the later-model-change and branch-reseed controls.
- `session-model-context-compacted.test.ts`: **16 passed** in 46.07 seconds.
- `session-model-context-window.test.ts`, `session-accessor.sqlite-model-context.test.ts`, and `session-actor-bounded-history.test.ts`: **17 passed** in 32.39 seconds.
- oxfmt, type-aware oxlint, core and `agents-sessions` typechecks, line-cap, test-lines, and diff checks pass. Net test growth is 23 lines, below the 400-line allowance.

The compacted matrix takes about 46 seconds because it drives the real SQLite worker through the existing 80-turn, large-payload scenarios. The new case shares that owning suite and takes about 1.1 seconds; it does not add a parallel test file.

The aggregate `check-changed` run exits 1 with the initial format finding and full-tree unused-export findings outside these three files. The format finding was fixed and rechecked. Candidate-owned typecheck, lint, and other guards passed, and no unrelated exports were changed.

Personal diff review covered the artifact-provider, pending-result, cache-reseed, and export boundaries. Two independent local review agents could not start because their configured model providers rejected the requested model names, so no independent local review is claimed.

No packaged Gateway or external provider run is claimed. The focused proof uses real session modules and isolated SQLite fixtures; PR CI remains the broad validation gate.

<details>

```sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/sessions/session-model-context-compacted.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

prs.title: fix(linux): let dashboard users grant microphone access
prs.body:
Closes #202024

## What Problem This Solves

Microphone input in the Linux companion's embedded Gateway dashboard fails with “Microphone access is blocked. Allow it in browser site settings to list inputs.” The embedded app has no browser site-settings permission control, leaving the user unable to grant access.

## User Impact

The registered Gateway dashboard can request microphone access through a native Allow/Deny dialog that identifies the Gateway origin. Deny is the default. Camera and screen capture are not granted, and ordinary embedded browsing tabs and widgets do not receive this handler.

**Runtime requirement:** this enables microphone consent and WebRTC for registered dashboards, but does not supply a WebRTC-capable engine. Full Talk was confirmed on Ubuntu 22.04.5 with a locally built WebKitGTK 2.55.0 development runtime using LibWebRTC. Stock installations are not guaranteed to support Talk; WebKitGTK 2.54 disables WebRTC during the backend transition. Use a regular browser when the system runtime lacks support. This PR does not bundle or upgrade WebKit.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Linux shell did not handle WebKit's media permission requests. The change installs an audio-only consent handler before a registered dashboard starts navigation and uses the existing Gateway document owner to admit requests. A pending dialog is cancelled on navigation or closure; accepting a stale dialog cannot grant access to another dashboard.

The dashboard settings explicitly enable media streams and WebRTC; microphone access still requires the native consent decision. The change adds no dependencies, stored permissions, Gateway configuration, or browser-engine packaging. Experimental runtime builds, library patches, and launch scripts are excluded.

## Evidence

- Follow-up on 2026-11-22: the reporter confirmed a real Talk session with microphone input and Bluetooth response playback using the same permission-enabled desktop binary plus `set_enable_webrtc(true)` and an unpatched WebKit main build at `7f49613cb85904e9ab361c1d9c7f36d34b35fb3d` (GTK3 API 4.1, `ENABLE_WEB_RTC=ON`, `USE_LIBWEBRTC=1`). No legacy WebKit/GStreamer fixes were applied to that engine. This is development-runtime evidence, not a claim about stock Ubuntu packages.
- That runtime also passed an independent localhost peer test with synthetic capture: outgoing/incoming audio, data echo, and advancing HTML audio playback, including an answer without the MID RTP extension. An isolated actual OpenClaw launch reported `RTCPeerConnection: function; offer: offer; bundle: true`. Synthetic tests do not establish physical microphone or speaker quality; the reporter's live session provides that separate confirmation.
- The follow-up source delta is one settings call. Rust formatting passes; the previously built and tested experimental binary already contains this exact call. Existing consent/build proof below is retained from the original permission revision, rather than presented as newly rerun.

- Reproduced the failure through the actual Linux desktop binary on base `cd2ae19272a3ee7be456385fa7efc56d6e2109a6`, using an isolated local HTTP dashboard fixture: `getUserMedia({audio:true})` returned `NotAllowedError` without a prompt. The patched desktop binary displays the native consent dialog. The reporter also confirmed the prompt in their actual Gateway dashboard.
- The native GTK/WebKit regression passes with synthetic capture devices: Allow returns an audio track; Deny, combined audio/video, and an unadmitted origin all reject. It never records a physical microphone. The test is explicitly display-dependent and must be invoked with `--ignored --test-threads=1`.
- All 53 existing `gateway_windows::` tests pass.
- Locked Linux debug build, Rust formatting, targeted documentation formatting, and patch whitespace checks pass.
- Author simplification/code review completed. Local autoreview and ClawSweeper are not installed; no independent review is claimed. The prior hosted review found no code defects and requested desktop Allow/Deny and baseline evidence. The follow-up results below address those proof requests. A maintainer capability decision and review of the updated revision remain outstanding.

### Desktop permission results (2026-11-22)

Collected after the review, through the actual OpenClaw Linux executable and its registered dashboard path, using a localhost HTTP fixture and a separate temporary HOME/XDG profile for each decision. The reporter selected the native dialog buttons. The page calls `getUserMedia({audio:true})`, reports track kinds or the exception name to the fixture, and immediately stops all granted tracks. No audio is recorded or uploaded.

```text
Original pre-permission desktop: Baseline: NotAllowedError
Patched desktop, Allow:          Allow: allowed:audio
Patched desktop, Deny:           Deny: NotAllowedError
```

The baseline executable was freshly built from the pre-permission app sources at `cd2ae19272a3ee7be456385fa7efc56d6e2109a6`. Both the baseline comparison and patched desktop used the same local WebKitGTK 2.55.0 runtime described above. The patched executable contains the exact permission module now on PR head `8bdd795c367bac38acad4ff6836efc7cf564537e`. Each case used a fresh app process/profile; a first attempt to test Deny then Allow within one page retained denial and was not used as Allow evidence.

The committed native regression was rerun with system WebKit. A temporary negative control omitted the test fixture's call to install the permission handler, reproducing the pre-fix lack of a handler; this is explicitly a negative control, not an unchanged test run against a baseline that lacks the new module.

```text
Handler omitted:
  assertion left == right failed
  left:  Some("NotAllowedError")
  right: Some("allowed:audio")
  FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed

Handler restored:
  microphone_linux::tests::webkit_microphone_consent ... ok
  1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored
```

The restored regression covers Allow, Deny, combined audio/video rejection, and an unadmitted origin. Temporary source changes were restored; the checkout is clean. Earlier fixture runs encountered temporary-directory cleanup errors involving the desktop portal mount after delivering their capture results; the final Deny and matched-runtime baseline runs both exited successfully. This evidence establishes the permission behavior, while the separate reporter-confirmed Talk session establishes real microphone/Bluetooth use. The maintainer capability decision remains outstanding.

The screenshots below show the real desktop app displaying a synthetic dashboard fixture, not a full authenticated Talk session. The “after” image is the native dialog; the “before” image is the dashboard's rejected capture result. Images contain only fixture content.

### Before

![Before: microphone capture fails without a consent prompt](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/861b9824-6deb-4027-9ade-13e97b8f9128)

### After

![After: the Linux app offers Deny and Allow for microphone access](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/08b2274d-8618-4337-a214-684ad1b5d1eb)

<details>
<summary>Focused verification commands</summary>

```sh
cd apps/linux/src-tauri

WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=1 WEBKIT_DISABLE_COMPOSITING_MODE=1 \
```
